story.title: Milo, Juno, and the Brick That Clicked
story.subtitle: A bedtime trip to where LEGO began.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Glowing Brick
chapters.text:
Milo and Juno sat on the carpet, way past bedtime. They were building a LEGO shark. Juno made it stomp like a dinosaur.

Milo snapped one more brick onto the fin. CLICK.

The brick blinked. Then it glowed bright yellow.

"Whoa," whispered Milo. "Did you see that?"

The brick hummed, like a tiny bee. Juno poked it with one finger. "It's warm!"

Suddenly the brick popped open, like a tiny door. A soft wind blew out, smelling like fresh wood.

"I think it wants us to go in," said Milo.

He grabbed Juno's hand. They climbed through the glowing brick. WHOOSH! They tumbled into a little wooden workshop. Sawdust floated in the air.

A kind man in an apron looked up from his workbench. He was carving a little wooden duck.

"Well now," he said, smiling. "Visitors! I am Ole Kirk Christiansen. Welcome to my workshop, in Billund, Denmark."

"What year is it?" asked Milo.

"It is 1932," said Ole Kirk. "I make wooden toys here. And stepladders, too!"

Juno giggled. "A stepladder is not a toy!"

"No," laughed Ole Kirk. "But a boy still needs to reach the cookie jar."

Milo picked up a wooden toy. "I like making things too. With LEGO bricks!"

"Then you and I," said Ole Kirk, "are going to get along very well."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Play Well
chapters.text:
The next morning, Ole Kirk nailed up a brand new sign.

"What does it say?" asked Juno.

"It says LEGO," said Ole Kirk. "That is my company's new name!"

Milo tilted his head. "LEGO? What does that mean?"

Ole Kirk grinned. "It comes from two Danish words, leg godt. That means 'play well.'"

"Play well," said Juno slowly. "I like that."

"Some people say lego is also a very old word that means 'I put together,'" said Ole Kirk. "That might just be a fun coincidence. But really, I just wanted a name about playing well."

Milo clapped his hands. "Play well! That should be everybody's rule."

"I think so too," said Ole Kirk. He handed Milo a little hammer. "Want to help me hang the sign straight?"

Milo held it while Ole Kirk hammered. BANG, BANG, BANG.

The sign hung perfectly straight, right over the door.

"There," said Ole Kirk. "LEGO. 1934. Play well."

Juno jumped up and down. "PLAY WELL!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Plastic Machine
chapters.text:
A few minutes later for Milo and Juno, the workshop looked different. A big, clanking machine stood in the corner.

"What is THAT?" asked Milo, eyes wide.

"A plastic machine!" said Ole Kirk. "In 1947, we started making toys from plastic, not just wood."

Juno sniffed the air. "It smells funny."

"Plastic gets soft and squishy when it's hot," said Ole Kirk, "then turns hard when it cools. We can push it into any shape we like."

Milo pressed a button, just to see.

CLUNK. WHIRRRR. The machine squeezed out a little plastic brick.

"My bricks!" shouted Milo, catching it.

"Careful, careful," laughed Ole Kirk, smiling anyway. "You found the lever before I even showed you. We were one of the very first toy companies in Denmark with a machine like this."

Juno held the warm little brick like a treasure. "It's so smooth!"

"Someday," said Ole Kirk, "that little brick is going to change everything."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Bricks That Almost Click
chapters.text:
Ole Kirk led them to a long table covered in little plastic bricks with bumps on top.

"These are new," he said. "We call them Automatic Binding Bricks."

Juno frowned. "That's a long name for a tiny brick."

"You're right," chuckled Ole Kirk. "Let's just call them bricks."

Milo picked one up. It had round bumps on top, but underneath it was just hollow and empty.

He stacked two bricks together. They sat on top, wobbled, then fell. CLATTER.

"Hmm," said Milo. "They don't hold very tight."

"Not yet," said Ole Kirk. "This is only 1949. We are still figuring it out."

"What if," said Milo slowly, "there was something underneath, to grab onto the bumps?"

Ole Kirk's eyebrows shot up. "That," he said, "is exactly the question my son keeps asking."

"Can we meet him?" asked Juno.

Ole Kirk smiled. "Follow me."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Tubes Underneath
chapters.text:
A man with kind eyes and a pencil behind his ear looked up from a workbench full of brick pieces.

"This is my son," said Ole Kirk. "Godtfred Kirk Christiansen."

"I heard you have a good question," said Godtfred, smiling at Milo.

Milo nodded. "What if there were little tubes inside the brick? To hug the bumps underneath?"

Godtfred's eyes lit up. He grabbed a pencil and sketched tiny round tubes inside a brick.

"Let's try it," he said.

He pressed two new bricks together.

CLICK!

He pulled. They held tight.

"IT CLICKS!" yelled Milo and Juno together.

"It does!" laughed Godtfred. "On January 28th, 1958, we are making this our brick, forever."

Milo turned the brick over in his hands. "Will bricks always fit together, even way later?"

"Even way, way later," said Godtfred. "A brick made today will still click with a brick made far in the future."

Juno gasped. "That's forever friends!"

"Exactly," said Godtfred, grinning. "Forever friends."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: A Whole Brick Town
chapters.text:
The Spark Brick in Milo's pocket buzzed again. WHOOSH! The workshop spun away, and they landed somewhere new, a whole park made of bricks.

"Whoa," breathed Milo. "Is that a brick castle?"

"And a brick elephant!" squealed Juno, pointing.

A cheerful voice called out. "Welcome to LEGOLAND!"

It was Godtfred again, a little older now, wearing a sun hat.

"We opened this park in 1968," he said, "right next to our very first factory, here in Billund."

Milo spun in a circle, looking at everything. "You built a whole town out of bricks!"

"We did," said Godtfred. "Go on, take a closer look."

Milo ran to a brick shark statue and gasped. "A LEGO shark! Just like mine!"

Juno found a brick dinosaur and stomped around it, roaring. "Hello, cousin!"

Godtfred laughed so hard he had to sit down on a brick bench. "You two fit right in here."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Bricks for Little Hands
chapters.text:
Juno tugged Godtfred's sleeve. "My bricks are too teeny for my fingers sometimes."

Godtfred crouched down. "I know just the thing. Come with me."

He led them to a shelf with bigger, chunkier bricks.

"These are called DUPLO," he said. "We made them in 1969, just the right size for little hands like yours."

Juno grabbed a big blue brick and clicked it onto another. CLICK!

"I did it all by myself!" she cheered.

"And the best part," said Godtfred, "DUPLO bricks still fit with the regular LEGO bricks too. Big or small, everything clicks together."

Milo set one of his tiny bricks on top of Juno's giant one. It fit perfectly.

"See?" said Milo. "Big sister bricks and little sister bricks!"

Juno giggled. "I'm not little! I'm four!"

"You're the perfect size," said Godtfred, smiling, "for DUPLO."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Little Yellow Person
chapters.text:
On the shelf next to the bricks stood a tiny yellow person, no bigger than Milo's thumb.

"Who's that?" asked Milo, picking it up gently.

"Our newest friend," said Godtfred. "We call him a minifigure, a tiny LEGO person. In 1978, we gave him bendy arms, and a head and hat you can swap around."

Milo popped the little hat off and put on a different one. "He can be a pirate now!"

"Or a shark tamer!" said Juno, giggling.

The tiny figure's hands clicked perfectly around a brick, holding it up like a trophy.

"He looks happy," said Juno.

"Play well," said Godtfred, winking.

The Spark Brick in Milo's pocket buzzed one last time, warm and golden.

"I think it's time to go home," said Milo.

Godtfred shook both their hands. "Thank you for all your good questions. Come back and play well again sometime."

WHOOSH! The workshop and the park spun away like a spinning top.

Milo and Juno landed back on their own carpet, their half-built LEGO shark still waiting for them. The little yellow minifigure sat right beside it, holding one tiny brick.

Juno yawned a dinosaur-sized yawn. "Did that really happen?"

Milo squeezed the glowing brick, now cool and quiet. "I think it did."

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Milo. Goodnight, Juno. Play well.

true_facts.text: **Ole Kirk Christiansen** started his toy workshop in **Billund** in **1932**, making wooden toys and stepladders.
In **1934** he named his company **LEGO**, from Danish words meaning **"play well."**
The word *lego* might also be an old word that means "I put together" — but that could just be a fun coincidence.
In **1947** the workshop got a **plastic machine** so they could make toys from plastic, not just wood.
In **1949** they made bricks with **bumps on top**, but the bricks didn't hold together very tight yet.
**Godtfred**, Ole Kirk's son, added **tiny tubes underneath** the bricks so they would click and hold tight, in **1958**.
A brick from **1958** still clicks perfectly with a brick made today.
The first **LEGOLAND** park opened in **1968**, right next to the very first factory in **Billund**.
Bigger, chunkier **DUPLO** bricks came out in **1969**, just the right size for little hands — and they still click with regular bricks.
The first tiny LEGO people, called **minifigures**, got bendy arms and swappable heads and hats in **1978**.

story.title: Theo and the First Save File
story.subtitle: One night, one glitchy screen, and fifty years of video games.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Green Line That Played Tennis (1958)
chapters.text:
Theo was not asleep. He was in Roblox Studio, testing a double-jump script for the eleventh time, and it still made his character faceplant into a wall.

He hit play again. The screen flickered. Then it went fully green-and-black, like an old computer that time forgot.

A single glowing dot bounced out of the monitor and landed on his desk. It looked like a tiny ball of pixels, if a pixel could look smug.

"Name's Blip," it said. "You just loaded me up. Want to see where games actually started?"

Before Theo could answer, the green lines on the screen arranged themselves into a court with a net and a bouncing dot — tennis, but made of light.

"This is **Tennis for Two**," Blip said. "Built in **1958** by a scientist named William Higinbotham, on a machine called an **oscilloscope** — normally it just drew wiggly lines to check electricity, but he turned it into a tennis game instead."

Theo squinted at the screen. "The ball doesn't bounce off the net. It just disappears if it hits the middle line."

"Yep," said Blip. "No graphics budget for that yet."

"That's basically my first build," Theo admitted. "One platform, no art, still fun."

Blip spun in a happy little loop. "Exactly. You get it. Ready to load the next save?"

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Two Ships and One Very Patient Computer (1962)
chapters.text:
The green court folded away, and a new screen buzzed to life — this one showed two little ships shooting at each other in space.

"**Spacewar!**," Blip announced. "Made in **1962** by a college student named Steve Russell and his friends, on a giant computer called a **PDP-1** — basically a refrigerator-sized box that took up a whole room just to run one game."

Theo watched the ships loop around a star in the middle, swapping fire. "Wait, it's two players? Against each other?"

"First one of its kind," Blip said.

"That's like me and my cousin playing soccer against each other instead of just kicking a ball at a wall," Theo said. "It's way better with somebody to beat."

"Funny you say that," said Blip. "Multiplayer was kind of the whole point."

One of the ships drifted too close to the star and got pulled in.

"Gravity well," Blip said. "It'll eat your ship if you're not careful."

Theo grabbed the mouse without thinking and nudged the surviving ship clear of the star, just like dodging a defender. It worked. The ship lived.

"Nice save," said Blip. "Ready for the next one? This one's got cardboard in it."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Box Wrapped in Wood-Print Tape (1972)
chapters.text:
The screen now showed a cluttered workshop and a plain brown box covered in fake wood-grain tape.

"Meet Ralph Baer," Blip said. "An engineer who had one big idea: what if you could play a game right on your own TV?"

"That's it? That's the box?" Theo asked.

"That's the **prototype**," Blip said — "a rough first version you build to test an idea before the real thing."

"I've got, like, forty prototypes of my obby in Studio," Theo said. "None of them look that ugly, though."

"Ugly works," Blip said. "In **1972**, Baer's box became the **Magnavox Odyssey** — the first ever video game **console**, a machine built just for playing games, plugged straight into your TV."

Theo leaned closer. "So before this, games only lived on huge lab computers?"

"Exactly. Baer brought it home."

"What if you could play more than one game on it, though?" Theo asked. "Like swapping between my different Roblox places?"

Blip's glow brightened. "Funny you should ask. Hang on to that thought."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Machine That Choked on Quarters (1972)
chapters.text:
The scene shifted to a noisy arcade, lit by one buzzing bulb and a single cabinet in the corner.

"Also in **1972**," Blip said, "two guys named Nolan Bushnell and Ted Dabney started a company called Atari and put out an arcade game called **Pong**."

On the screen, two white paddles knocked a square dot back and forth. BEEP. BOOP. BEEP.

"That's it?" Theo said. "Just paddles and a square?"

"People went nuts for it," Blip said. "Story goes, one early Pong machine jammed completely — so stuffed with quarters it couldn't close. Might be a bit of an exaggeration, honestly, but it tells you how fast people fell in love with it."

Theo tapped the cabinet. A little coin slot rattled. "Let's find out," he said, and started dropping imaginary quarters in, counting under his breath like he was counting laps at practice.

At twenty he grinned. "Okay, I believe it could jam. This thing's basically a piggy bank with graphics."

Blip laughed, a sound like a dial-up tone. "Ready for cartridges?"

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: One Box, Many Games (1977–1978)
chapters.text:
The arcade melted into a living room with a TV and a stack of flat plastic cases.

"**1977**," Blip said. "The **Atari 2600**. Instead of one game built in forever, you could plug in a **cartridge** — a little plastic case with a whole game stored inside, kind of like swapping SD cards."

Theo picked one up. "So it's like my Roblox places, except you need an actual physical thing to switch games?"

"Before the internet, yeah. You wanted a new game, you bought a new cartridge."

He slotted one in. The screen filled with rows of blocky aliens marching down, and a little cannon at the bottom.

"**Space Invaders**," Blip said. "Made in **1978** by a designer named Tomohiro Nishikado. It caused an absolute craze — arcades everywhere packed with kids trying to beat it."

The aliens sped up as they got lower, beeping faster and faster. Theo's thumb found the fire button on instinct, same reflex as a last-second penalty save.

He cleared the bottom row just before it reached him.

"Nice reflexes," said Blip. "Goalkeeper training pays off, huh."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Pizza, a Pile of Cartridges, and a Comeback (1980–1983)
chapters.text:
A yellow circle with a wedge missing chomped across the next screen, gobbling little dots.

"**Pac-Man**," Blip said. "Made in **1980** by Toru Iwatani. Story goes he got the idea from a pizza missing a slice — nobody's totally sure that's true, but it's a good story, so it stuck."

Theo watched Pac-Man dodge four colorful ghosts. "Okay, that's actually kind of genius. Simple shape, instant character."

Then the screen glitched, and a pile of plastic cartridges appeared, dumped in a messy heap.

"**1983**," Blip said, quieter now. "Too many rushed, low-quality games flooded the stores. People stopped trusting new releases, and the whole market in North America shrank fast. They call it the **crash**."

"That's rough," Theo said. "Like if everyone started uploading unfinished Roblox games and people just... stopped playing new stuff."

"Exactly like that," said Blip. "Some of those unsold cartridges — including a game based on E.T. — ended up buried in a landfill in New Mexico. People thought that one was just a legend too, until diggers found the actual cartridges in **2014**."

"So it was true the whole time?"

"That one was true the whole time," Blip said. "Good games always find a way back, though. Watch this."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: A Plumber, a Falling Block, and a Comeback (1984–1985)
chapters.text:
A small mustached man in overalls jumped over a mushroom-shaped enemy, bouncing a brick with his head.

"**1985**," Blip said. "**Nintendo** brought the market back with a console called the **NES**, bundled together with a game called **Super Mario Bros.**"

"Mario," Theo said. "Obviously. Everyone knows Mario."

"Designed by Shigeru Miyamoto," Blip said. "He imagined a jumping hero — turned out to be the most famous character games have ever made."

On the screen, Mario leapt a gap. Theo's hand jumped with him, same timing he used lining up a free kick.

"And a year earlier," Blip added, as the screen split into falling blocks, "a scientist in Moscow named Alexey Pajitnov made **Tetris**, in **1984**. Blocks fall, you fit them together, lines clear."

Theo watched a long I-shaped block drop. "Rotate it and drop it on the left," he said instantly. "That gap needs the long one."

The line cleared. Blip blinked in surprise. "You've literally never played this."

"I build puzzle levels in Studio," Theo said. "Shapes fitting together is kind of my whole thing."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Blue, Shiny, and Connected (1991–2006)
chapters.text:
A blue hedgehog zipped across the screen so fast it left a streak of color.

"**Sonic the Hedgehog**," Blip said. "Sega's answer to Mario, made in **1991** — fast mascot for a company that wanted speed to be the whole pitch."

The screen then flickered to a gray console with a disc tray sliding open.

"**1994**," Blip said. "Sony's **PlayStation**. It used **CDs** instead of cartridges — shiny discs that held way more space, so games suddenly had real voices and smoother video."

Next, two computers lit up side by side, connected by a cable.

"**1993**," Blip said, "a shooter called **Doom** got people wiring computers together in the same room just to play against each other. They called it a **LAN party** — like a sleepover, but everyone brought their own keyboard."

"We basically do that with Roblox," Theo said. "Minus the cables."

Last, a white remote appeared, and on screen a tiny tennis racket swung whenever Theo swung his arm.

"**2006**," Blip said. "Nintendo's **Wii**. **Motion controllers** — it reads how you actually move, so your arms do the work instead of just your thumbs."

Theo swung like he was heading a corner kick. The on-screen racket swung with him. "Okay," he said, "that one's just fun."

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Back to the Room, Achievement Unlocked (2011–Now)
chapters.text:
The last screen Blip pulled up looked almost exactly like Theo's own desktop: blocky green hills, a blocky sun.

"**Minecraft**," Blip said. "Made in **2011** by a Swedish developer who went by Notch. It's gone on to become the best-selling video game ever made."

"Everybody's played Minecraft," Theo said. "Even my grandma's played Minecraft."

"That's kind of the point," said Blip. "Started with one guy building blocks on his own computer. Now it's basically everywhere."

The screen zoomed out to a glass building, shelves full of old consoles and cartridges behind glass cases.

"The **World Video Game Hall of Fame**," Blip said. "Opened in **2015**, at a museum called The Strong, in Rochester, New York. Every game you just saw tonight has a spot in there somewhere."

Theo looked at the whole lineup — the green tennis line, the two ships, the brown box, the paddles, the aliens, Pac-Man, Mario, Tetris, Sonic, the blocky hills — all of it leading, somehow, exactly to his own messy Roblox Studio window.

"So every game I build," he said slowly, "is just the next save file after all of this."

"Now you're getting it," Blip said, already fading back toward the screen. "Press start on your own, Theo."

The green-and-black flicker cleared. Theo's ordinary desktop was back, Roblox Studio still open, his double-jump script sitting there, unfinished, waiting.

He looked at it differently now.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow, he had a game to finish building.

true_facts.text: **Tennis for Two** was built in **1958** by scientist William Higinbotham, shown on a machine called an **oscilloscope**.
**Spacewar!** was made in **1962** by college student Steve Russell and friends, on a giant computer called a **PDP-1**.
Engineer **Ralph Baer** built a rough first test version — a **prototype** — called the Brown Box in the late 1960s.
Baer's box became the **Magnavox Odyssey** in **1972**, the first home video game **console** ever made.
Also in **1972**, Nolan Bushnell and Ted Dabney started **Atari** and released the arcade game **Pong**.
In **1977**, the **Atari 2600** let players swap in plastic **cartridges** instead of being stuck with one game.
**Space Invaders** was made in **1978** by designer Tomohiro Nishikado, and it caused a huge arcade craze.
**Pac-Man** was made in **1980** by Toru Iwatani — the story that pizza inspired its shape might not be totally true, but it's a fun one.
In **1983**, too many rushed, low-quality games flooded stores and the video game market in North America shrank — people call it the **crash**.
Nintendo's **NES** launched in **1985**, bundled with **Super Mario Bros.**
**Shigeru Miyamoto** designed Super Mario Bros. in **1985**, starring the plumber Mario.
**Tetris** was invented in **1984** by scientist Alexey Pajitnov at a computer center in Moscow.
**Minecraft** was released in **2011** by developer Notch, and it became the best-selling video game ever.
The **World Video Game Hall of Fame** opened in **2015** at a museum called The Strong, in Rochester, New York.

story.title: Milo, Juno and the Brick That Found Sharks
story.subtitle: A swim through five hundred million years of fins

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Brick That Turned Blue
chapters.text:
Milo and Juno sat on the carpet. They were building a brick tower. It was the tallest one yet.

Suddenly, one brick glowed red. It was the very same brick from last week. The one that went CLICK and held.

"It's doing the thing!" Juno shouted.

The brick buzzed in Milo's hand. Then it turned bright blue, like the sea.

CLICK! A tiny brick shark popped up. He had a big smile and shiny eyes.

"Hello!" he said. "I'm Finn. Want to see real sharks?"

"YES!" said Juno.

Finn's tail spun like a little propeller. WHOOOOSH! The carpet melted into blue water.

Milo reached out and touched Finn's back. It felt bumpy, like sandpaper.

"Real shark skin feels like that too," said Finn. "Rough, like sandpaper. It helps sharks zoom through the water."

Then Milo noticed something else. "Finn, your bones feel bendy. Not hard, like mine."

"Good catch!" said Finn. "Shark bones are made of cartilage. That's bendy stuff, like the bendy part of your ear. Squish your ear and feel it!"

Milo squished his own ear. "Whoa, bendy!"

"Exactly," grinned Finn. "Ready to swim?"

"READY!" yelled Juno.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: So Many Shark Friends
chapters.text:
They swam through the blue water. Little fish zipped past them.

"Look!" said Milo. "A spotted one! A stripy one! A tiny one!"

Juno counted on her fingers. "One, two, three... I runned out of fingers!"

Finn laughed, a bubbly laugh. "You'll need way more fingers. There are more than **500 different kinds of sharks** swimming in our oceans."

Milo's mouth popped open. "Five hundred?! That's more than all my LEGO bricks!"

"Some are tiny as your hand," said Finn. "Some are longer than a school bus."

Juno spotted a shark with a flat, wide head zooming by. "That one looks funny!"

"We'll meet him later," said Finn, winking.

Milo spun in the water like a happy fish. "Five hundred shark friends. We better say hi to lots of them!"

"SPLOOSH!" yelled Juno, splashing her hands.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Older Than Dinosaurs
chapters.text:
Juno loved dinosaurs more than anything. "Finn, were there sharks when dinosaurs were alive?"

Finn gave a big shark smile. "Even older than that, Juno! Sharks swam in the ocean more than **400 million years ago**. That's before dinosaurs. Before even trees!"

Juno's eyes went wide as dinner plates. "Sharks are OLDER than my dinosaurs?!"

"Way older," said Finn.

Milo thought hard about it. "So sharks saw the very first dinosaur ever hatch?"

"They might have!" laughed Finn.

Juno did a happy dino-stomp dance in the water. Little bubbles popped up around her feet.

"Sharks win! Sharks win!" she cheered.

Milo high-fived her floaty fin. "Dinosaurs are still cool, though."

"Everyone here is cool," said Finn. "Follow me. Next stop is a BIG one."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Gentle Giant
chapters.text:
A shadow fell over them. Milo looked up. And up. And up.

"That's the **whale shark**," said Finn. "The biggest fish in the whole sea. Longer than **40 feet** — longer than a school bus!"

Juno hid behind Milo's arm, just for one second. "Is it scary?"

The whale shark opened its huge mouth. Tiny bits of food floated in and got slurped right up.

"Nope!" said Finn. "He only eats teeny tiny bits of food floating in the water. Smaller than a crumb!"

Milo relaxed all over. "He's like a big gentle vacuum cleaner!"

Juno giggled and waved at the giant shark. The whale shark blinked slowly and swam on by.

"Bye, big buddy!" Juno shouted.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Smile Wide
chapters.text:
Next they met a sleek gray shark with a toothy grin.

"This is the **great white shark**," said Finn. "He can grow as long as **20 feet**. Look at those teeth!"

Milo leaned in close. The teeth were shaped like little triangles, with bumpy edges like a saw.

"Why are they bumpy?" asked Milo.

"Good question," said Finn. "That shape helps him eat his dinner."

Then Milo noticed something wobbly. "Finn, is that tooth loose?"

"Sharp eyes!" said Finn. "Sharks lose teeth all the time. A new one always slides forward to take its place. Sharks grow thousands of teeth in one whole life!"

Juno gasped. "Thousands?! I only have baby teeth and grown-up teeth!"

"Sharks are extra fancy," laughed Finn.

The great white gave one more toothy grin and swam off, happy as can be.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Tooth as Big as a Hand
chapters.text:
They swam down, down, past old rocks and sand.

Milo spotted something shiny in the sand. He picked it up. It was a giant tooth, as big as his whole hand!

"Whoa! Whose tooth is THIS?" Milo asked.

"That," said Finn, "belonged to **Megalodon**. A giant shark who lived long, long ago."

"Where is he now?" asked Juno.

"He isn't around anymore," said Finn gently. "That's called **extinct**. It means he's all gone now."

"Like... gone gone?" asked Juno softly.

"Gone gone," said Finn. "But we still know about him because of teeth like this one. Old teeth left behind in rock are called **fossils**. They're like clues from long ago."

Milo held the tooth up proudly. "I found a clue!"

"You sure did," said Finn. "Great big discovery, Milo."

Juno patted the tooth softly. "Night night, old shark."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Wraparound Eyes and the Shark Lady
chapters.text:
The funny flat-headed shark from before swam closer.

"This is a **hammerhead shark**," said Finn. "His head is wide and flat, like a hammer. That means his eyes are far apart."

Juno giggled. "His head IS a hammer!"

"Why's that good?" asked Milo.

Finn grinned wide. "Wide eyes mean he can see almost all the way around himself. A wraparound view!"

Milo tried spreading his arms out wide like a hammerhead's head, wobbling through the water.

Finn chuckled. "There once was a scientist named **Eugenie Clark**. People called her the Shark Lady. She studied sharks for years and years. She showed everyone that sharks are curious, and can even learn tricks — just like a puppy!"

"Sharks are smart!" said Milo.

"Smart AND friendly," said Finn. "Now, little swimmers — time to go home."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Back on the Carpet
chapters.text:
Finn's tail spun again. WHOOOOSH! The water swirled into carpet and lamps and pillows.

CLICK! Milo and Juno landed softly on their bedroom floor.

Milo opened his hand. The giant tooth was gone. In its place sat a small, shiny gray LEGO brick, shaped just like a tooth.

"A souvenir!" said Milo, grinning.

Juno yawned a big dinosaur yawn. "Sharks are older than dinosaurs... and I waved at a whale shark..."

Finn, now a tiny brick again, gave one last wink before going still and quiet on the carpet.

Milo placed the new tooth-shaped brick on top of their tower. It clicked right into place and held.

"Goodnight, sharks," whispered Juno, snuggling into her blanket.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Milo. Goodnight, Juno. Play well.

true_facts.text: Shark bones are made of **cartilage**, bendy stuff like the bendy part of your ear.
Shark skin feels rough, like **sandpaper**, and helps them zoom through the water.
There are more than **500 different kinds of sharks** swimming in the ocean today.
Sharks were swimming in the ocean more than **400 million years ago**, before dinosaurs.
The **whale shark** is the biggest fish in the sea, longer than a school bus, and it eats only tiny bits of food.
The **great white shark** can grow up to **20 feet** long and has triangle-shaped teeth.
Sharks lose teeth all the time, but new ones slide forward, so they grow **thousands of teeth** in one life.
**Megalodon** was a giant shark that lived long ago and is **extinct**, meaning it isn't around anymore.
We know about Megalodon from giant **fossil teeth**, old teeth left behind in rock.
The **hammerhead shark** has a wide, flat head that spreads its eyes apart for a wraparound view.
A scientist named **Eugenie Clark**, called the Shark Lady, showed that sharks are curious and can learn tricks.

story.title: Theo and the First Kickoff
story.subtitle: A Player One Adventure Through the History of Soccer

chapters.heading: Level 1: Loading… China, 2,000 Years Ago
chapters.text:
The ball thumped off Theo's knee for the ninth time in a row — new record — when his laptop screen flickered from Roblox blue to a crawling, static green.

It had been exactly one week since a message had glowed on that same screen: THE NEXT LEVEL IS YOURS TO BUILD. Theo had been waiting for round two ever since.

"Player One!" squeaked a tiny green shape, snapping together pixel by pixel until Bit stood on the keyboard, waving both blocky arms. "BZZZT. Miss me? Don't answer that, obviously you did."

The floor dropped away like a loading screen, and Theo landed in a dusty courtyard somewhere that smelled like woodsmoke. Men in long tunics were kicking a stitched leather ball back and forth, aiming it through a small hole in a net strung between two poles — no hands allowed.

"Whoa — no goal, just a *hole*?" Theo said, catching the ball on his chest out of pure reflex.

"This is **Cuju**," Bit said. "Played in **China over 2,000 years ago** — that's more than twenty human lifetimes back. One of the very first kicking games anybody ever wrote down. You just joined the oldest save file in soccer."

A player waved Theo over, pointing at the net hole, clearly daring him. Theo lined up, remembered every penalty he'd ever practiced, and struck it clean. The ball threaded the hole with a soft **THWAP**.

The courtyard erupted. A single golden coin popped out of nowhere and spun into Theo's palm, warm as sunlight.

"First save point," Bit said, eyes glowing. "Keep collecting — these fuse into something good at the end. Now come on, Player One. We've got about twenty-two centuries to cover before bedtime."

chapters.heading: Level 2: Banned in London, Rewritten at Cambridge
chapters.text:
The next doorway dumped Theo into a muddy English field in the middle of total chaos.

Dozens of men were chasing a ball through the streets of a whole town, shoving past fences, smashing through a market stall. Someone's cart tipped over. Nobody seemed to be following any rule at all.

"This can't be soccer," Theo said, dodging an elbow. "This is just a riot with a ball in it."

"Close," Bit said. "It's called **mob football**, and it got so out of hand that **King Edward II banned it in London in 1314**. Too much property got wrecked. Too many shins got kicked that weren't attached to the ball."

Theo watched two players collide and laughed despite himself. "Somebody needs to write this down. Like, actual rules. You can't just *vibe* a sport."

The field dissolved into a tidy college lawn, where a group of students in jackets were arguing over a notebook.

"Funny you should say that," Bit said. "In **1848**, Cambridge University students sat down and wrote the **Cambridge Rules** — the first real attempt at one rulebook everybody could agree on, instead of every town playing its own made-up version."

One student held the notebook out toward Theo, as if asking a stranger to settle an argument. Theo pointed at a messy line about handling the ball and crossed it out clean. The students nodded like that solved everything.

Another coin dropped into his hand.

"Guess somebody just helped invent the world's first rulebook," Bit said. "No pressure."

chapters.heading: Level 3: The Rulebook of London
chapters.text:
A clock tower chimed somewhere in fog as Theo and Bit stepped into a wood-paneled tavern room packed with serious-looking men and a lot of pipe smoke.

"Gentlemen," one man was saying, tapping a pen against paper, "shall football be a game of the feet, or a game of the hands?"

"That's **Ebenezer Cobb Morley**," Bit whispered. "On **26 October, 1863**, right here in London, he and some other clubs started the **Football Association** — the FA. The big rule they landed on: no carrying the ball with your hands."

"Wait," Theo said. "So before this, people could just... pick it up?"

"Some clubs wanted to. Morley's side said no. He personally sat down and wrote the first official **Laws of the Game** — the rulebook soccer still follows the shape of today."

Schoolboys outside the window were calling it something funny — shortening "association football" into a nickname.

"Assoc... soc..." Theo sounded it out. "Soccer. They turned it into *soccer*."

"Nicknamed in **1880s** England," Bit confirmed, delighted. "You just worked out where the whole word came from."

Morley slid the finished rulebook across the table, and the other men signed it one by one, shaking hands like a deal closing. Theo leaned in and tapped the paper for luck.

The ink glowed gold for a second, and a coin rolled off the page into his hand.

"Save complete," Bit said. "Soccer finally had a rulebook. Now it needed something to *play for*."

chapters.heading: Level 4: The Oldest Ball and the First Rivals
chapters.text:
Stone walls rose around them — a castle, cold and echoing.

"Stirling Castle," Bit said. "Scotland."

Theo spotted something wedged behind a wooden beam: a lumpy, hand-stitched ball, deflated flat as a pancake. "Is that... a soccer ball?"

"Found hidden exactly there. It's made from a pig's bladder stuffed into leather, and it might date back to the **1540s** — which would make it the **oldest football in the world**."

"It looks like it lost a fight with a dog," Theo said, poking it carefully.

The castle dissolved into a roaring stadium. Men in long shorts lined up for kickoff.

"**1871**," Bit said. "The very first **FA Cup** — a knockout competition, win or go home — and it's still played every single year since. Oldest football competition on Earth."

The scene blinked forward. Now the shirts read SCOTLAND and ENGLAND.

"And **1872**, Glasgow," Bit went on. "First official match between two countries. Final score?"

Theo studied the scoreboard, which stubbornly refused to change. "Zero-zero? Nobody scored? That's... anticlimactic."

"Welcome to soccer," Bit said. "Sometimes the most historic goal is the one nobody gets."

Theo grinned and jogged onto the pitch anyway, stealing a loose ball and dribbling it in a slow victory lap nobody asked for. The crowd, somehow, loved it. A coin landed in his pocket like applause.

chapters.heading: Level 5: The League and the World
chapters.text:
A train yard. Smoke. A man with a clipboard, counting clubs on his fingers.

"**1888**," Bit said. "William McGregor organizes the **Football League** — the first league in the world, where clubs play each other on a real schedule all season, not just once-off matches."

Theo watched fixtures get chalked onto a board, team names stacking into a table. "So before this, clubs just... played whoever, whenever?"

"Pretty much. McGregor's the reason soccer got a *calendar*."

The scene jumped to Paris, a room full of men from seven different countries arguing in at least four languages at once, somehow agreeing anyway.

"**1904**," Bit said. "**FIFA** gets founded — the organization that still runs soccer's biggest rules and tournaments worldwide, for every country, not just England."

One official slid a stack of papers toward Theo, clearly needing a tie-breaking vote on something. Theo scanned it, then simply pointed at the word WORLD circled at the top.

"If it's for everybody," he said, "shouldn't there be a tournament for, like, the whole world?"

The room went quiet. Then the FIFA men looked at each other and started nodding, fast.

"Theo," Bit said slowly, "I think you just talked them into the idea they were already having."

A coin dropped, heavier than the others.

chapters.heading: Level 6: Uruguay, 1930
chapters.text:
Heat. Flags. A stadium packed so tight Theo could barely see the pitch.

"**1930**, Montevideo, **Uruguay**," Bit said. "The very first **FIFA World Cup**. Teams actually sailed across the ocean on boats to get here."

A man in a sharp suit paced the sideline, clutching a small golden statue like it was made of glass.

"That's **Jules Rimet**," Bit said. "FIFA's president. He's the one who pushed hardest to make this whole tournament happen — so hard they named the trophy after him."

The final whistle blew. Uruguay had beaten Argentina, and the home crowd went absolutely sideways with joy — flags thrown, strangers hugging, someone's hat sailing into the stands.

Rimet turned, searching the chaos for somewhere safe to set the trophy down, and Theo — closest, fastest — cupped both hands under it before it could tip.

"Careful with that," Theo said. "That thing's gonna matter for like a hundred years."

Rimet laughed, said something in French Theo didn't catch, and let him hold it one extra second before taking it back.

A coin, gold and round as a tiny trophy itself, dropped into Theo's hand.

"First World Cup, officially saved," Bit said.

chapters.heading: Level 7: The Trophy Goes Missing
chapters.text:
London again, decades later. A glass display case stood empty except for a sign and a very worried-looking security guard.

"**1966**," Bit said. "England's hosting the World Cup — and about to win their only title ever. But right before it starts, someone steals the trophy clean out of this case."

Theo stared at the empty glass. "They just... took it?"

"Whole country panicked. Searched everywhere. Then, exactly one week later —"

A small black-and-white dog trotted past, sniffing at a hedge, and yanked something shiny out from under a garden wall with its teeth.

"No way," Theo said. "A *dog* found it?"

"A dog named **Pickles**," Bit confirmed, practically wheezing with laughter. "Soccer's biggest trophy, rescued by the goodest boy in England."

The scene swirled forward to a packed stadium, England in white, the final whistle, the trophy lifted high and gleaming, safe at last.

Theo pumped his fist along with eighty thousand strangers like he'd personally been there the whole time.

A coin landed, still warm from all that cheering.

chapters.heading: Level 8: Cards and Kings
chapters.text:
A referee stood at midfield, holding up two small rectangles of cardboard — one yellow, one red — studying them like he wasn't sure they'd work.

"**1970** World Cup," Bit said. "Referee **Ken Aston** invents yellow and red cards — copied straight off a traffic light. Yellow means slow down. Red means you're out of the game."

"That's kind of genius," Theo admitted. "No more arguing in six different languages about who got in trouble."

Across the pitch, a player in yellow and green moved like the ball was glued to his foot, slipping past three defenders without breaking stride.

"That's **Pele**," Bit said. "Brazilian. By the end of his career he's the only player ever to be on **three** World Cup-winning teams — **1958, 1962, and 1970**. Brazil ends up winning the whole tournament **five times total**: those three plus **1994** and **2002** — more than anybody else."

Pele flicked the ball up, balanced it on the back of his neck for a second, then let it drop and finished with a casual side-foot into the net. He turned, spotted Theo watching open-mouthed, and tossed him the match ball with a grin.

Theo juggled it twice before fumbling it, laughing at himself. "Okay. Respect."

A coin appeared before the ball even hit the grass.

chapters.heading: Level 9: The Game They Tried to Ban
chapters.text:
Theo expected another stadium. Instead he got a padlocked gate, chained shut in front of an empty field.

"That's not very welcoming," he said.

"It's not supposed to be," Bit said, voice quieter than usual. "Starting in **1921**, the FA banned women from playing on its official grounds — even though women's teams had been packing stadiums for years."

On the other side of the fence, a player was still practicing anyway, striking shot after shot against a bare wall.

"That's **Lily Parr**," Bit said. "One of the best players of her whole generation, banned ball or not. Her team, the **Dick, Kerr Ladies**, drew bigger crowds than plenty of men's games."

Theo grabbed the padlock and gave it one hard, useless yank, just to feel like he'd tried. "That's so unfair it's not even funny."

"It was," Bit agreed. "And it took **fifty years** before the FA admitted it. The ban was finally lifted in **1971**."

The gate swung open on its own, rusty hinge groaning, and the padlock clattered to the grass. Theo stepped through first, and the field beyond filled instantly with players and noise and color, like it had been waiting the whole time.

"**1991**, China," Bit said, grinning again. "The first official **Women's World Cup** — and the **United States** wins it."

Theo held the broken padlock up like a tiny trophy of its own before it melted into gold in his palm — one more coin, heavier than it looked.

chapters.heading: Level 10: Return
chapters.text:
The field folded away like a screen going dark, and Theo landed back on his bedroom carpet, soccer ball still resting against his foot exactly where he'd left it.

Bit stood on the keyboard, pixels flickering slower than usual. "Save file complete, Player One."

Theo opened his hand. Every golden coin — Cuju, Cambridge, Morley's rulebook, the first Cup, the League, FIFA, Uruguay, Pickles, Pele, Lily Parr's padlock — rolled together, clicked, and melted into one small glowing trophy sitting in his palm.

"That's thousands of years of kicking a ball around," Theo said, turning it over. "All the way from some dusty courtyard to a dog finding a stolen trophy."

"History's basically just soccer with extra steps," Bit agreed. Its eyes had gone glassy and a little too bright. "BZZZT. Dust in my circuits. Totally normal."

Theo set the little trophy carefully on his windowsill, next to his cleats. On the laptop screen, green letters blinked once: LEVEL COMPLETE.

"Same time next week?" Theo asked.

"Always, Player One," Bit said, already fading pixel by pixel. "Go get some sleep. You've got a penalty to take."

story.ending_line: Saturday's game couldn't come soon enough — Theo had a penalty to take, and thousands of years of history behind his boot.

true_facts.text: **Cuju**, a kicking game played in **China over 2,000 years ago**, is one of soccer's oldest known ancestors.
Medieval **mob football** got so wild that **King Edward II banned it in London in 1314**.
The **Football Association** was founded in London on **26 October, 1863**, and said players could not carry the ball with their hands.
The **FA Cup**, first played in **1871-72**, is the oldest football competition still running today.
**FIFA**, soccer's worldwide organization, was founded in **Paris in 1904**.
The first **World Cup** was held in **Uruguay in 1930**, and the host country beat **Argentina** in the final.
In **1966**, the World Cup trophy was stolen in London — then found safe **one week later** by a dog named **Pickles**.
**Brazil** has won the World Cup a record **five times**.
**Pele** is the only player ever on **three** World Cup-winning teams: **1958, 1962, and 1970**.
Referee **Ken Aston** invented yellow and red cards, copying the idea from a **traffic light**, debuting at the **1970 World Cup**.
**Lily Parr** was one of the best players of her time, starring for a team called the **Dick, Kerr Ladies**.
The FA's ban on women's football was finally lifted in **1971**, fifty years after it began.
The first official **Women's World Cup** was held in **China in 1991**, and won by the **United States**.

story.title: Juno, Milo, and Theo and the Rumbling Rock
story.subtitle: A sizzling, bubbling trip into the heart of a volcano

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Rock That Rumbled
chapters.text:
It was way past bedtime. Juno sat on the rug with her toy dinosaurs. Milo stacked LEGO bricks into a tower. Theo peeked at one more game on his tablet.

Then Juno's little toy volcano started to glow. It was supposed to be gray and still. Now it was orange and warm.

RUMBLE. The toy volcano shook on the rug.

CRACK! The top popped open. Out popped a tiny glowing fellow made of orange light.

"Hiya!" he said. "I'm Sizzle. I live in volcanoes. Want to see how they work?"

Milo grinned. "Is it like popping open a LEGO brick?"

"Kind of!" said Sizzle. "A **volcano** is a hole in the ground. Hot melted rock, ash, and bubbly gas sneak out of it."

"What's the hot rock called?" asked Theo.

"Down under the ground, it's called **magma**," said Sizzle. "Once it comes out on top, we call it **lava**."

Juno poked the warm little volcano. "Can we go inside?"

Sizzle winked. "Hold on tight."

The rug seemed to melt into mist. WHOOSH! The three kids shrank down, down, down — right into the rumbling rock.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Great Horseshoe
chapters.text:
They landed on a floating map, glowing like a video game screen. Theo's eyes went wide. "It looks like my Roblox world map!"

"Look closer," said Sizzle.

A curvy orange line glowed all around the edge of the ocean on the map. It curled like a horseshoe.

"Most volcanoes live where Earth's **plates** bump together," said Sizzle. "Plates are giant puzzle pieces that make up the ground we stand on."

Theo traced the glowing horseshoe with his finger. "It goes all the way around!"

"That's the **Ring of Fire**," said Sizzle. "About three out of every four volcanoes on Earth live right along it."

Milo counted little orange dots. There were so many near one country.

"That place has more volcanoes than anywhere else!" Milo shouted. "It's called Indonesia!"

"Milo found it!" cheered Sizzle. "You're right."

The map spun like a soccer ball, faster and faster, until it blurred into orange light.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Bubbling Island
chapters.text:
SPLOOSH! They landed on a warm, black beach. Steam puffed up from cracks in the ground.

"Where's the plate edge here?" asked Theo, looking around.

"There isn't one," said Sizzle. "This volcano grew over a **hotspot** — a warm, bubbly spot deep inside the Earth, far from any edge."

Juno pointed at the bubbling red glow nearby. "Is that one awake right now?"

"Very awake," said Sizzle. "This volcano is called **Kilauea**. It's one of the busiest on Earth. It has been erupting almost nonstop for years and years."

Milo, who loved sharks, leaned toward the water. "Does the lava go all the way into the ocean?"

"Sometimes it does," said Sizzle. "HISSSS — that's the sound it makes when hot lava meets cool sea water."

Juno hissed back, giggling. "HISSSS!"

Theo hissed too. Soon all three kids were hissing like little teakettles, while Sizzle laughed so hard his glow wobbled.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Biggest Mountain Ever
chapters.text:
Next they stood at the bottom of a mountain so wide, Theo couldn't see the edges.

"Whoa," he said. "That's not pointy like a normal mountain."

"This one is called **Mauna Loa**," said Sizzle. "It's the biggest active volcano on the whole planet, taller than four thousand of your soccer fields stacked straight up."

"Why is it so wide and flat on top?" asked Milo.

"Some volcanoes are wide and gentle, like this one," said Sizzle. "Others are tall and pointy, like a mountain called Fuji, far away in Japan."

Milo grabbed an invisible LEGO brick from the air and pretended to build. "I'm gonna build a wide one AND a pointy one!"

"Build both," laughed Sizzle. "Then you'll know every volcano shape there is."

Juno clapped her hands. The ground rumbled happily underneath them, like a giant cat purring.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Island That Was Born
chapters.text:
The scene swirled into cold mist and crashing waves.

"Brrr," said Juno. "Where are we now?"

"Iceland," said Sizzle. "Here, two big plates are pulling apart, slow as a stretchy toy."

Suddenly the sea began to boil. BOOM! Steam and rock shot up from under the water.

"Is a new island being made?" Theo asked, amazed.

"Yes!" said Sizzle. "In **1963**, this exact thing happened. A whole new island popped up from the sea. They named it **Surtsey**."

Juno watched the rock pile grow taller and taller, like a sandcastle building itself.

"It's making its own land!" Juno shouted.

"That's exactly right, Juno," said Sizzle. "No danger here — we're watching safely from far away."

The three kids cheered as the little island kept rising out of the fizzy, bubbling water.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Mountain on Mars
chapters.text:
CLICK. The world around them went dark and sparkly, full of stars.

"Are we in space?" Theo gasped. This was better than any game level.

"We are," said Sizzle. "Look down."

Below them sat a red, dusty planet with one enormous bump on it.

"That's **Mars**," said Sizzle. "And that bump is **Olympus Mons** — the biggest volcano anyone has ever found, anywhere."

"How big?" Theo asked, already knowing it would be huge.

"About thirteen and a half miles tall," said Sizzle. "Stack almost three of your tallest mountains and you still wouldn't reach the top."

Theo whistled. "That beats every level I've ever built."

Milo tried to imagine a LEGO tower that tall and just laughed. "We'd need ALL the bricks in the world."

Sizzle chuckled. "Every single one."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Watching the Wobbles
chapters.text:
Back on Earth, they stood beside a cozy little hut. Inside, people watched glowing screens.

"Who are they?" asked Milo.

"Scientists who study volcanoes," said Sizzle. "They use special machines that feel tiny wiggles in the ground. That tells them a volcano might wake up soon."

Juno looked at the dark dirt outside the hut. It was super dark and soft.

"Why does everything grow so big here?" she asked, pointing at tall, leafy plants.

"Old volcano ash turns into **fertile** dirt," said Sizzle. "That means dirt that helps plants grow big and strong. That's why some people live near volcanoes, even sleepy ones."

Juno patted the soft dirt. "It's like volcano food for plants!"

"Exactly like that," said Sizzle, beaming. "Juno, you said it perfectly."

The hut lights blinked gently, like a goodnight wave.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Back to the Rug
chapters.text:
WHOOSH! The warm wind spun them around and around.

Then — THUMP. Juno, Milo, and Theo landed right back on their own living room rug.

The toy volcano sat quiet again, gray and still. But right beside it was something new: one tiny, shiny orange rock, still warm to the touch.

"Sizzle left us a souvenir," Milo whispered, turning it in his fingers.

Theo grinned. "Best field trip ever. Better than any level."

Juno yawned a huge yawn and hugged her toy dinosaur close.

Milo set the little orange rock on his nightstand, right next to his LEGO tower.

"Goodnight, volcano," Juno whispered to the toy. "Rumble on."

Outside, the real world was quiet and cool, full of sleepy stars — just like the ones over that red, bumpy planet far, far away.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Juno. Goodnight, Milo. Goodnight, Theo. Rumble on.

true_facts.text: A **volcano** is a hole in the ground. Hot melted rock, ash, and gas sneak out of it.
Hot rock underground is called **magma**. Once it flows out on top, it's called **lava**.
Most volcanoes sit where Earth's **plates**, like giant puzzle pieces, bump together.
The **Ring of Fire** is a big horseshoe shape where most of Earth's volcanoes live.
**Indonesia** has more volcanoes than any other country.
**Kilauea** in Hawaii has been erupting almost nonstop for years and years.
**Mauna Loa** is the biggest active volcano on the whole planet.
Some volcanoes are wide and gentle, and some are tall and pointy, like Mount **Fuji**.
In **1963**, a brand-new island called **Surtsey** rose right up out of the sea near Iceland.
Iceland has lots of volcanoes because two giant plates there are slowly pulling apart.
**Olympus Mons** on Mars is the biggest volcano ever found, about thirteen and a half miles tall.
Scientists use special machines that feel tiny wiggles in the ground to know when a volcano might wake up.
Old volcano ash turns into **fertile** dirt, which helps plants grow big and strong.

new_recurring.name: Sizzle
new_recurring.rule: A tiny glowing lava-light guide who pops out of a warm, glowing toy or rock to lead the kids into science and history adventures. Cheerful, uses sound words, always resolves scary moments right away, and leaves a small warm keepsake at…

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: The kids returned to their rug to find the toy volcano quiet again, with a small warm orange keepsake rock left beside it by Sizzle.

request.care_notes: Focus on the wonder of how Earth works underneath: hot melted rock, pressure building up, and the dramatic release. Avoid detailed descriptions of lava destroying homes, people fleeing, or ash choking the air. Keep the tone of awe and curiosity rather than danger.

story.title: Juno and the Buzzy Dinosaur
story.subtitle: A tiny flight into a hive of busy bees

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Glowing Dinosaur
chapters.text:
Juno sat on her bedroom floor with her favorite toy dinosaur, Spike.

She gave him a squeeze. Spike's green skin began to glow! Yellow and black stripes popped up. Then — WHOOOOSH — two see-through wings popped out of his back.

'Whoa!' said Juno. 'Are you a bee now, Spike?'

'I am Buzz-Rex,' said the dinosaur, in a small buzzy voice. 'Half dino, half bee. Want to see how bees make honey?'

'Yes, please!' said Juno.

Buzz-Rex hummed. The room got small, small, smaller — and so did Juno! They zoomed out the window and into a hive, a house for thousands of bees.

In the middle sat one giant bee, with helpers all around her.

'That is the queen bee,' said Buzz-Rex. 'She can lay up to **2,000 eggs in one single day**.'

Juno counted on her fingers. One, two, three — then gave up, giggling. 'That's too many to count!'

'The queen doesn't count either,' buzzed Buzz-Rex. 'She just keeps laying.'

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Busy Bee Jobs
chapters.text:
A bee zoomed by, carrying a speck of yellow dust. Another bee stood guard at the door.

'Why is everybody so busy?' asked Juno.

'Worker bees take turns doing every job,' said Buzz-Rex. 'Cleaning. Guarding. Flying out for flowers. **Every single worker bee is a girl.**'

'I want a job too!' said Juno.

She puffed up her chest and stood by the door, buzzing like a tiny guard.

The real guard bee buzzed right back at her, like saying hello.

Buzz-Rex laughed his buzzy laugh. 'Good guarding, Juno.'

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Five Buzzy Eyes
chapters.text:
A little bee landed right on Juno's nose.

She looked up, straight into its face. 'It has lots of eyes!'

'Count them,' said Buzz-Rex.

Juno counted slowly. 'One, two, three, four... five!'

'**Bees have five eyes**,' said Buzz-Rex. 'Two big ones for seeing shapes. Three tiny ones on top, just for feeling light.'

Juno giggled. 'Five eyes is a lot of blinking.'

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Buzzing Wings
chapters.text:
BZZZZZ! The sound was everywhere.

Juno covered her ears, then peeked through her fingers. 'Why is it so loud?'

'Watch the wings,' said Buzz-Rex.

Juno squinted at a bee's wings. They moved so fast they turned into a blur.

'**Bee wings flap two hundred times every second**,' said Buzz-Rex. 'All that flapping makes the buzz.'

Juno flapped her own arms as fast as she could. She only made three flaps before flopping down, dizzy. 'I give up!' she laughed.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Six-Sided Room
chapters.text:
Inside the hive, Juno found a golden wall full of tiny rooms.

She touched one gently. 'What shape is this?'

'Count the sides,' said Buzz-Rex.

Juno traced her finger around. 'One, two, three, four, five, six!'

'**Each little room has six sides**,' said Buzz-Rex. 'That shape holds the most honey, using the least wax.'

'IT HAS SIX SIDES!' Juno shouted, loud enough to make two bees jump.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Flower Juice to Honey
chapters.text:
Buzz-Rex flew Juno outside, right over a field of flowers.

Bees landed on every petal, drinking sweet flower juice called **nectar**.

'One bee only makes a tiny, tiny bit of honey her whole life,' said Buzz-Rex. 'About **one-twelfth of a teaspoon**.'

Juno frowned. 'Then how do we get a whole jar?'

'Lots of bees, visiting lots of flowers,' said Buzz-Rex. '**About two million flower visits** make just one pound of honey.'

Juno looked out at the huge field. 'That's a LOT of buzzing.'

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Bees with the Dinosaurs!
chapters.text:
Buzz-Rex held up a chunk of golden-brown rock. Something tiny was stuck inside it.

'Look close,' he said.

Juno pressed her nose to the rock. 'It's a bee!'

'**This bee got stuck in sticky tree goo, a hundred million years ago**,' said Buzz-Rex. 'The goo turned hard, like a see-through window. Guess who else was alive back then?'

Juno gasped. 'DINOSAURS?!'

'Dinosaurs,' said Buzz-Rex, wiggling his tail. 'Bees have been buzzing since before you were even a thought.'

Juno hugged the rock like treasure.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Back to the Carpet
chapters.text:
Buzz-Rex showed Juno an old, old picture carved in stone. People in the picture were gathering honey from a hive.

'People have loved honey for a really, really long time,' said Buzz-Rex.

'Does honey ever go bad?' asked Juno.

'Almost never,' said Buzz-Rex. '**Honey found in jars thousands of years old is still good to eat.**'

Juno yawned a big dinosaur yawn.

Buzz-Rex hummed softly. The world grew bigger, bigger, biggest. Juno landed back on her own bedroom floor. Spike was snug in her arms again.

On the carpet beside her sat one tiny golden bead. It glowed, just a little, like a goodnight wink.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Juno. Buzz and dream sweet.

true_facts.text: A queen bee can lay up to **2,000 eggs in one day**.
Every worker bee in the hive is a girl, and they take turns doing all the jobs.
Bees have **five eyes** — two big ones and three tiny ones on top.
A bee's wings flap **two hundred times every second**, and that makes the buzzing sound.
Honeycomb rooms have **six sides**, which holds the most honey with the least wax.
One bee makes only about **one-twelfth of a teaspoon** of honey in her whole life.
It takes about **two million flower visits** to make just one pound of honey.
A bee stuck in old tree goo shows bees were buzzing around **when dinosaurs were alive**.
Honey found in jars **thousands of years old** is still good to eat.
Long ago, people drew pictures of themselves gathering honey from bees.

new_recurring.name: Buzz-Rex
new_recurring.rule: A toy dinosaur that glows, sprouts bee wings, and shrinks Juno down whenever she squeezes him at bedtime. He guides her through a true fact adventure and always leaves one small glowing keepsake on her bedroom floor when they return.

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Juno returned to her bedroom floor with a tiny glowing golden bead beside her toy dinosaur Spike, after flying through a beehive with her new guide, Buzz-Rex.
