story.title: Theo and the Sputnik Signal
story.subtitle: A midnight build turns into the real race to space.

chapters.heading: Level 1: Sputnik's Beep (1957)
chapters.text:
Theo was belly-down on his bedroom carpet at 11:52 p.m., laptop propped on a pillow, headphones clamped over his ears like he was defusing a bomb.

On the screen, a little rocket sat on a launchpad he had spent two hours building in Roblox Studio. Every time he hit Play, the rocket sank through the floor like it was made of wet sand.

"Come ON," Theo muttered, dragging the collision box wider for the ninth time. "You're a rocket. Rockets don't fall through the ground."

He hit Play again. The rocket sank. Again.

He yanked his headphones off to rub his eyes — and that was when he heard it anyway, thin and tinny, leaking out of the speakers even though the game wasn't making a sound.

Beep. Beep-beep. Beep.

The screen flickered. Not a normal flicker — a green-and-black flicker, like someone had reached back in time and dragged an old computer terminal into his bedroom.

A shape blinked into the corner of the screen: a small pixel satellite, round as a beach ball, with four thin antennas trailing off it like whiskers. A chat bubble popped up beside it.

BEEP. BEEP. HELLO, it read.

Theo did not scream, which he would like on the record. He did lean back about a foot.

"...Hello?" he said. "Are you a glitch?"

I AM NOT A GLITCH, the bubble said, sounding faintly offended for something made of pixels. I AM PIP. YOU HAVE BEEN BUILDING ROCKETS ALL NIGHT. DO YOU KNOW WHERE THE FIRST ONE ACTUALLY WENT?

Theo blinked. "...Into orbit?"

CLOSE, Pip beeped. TUNE ME IN AND I'LL SHOW YOU.

A little dial appeared, like an old radio. Theo — who had spent enough nights messing with audio settings in Roblox Studio to know a frequency slider when he saw one — nudged his mouse slowly until the beeping outside his headphones lined up with the beeping inside them.

CLICK.

The screen opened, like a loading screen, into a black sky scattered with stars, and a silver ball the size of a beach ball sailing through it, trailing a thin radio signal like a kite string.

"That's..." Theo squinted. "That's Pip. That's literally you."

NOT ME, said Pip. MY GREAT-GREAT-GRANDFATHER. **SPUTNIK 1.** **OCTOBER 4, 1957.** THE SOVIET UNION LAUNCHED HIM — THE FIRST MAN-MADE OBJECT EVER TO GO AROUND THE EARTH.

"Around the Earth," Theo repeated. "Like, going in circles forever?"

AN **ORBIT**, Pip explained, is just a big circle a thing makes around a planet because it keeps falling and missing the ground, over and over. SPUTNIK WAS ONLY **58 CENTIMETERS WIDE.** SMALLER THAN YOUR DESK CHAIR. ALL IT DID WAS GO BEEP.

"That's it? It just beeped?"

THAT'S IT. AND PEOPLE ALL OVER THE WORLD PICKED UP THE BEEP ON ORDINARY RADIOS.

Theo looked at the little silver ball sailing through the dark, beeping its heart out, and suddenly his glitchy rocket didn't feel so embarrassing. "Okay," he said. "That's actually unbelievably cool."

ROUND ONE, said Pip, and the stars rearranged into a corridor of glowing doors. THERE ARE MORE LEVELS. TRY TO KEEP UP.

chapters.heading: Level 2: Laika's Orbit (1957)
chapters.text:
The next door didn't open so much as ping, the way a Roblox server does when a friend joins.

Theo stepped through — or whatever you call it when your brain is apparently inside a loading screen — into a close, round little chamber with padded walls and a tiny window. Wagging in the middle of it, impossibly calm, sat a brown-and-white dog with her ears pricked forward.

"That is a dog," Theo said. "In space. Please tell me that's a hologram."

SHE IS **LAIKA**, Pip beeped. **NOVEMBER 3, 1957.** ONE MONTH AFTER SPUTNIK, THE SOVIETS LAUNCHED **SPUTNIK 2** — AND SHE WAS INSIDE. FIRST LIVING CREATURE TO ORBIT EARTH.

Theo crouched by the little window, careful not to touch the glass. "She just... went around the whole planet. By herself."

NOT ALONE, Pip said. SCIENTISTS ON THE GROUND WATCHED OVER HER THE WHOLE TIME. SHE BECAME FAMOUS AROUND THE WORLD — A SMALL DOG WHO DID SOMETHING NO LIVING THING HAD EVER DONE BEFORE.

Theo studied the capsule itself — round, snug, no steering wheel, nothing to grab onto. It looked nothing like his Roblox rocket, which was basically a cylinder standing on a flat plate.

"Why's it round?" he asked. "Shouldn't it be pointy? Aerodynamic?"

ASK YOURSELF, Pip said, WHICH SHAPE SURVIVES A CRASH LANDING BETTER — A CORNER, OR A CURVE?

Theo thought about every Roblox build that had ever fallen off a cliff. The sharp-edged ones always snapped apart. The round ones bounced.

"...A curve," he said slowly. Then, faster: "Wait. My rocket's been falling through the floor because the bottom's a flat square. If I round the edges—"

HE'S CATCHING ON, Pip told the dark, like he was narrating to an audience only he could see.

Theo grinned and waved at Laika's little window, and the pup tilted her head, like she was waving back from decades and a few hundred miles up.

"Good girl," Theo said softly. "You did something nobody had ever done."

The chamber faded, the way a loading bar finishes, and the corridor of doors reappeared.

ROUND TWO, said Pip. NEXT STOP — AMERICA PANICS.

"That's an oddly specific level name," Theo said.

IT'S HISTORICALLY ACCURATE, said Pip, which is somehow worse.

chapters.heading: Level 3: The Invisible Belt (1958)
chapters.text:
The next door opened onto a cramped room full of people in short-sleeved shirts, staring at a chart that jumped and spiked like a heart monitor having a bad night.

"Okay, this looks like a glitchy leaderboard," Theo said.

IT'S BETTER THAN A LEADERBOARD, said Pip. SPUTNIK SCARED THE UNITED STATES SO BADLY THEY BUILT A WHOLE NEW SPACE AGENCY. **NASA** STARTED WORKING ON **OCTOBER 1, 1958.**

"Because of one beeping ball?"

BECAUSE OF ONE BEEPING BALL, Pip confirmed. AND EVEN BEFORE NASA OFFICIALLY EXISTED, THE U.S. LAUNCHED ITS OWN FIRST SATELLITE — **EXPLORER 1**, ON **JANUARY 31, 1958.**

The jumpy chart filled the screen again, lines spiking every time a little animated satellite crossed a certain patch of sky.

"What's making it spike like that?" Theo asked. "Is the satellite lagging?"

NOT LAGGING. Explorer 1 found something nobody knew was there — an invisible ring of charged particles wrapped around the Earth, held in place by the planet's own magnetism. Scientists later named it the **Van Allen radiation belt**.

"So it's like an invisible wall," Theo said, "that you'd only find by accident. By flying straight into it."

EXACTLY LIKE THAT, Pip said. WHICH REMINDS ME.

A thin, shimmering line appeared across the floor, right where Theo would have walked if he'd kept moving. He stopped just short of it.

"Is that—"

AN INVISIBLE WALL. YES. TRY NOT TO WALK THROUGH HISTORY. IT GETS MESSY.

Theo laughed and stepped around it — and froze. "Wait. That's it. That's why my rocket keeps falling through the floor. I never added a collision wall under the pad. I just assumed the floor would catch it."

YOU CAN'T SEE GRAVITY EITHER, Pip pointed out. DOESN'T MEAN IT ISN'T THERE.

"You're surprisingly wise for a beach ball," Theo said.

I CONTAIN MULTITUDES, said Pip, and the room folded away like a tab closing.

chapters.heading: Level 4: One Hundred Eight Minutes (1961)
chapters.text:
The new room was snug and round again, but bigger, with a single curved seat and a porthole showing the whole blue curve of Earth outside.

A man in a white helmet grinned through the glass of the capsule, like he was having the best day of his life, which, as it turned out, he kind of was.

"Who's that?" Theo asked, already liking him.

**YURI GAGARIN.** SOVIET PILOT. **APRIL 12, 1961** — THE FIRST HUMAN BEING TO FLY INTO SPACE, RIDING A CAPSULE CALLED **VOSTOK 1** ALL THE WAY AROUND THE EARTH. ONE FULL LOOP. ABOUT **108 MINUTES.**

Theo, who had spent roughly eleven hundred Saturdays on a soccer field, did the math automatically. "That's longer than a whole match. He went around the entire planet in less time than it takes my team to lose in overtime."

PUT YOUR SKILLS TO USE, said Pip, and a glowing stopwatch appeared, already counting down from 108:00.

Theo watched it tick, picturing it like a match clock — first half, second half, the whistle. By the time it hit zero, Gagarin's capsule was already arcing back toward the ground, parachute blooming.

"That's insane," Theo breathed. "One lap and you're already a legend."

THREE WEEKS LATER, ANOTHER PILOT WENT UP TOO — **ALAN SHEPARD**, THE FIRST AMERICAN IN SPACE, ON **MAY 5, 1961.** HIS FLIGHT WAS SHORTER AND NEVER WENT ALL THE WAY AROUND. BUT IT STILL COUNTED.

"Sounds like Gagarin got the full match and Shepard got a penalty shootout," Theo said.

THAT'S UNFAIRLY ACCURATE, said Pip.

The scene shifted to a podium, a man in a dark suit speaking to a crowd that stretched farther than Theo could see.

ON **MAY 25, 1961**, said Pip, more quietly, PRESIDENT **JOHN F. KENNEDY** STOOD UP AND TOLD HIS COUNTRY TO LAND A PERSON ON THE MOON — AND BRING THEM HOME SAFE — BEFORE THE DECADE ENDED.

"That's like telling your whole team you're winning the championship before the season even starts," Theo said, "when you don't even have the players yet."

PRETTY MUCH. AND BEHIND THE SCENES, TWO DESIGNERS WERE RACING TO MAKE IT HAPPEN. ON THE SOVIET SIDE, **SERGEI KOROLEV** RAN THE WHOLE ROCKET PROGRAM — BUT HIS NAME WAS KEPT SECRET UNTIL HE DIED IN 1966. NO ONE EVEN KNEW HIS FACE.

"A secret genius," Theo said slowly. "Like a modder who builds the best game on the platform and never puts their name on it."

ON THE OTHER SIDE, **WERNHER VON BRAUN** LED THE AMERICAN TEAM BUILDING THE ROCKET THAT WOULD EVENTUALLY TRY FOR THE MOON.

Theo looked at the stopwatch, frozen at 00:00, and felt something tighten pleasantly in his chest — the same feeling he got when a build finally, finally worked. "Okay," he said. "I need to see if they actually did it."

PATIENCE, said Pip. THERE ARE STILL LEVELS LEFT.
chapters.shout_line: HE WENT AROUND THE ENTIRE PLANET?!

chapters.heading: Level 5: Forty-Eight Laps (1963)
chapters.text:
The next door opened on a woman strapped into a capsule, grinning the exact same unstoppable grin Gagarin had worn.

**VALENTINA TERESHKOVA**, said Pip. **JUNE 16, 1963.** FIRST WOMAN IN SPACE. SHE FLEW ABOARD **VOSTOK 6** AND WENT AROUND THE EARTH NOT ONCE, BUT **FORTY-EIGHT TIMES.**

Theo whistled. "Forty-eight? That's not a flight, that's a whole season."

A little counter appeared beside the capsule, ticking upward: 1... 2... 3...

"Hang on," Theo said, watching it climb, "let me guess where it stops." He thought about laps around a soccer pitch, about how his legs usually started complaining after ten, and multiplied it out in his head. "Forty-eight."

The counter stopped. 48.

THAT'S CORRECT, said Pip, sounding almost smug on Theo's behalf. SHE HAD BEEN AN ORDINARY FACTORY WORKER BEFORE SHE TRAINED TO FLY. NOT A TEST PILOT. NOT MILITARY. JUST SOMEONE WHO WANTED IT ENOUGH.

"So she just... leveled all the way up," Theo said. "From the factory floor to actual orbit."

PUT LIKE THAT, said Pip, IT SOUNDS EASY. IT WAS NOT EASY.

Theo watched her capsule sail past the window forty-eight invisible times in his mind and felt oddly proud of a woman he'd known about for exactly ninety seconds. "She's basically the final boss of persistence," he said.

A GOOD WAY TO PUT IT, said Pip, and for once didn't argue.

chapters.heading: Level 6: Ten Minutes Outside (1965)
chapters.text:
The next room had no walls at all — just a capsule floating in black space, and, drifting just outside it at the end of a long cord, a figure in a bulky white suit.

Theo's stomach did a small flip. "Is he just... out there? With nothing around him?"

**ALEXEI LEONOV**, said Pip. **MARCH 18, 1965.** FIRST HUMAN EVER TO LEAVE HIS CAPSULE AND FLOAT FREE IN SPACE — WHAT WE CALL A **SPACEWALK.** HE WAS OUTSIDE FOR ABOUT TEN MINUTES.

"Ten minutes doesn't sound that long," Theo said, eyeing the thin cord connecting the floating man to the capsule, the only thing between him and absolutely nothing. "But that cord is doing a LOT of work."

THAT'S THE **TETHER**, said Pip. A STRONG LINE THAT KEEPS AN ASTRONAUT ATTACHED TO THEIR SHIP SO THEY DON'T DRIFT AWAY FOR GOOD.

Theo stared at it, and something clicked in his brain. "That's an anchor point," he said. "My rocket keeps wobbling because I never anchored the fuel tank to the frame. It's just balanced there. One bump and it's gone."

HISTORY: STILL HELPFUL, said Pip.

Leonov drifted gently back toward the capsule, hand over hand along the tether, and climbed back inside, safe. The whole thing had lasted ten minutes and ended exactly the way it was supposed to.

"Ten minutes floating in actual space and he just climbs back in like he's done on the trampoline," Theo said. "Unbelievable."

MOST OF HISTORY, said Pip, IS PEOPLE BEING BRAVER THAN THEY HAD ANY RIGHT TO BE, AND THEN GOING HOME FOR DINNER.

chapters.heading: Level 7: Earthrise (1968)
chapters.text:
The next door didn't open onto a room at all. It opened onto nothing — then, suddenly, onto everything: a dusty gray horizon curving away below, and above it, impossibly, a small blue marble rising into a black sky.

Theo forgot to say anything for a second, which almost never happened.

**DECEMBER 1968**, said Pip, quieter than usual. **APOLLO 8.** THE FIRST ASTRONAUTS TO FLY ALL THE WAY TO THE MOON AND ORBIT AROUND IT. ONE OF THEM, **WILLIAM ANDERS**, LOOKED OUT THE WINDOW AND SAW THAT.

"That" was Earth, rising over the Moon's gray edge like a sunrise, except blue and white and swirled with cloud, smaller than Theo had ever imagined a whole planet could look.

"He just... saw it happen?" Theo said. "Nobody had ever seen that before?"

NOBODY. HE GRABBED A CAMERA AND TOOK THE PICTURE RIGHT THERE. IT'S CALLED **EARTHRISE**, AND IT'S ONE OF THE MOST FAMOUS PHOTOS EVER TAKEN.

Theo thought about every screenshot he'd ever taken of his own builds — the little camera icon he mashed the second something finally looked right. "I get that," he said. "You build this whole thing and then one angle just... makes you stop."

He raised an imaginary camera, framed the rising Earth exactly the way Anders must have, and mimed the click.

NOT BAD, said Pip. YOU'D HAVE MADE A DECENT ASTRONAUT.

"I'd have made a decent photographer," Theo corrected. "Let's not get ahead of ourselves."

The little blue Earth kept climbing silently over the gray horizon, and for a moment neither of them said anything else, because some things don't need a joke after them.

chapters.heading: Level 8: The Giant Leap (1969)
chapters.text:
The next door thundered open — actual thunder, a wall of sound and fire, the biggest rocket Theo had ever seen standing on a pad like a skyscraper that had decided to go somewhere.

"How big IS that thing?" Theo shouted over the roar.

THE **SATURN V**, Pip beeped back. **363 FEET TALL.** TALLER THAN THE STATUE OF LIBERTY. IT'S THE ROCKET THAT GOT THEM THERE.

The rocket climbed, impossibly, almost gently, trailing fire — and the scene jumped, the way levels do, straight to a gray dusty surface, a ladder, and a boot, reaching down.

"Wait," Theo said. "Is this—"

**JULY 20, 1969.** **APOLLO 11.** AND THAT'S **NEIL ARMSTRONG**, ABOUT TO BECOME THE FIRST PERSON EVER TO WALK ON THE MOON.

The boot touched down. Dust puffed up around it in complete silence, because there's no air on the Moon to carry a sound.

"That's one small step for man," crackled a voice, "one giant leap for mankind."

Theo didn't say anything clever. For once, he just watched.

BUZZ ALDRIN CLIMBED DOWN AFTER HIM, said Pip. THEY WALKED AROUND TOGETHER DOWN THERE. MEANWHILE THEIR THIRD CREWMATE, **MICHAEL COLLINS**, STAYED UP IN THE COMMAND MODULE — NAMED **COLUMBIA** — ORBITING THE MOON ALL ALONE, WAITING TO BRING THEM ALL HOME.

"He didn't even get to walk on it?" Theo said. "That's rough."

SOMEBODY HAD TO FLY THE SHIP, Pip said. NOT EVERY HERO GETS THE SCREENSHOT. SOME OF THEM JUST KEEP EVERYONE ELSE ALIVE.

Theo thought about every multiplayer build he'd ever done where he was the one holding the server together while a friend grabbed the glory — and decided Michael Collins was, in fact, the real MVP.

The two boots on the dust kept walking, bouncing slightly in the lighter gravity, and Theo watched with his mouth slightly open, feeling like he'd just watched the final level of the best game ever made — except it was real, and it had happened before his own parents were even born.

"They actually did it," Theo said. "Kennedy's whole deadline thing. They actually did it."

BEFORE THE DECADE ENDED, said Pip. WITH TWO YEARS TO SPARE.

chapters.heading: Level 9: The Fix and the Handshake (1970–1975)
chapters.text:
The next room started calm — a capsule gliding smooth and quiet toward a gray dot that was obviously the Moon — and then, without warning, something inside it went BANG, and warning lights flooded the little cabin red.

Theo flinched. "Whoa — what happened?"

**1970.** **APOLLO 13.** AN OXYGEN TANK EXPLODED ON THE WAY TO THE MOON AND CRIPPLED THE WHOLE SHIP. THEY HAD TO TURN BACK.

"Are they okay?" Theo asked immediately, because that mattered more than anything else in the room.

THEY'RE OKAY, said Pip, fast and firm, like it wanted that part understood before anything else. ENGINEERS BACK ON EARTH WORKED OUT A FIX USING WHAT THE ASTRONAUTS ALREADY HAD ON BOARD, AND TALKED THEM THROUGH IT, STEP BY STEP. THE WHOLE CREW MADE IT HOME SAFE.

Theo let out a breath he hadn't noticed he was holding. "So it's like — the server crashes, but instead of losing everything, somebody figures out how to rebuild it out of spare parts while you're still inside it."

THAT'S UNCOMFORTABLY EXACT, said Pip. AND KIND OF THE WHOLE POINT. SOMETIMES THE BEST PART OF A STORY ISN'T THAT NOTHING WENT WRONG. IT'S THAT PEOPLE FIGURED IT OUT ANYWAY.

The battered little capsule splashed safely into blue ocean, and the scene dissolved into one last room — two spacecraft, docked nose to nose in orbit, a hatch sliding open between them.

**JULY 17, 1975**, said Pip. **APOLLO-SOYUZ.** AN AMERICAN SHIP AND A SOVIET SHIP MET UP IN ORBIT AND DOCKED TOGETHER. THE CREWS OPENED THE HATCH AND SHOOK HANDS. THAT'S HOW THE SPACE RACE ENDED.

Two astronauts floated through the hatch and clasped hands in midair, grinning, upside down relative to each other, which in zero gravity didn't matter at all.

"After everything," Theo said slowly, "beeping satellites and secret rocket designers and a guy floating in actual space on a rope — it just ends with a handshake?"

IT ENDS WITH A HANDSHAKE, Pip agreed. SEEMED LIKE A GOOD PLACE TO STOP RACING AND START WAVING.

The corridor of doors folded up behind them like a closing tab, and the green-black flicker rose around Theo's room again, and then — ordinary lamplight. His carpet. His laptop, still open, the cursor blinking in Roblox Studio exactly where he'd left it.

He looked at his rocket. Rounded base now. An invisible wall under the pad. A tether holding the fuel tank to the frame.

He hit Play.

The rocket sat on the pad for one heart-stopping second — and then it lit, and climbed, smooth and steady, all the way up past the render distance.

"YES," Theo said, loud enough that it was lucky nobody else was awake to hear it. "YES. FINALLY."

In the corner of the screen, for just a second, a tiny pixel satellite blinked once, beeped twice, and faded out.

"Night, Pip," Theo said to the empty screen, grinning like an idiot. Then he saved his file, like a sensible astronaut radioing home, and finally — finally — went to bed.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow there'd be a new level to build — and somewhere, Theo figured, Pip would already be listening for his next beep.

true_facts.text: Sputnik 1 was the first man-made object to orbit Earth, launched by the Soviet Union on **October 4, 1957**.
Sputnik 1 was only **58 centimeters wide** — smaller than a desk chair — and it just sent out a steady beep.
A month later, the dog **Laika** rode Sputnik 2 into orbit, the first living creature ever to circle the Earth.
Sputnik scared the United States into building a brand-new space agency, **NASA**, which started working on **October 1, 1958**.
America's first satellite, **Explorer 1**, launched **January 31, 1958**, and discovered an invisible ring of radiation wrapped around Earth, later called the **Van Allen belt**.
**Yuri Gagarin** became the first human in space on **April 12, 1961**, circling the whole Earth once in about **108 minutes**.
**Alan Shepard** became the first American in space on **May 5, 1961**, though his flight was shorter and didn't go all the way around.
On **May 25, 1961**, President **John F. Kennedy** challenged the country to land someone on the Moon and bring them home safe before the decade ended.
**Valentina Tereshkova** became the first woman in space on **June 16, 1963**, circling the Earth **forty-eight times**.
**Alexei Leonov** made the first spacewalk on **March 18, 1965**, floating outside his capsule on a tether for about ten minutes.
In **December 1968**, the Apollo 8 crew became the first people to orbit the Moon, and astronaut **William Anders** snapped the famous **Earthrise** photo.
On **July 20, 1969**, **Neil Armstrong** became the first person to walk on the Moon, calling it a giant leap for mankind.
In **1970**, an oxygen tank exploded aboard **Apollo 13**, but engineers on the ground helped the crew fix the problem and return home safely.
The Space Race ended on **July 17, 1975**, when an American and a Soviet spacecraft docked in orbit and their crews shook hands.

story.title: Maya and the Glowing Porthole of the Titanic
story.subtitle: A bedtime voyage through the biggest ship of her time

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Glowing Porthole
chapters.text:
Maya lay on her bedroom floor, pencil in hand, drawing a boat with three funnels and tiny flags. It was way past bedtime, but the drawing was almost done.

Her pencil gave a tiny **CLICK**, and the page glowed gold.

A round brass porthole shimmered on her wall, like a window made of water and sunshine. A kind, crackly voice came through it. "Evening, sailor. Fancy seeing something real?"

"Who's there?" Maya whispered.

"Call me Pip," said the porthole. "I show boats. Real ones. Want to see the start of the biggest one ever built?"

Maya grinned and climbed through.

She landed in a noisy **shipyard** — a place by the sea where workers build ships — in Belfast, Ireland. Hammers banged. Sparks flew like tiny orange stars.

"This is where Titanic was born," said Pip. "Built right here at the **Harland & Wolff** shipyard."

Maya looked up at a giant metal beam stretching along the ground like a spine.

"That's the **keel**," said Pip. "The very first bone of the ship. Workers laid it down on **March 31, 1909**."

Maya traced its shape with her finger. "It's so long!"

"When she's done," said Pip, "Titanic will stretch **882 feet** — almost three football fields. The biggest ship afloat."

Maya spotted two more half-built ships nearby, shaped just the same.

"Wait," she said. "Are those her sisters?"

Pip chuckled. "Sharp eyes. Titanic was the middle sister of three — **Olympic** came first, **Britannic** after."

Maya grinned, already sketching all three in a row. "Triplets. Just bigger."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Four Smokestacks, Sixteen Boxes
chapters.text:
Two years later, Pip brought Maya back for the loudest **CLANG** she'd ever heard.

Grease covered the launching ramp. Thousands of people cheered. On **May 31, 1911**, Titanic slid backward into the water with a **SPLOOSH**.

Maya counted the tall smokestacks poking the sky. "One, two, three, four!"

"Good counting," said Pip. "But only three ever puffed real smoke. The fourth was just for looks, to make her seem even grander."

Maya giggled. "A pretend chimney!"

Down below, a worker showed her inside the hull, where metal walls divided the ship into sealed rooms.

"These are **watertight compartments**," the worker explained. "Sixteen of them. If water gets into one, the rest stay dry, and the ship still floats."

"So she can't ever sink?" Maya asked.

"People called her **nearly unsinkable**," said Pip gently. "Nearly. Not the same as never."

Maya frowned, thinking hard. "What if a lot of them fill up at once?"

Nobody had a good answer. The worker just shrugged and went back to his rivets.

Maya tucked the question away, like a pebble in her pocket, and kept drawing little boxes inside her picture of the ship, just in case she needed them later.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Flags at Southampton
chapters.text:
Horns blasted so loud Maya covered her ears, then laughed.

It was **April 10, 1912**, and the dock at Southampton, England, was bursting with people waving handkerchiefs and hats.

"She's off to New York City," said Pip, "on her very first trip."

Maya waved an imaginary flag of her own. Sailors in crisp white shirts carried trunks and hatboxes up the gangway.

A small fluffy dog trotted past in someone's arms.

"Aw, a puppy gets to go too?" Maya said.

"A few lucky pets came aboard," said Pip. "Keep an eye out for that one."

Maya grinned and gave the little dog a wave as it bounced up the ramp, its owner laughing at how fast its tail wagged.

The ship's whistle let out one enormous **WHOOOOSH**, and slowly, slowly, Titanic pulled away from the dock, sliding into open water like the biggest toy boat in the world.

Maya hopped on her tiptoes, watching until the ship was just a dark shape on the horizon, getting smaller with every second.

"Next stop," said Pip, "the middle of the ocean."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Shape in the Dark
chapters.text:
Four days later, the night was quiet and very, very cold.

Maya peered through Pip's porthole at a flat black sea. It was **11:40 p.m. on April 14, 1912**.

Something pale drifted ahead, barely visible.

"Pip — there! A shadow on the water!" Maya pointed, her heart thumping.

High in the crow's nest, a lookout spotted it in that same moment and rang the warning bell, three sharp dings.

Too late to turn all the way, the ship's side scraped along a giant **iceberg** — a mountain of floating ice — with a long, low groan.

Maya held her breath. "Is it going to sink?"

"Not yet," said Pip steadily. "The compartments are doing their job. But water's getting into more of them than anyone hoped."

Down in the boiler rooms, crew worked fast, pumping water, keeping the lights and radios running.

Maya let her breath out slowly. "Okay. Okay. There's still time."

"There is," said Pip. "And time is exactly what they need."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Dot Dot Dot
chapters.text:
Up in the radio room, two operators named **Jack Phillips** and **Harold Bride** tapped out messages as fast as their fingers could fly.

Maya watched the little sparks jump off their key. "What are they doing?"

"Sending a **distress call**," said Pip. "A radio message asking any nearby ship to come help. They used the old signal, **CQD**, and a brand new one too, called **SOS**."

Maya tapped the porthole frame herself, three short, three long, three short. "Like that?"

"Exactly like that," said Pip, sounding impressed.

Out on deck, passengers wrapped in blankets heard music drifting through the cold air. A small band, led by a man named **Wallace Hartley**, kept playing to help keep everyone calm.

"People always said they played right to the very end," said Pip. "Nobody's completely sure that part is true, but it's the kind of brave thing worth remembering."

Maya listened to the faint, brave little tune and found she wasn't quite so worried anymore either.

"Keep playing," she whispered. "Smooth sailing."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Not Enough Boats
chapters.text:
Crew began lowering lifeboats, one by one, down the ship's tall side.

Maya counted them swinging down. "There aren't very many."

"You're right," said Pip. "Titanic only carried enough lifeboats for about **1,178** people, far fewer than everyone aboard."

Maya's chest tightened. "That's not fair."

"No," said Pip. "It wasn't. People fixed that rule afterward, I promise."

In one boat, a passenger named **Margaret Brown** grabbed an oar and rowed hard alongside the crew, keeping everyone's spirits up. People later called her the **"Unsinkable Molly Brown."**

"She's not even a sailor and she's rowing!" Maya cheered.

Nearby, the same little fluffy dog from the dock got tucked safely inside someone's coat and lowered into a boat of its own.

"It's okay, it's okay," Maya murmured, as if the dog could hear her all the way from home.

On the bridge, Captain **Edward Smith** stayed at his post, helping guide passengers toward safety instead of saving a seat for himself.

"That's what a good captain does," said Pip quietly.

Maya nodded, suddenly very proud of a man she'd never even met.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: A Light on the Water
chapters.text:
The sky was turning from black to grey. Maya scanned the horizon hard.

"Pip — there! A tiny light, way out there!"

Pip's porthole zoomed in like a telescope. "Good eyes again, Maya. That's the **Carpathia**."

The steamship had raced through the night after hearing the distress call, and now she was close enough to help.

One by one, cold and tired passengers climbed aboard her decks, wrapped in warm blankets, handed steaming mugs of tea.

Maya watched a woman hug a little girl so hard she nearly knocked her over.

"They made it," Maya whispered. "They actually made it."

"Many did," said Pip, "thanks to that call for help, and a crew that didn't stop rowing."

The sun came all the way up, gold and warm, lighting a sea with nothing left on it but lifeboats, blankets, and very relieved people wrapped inside them.

Maya let out a long breath. "That was close."

"It was," Pip agreed. "Close enough that people made sure it would never happen quite that way again."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Deep, Deep Down
chapters.text:
Pip's porthole flickered, pages of calendar flipping fast.

"After that night," said Pip, "ships changed their rules forever. Every ship now has to carry enough lifeboats for every single person aboard. Boats started watching for icebergs too, so captains always get warned in time."

Maya nodded firmly. "Good. That pebble question I had, about too many compartments flooding, somebody finally fixed it."

"They did," said Pip. "Took a while. But they did."

Then the porthole glowed a deep, deep blue, the color of the very bottom of the ocean.

"On **September 1, 1985**," said Pip, "an explorer named **Robert Ballard** finally found her."

Maya gasped at a grainy, ghostly picture: a huge shape resting on the seafloor, **12,500 feet** down, further under the water than Maya could really imagine.

She squinted at the picture. "It looks like... two pieces?"

"Good eye," said Pip. "She broke into two main parts on the way down. She rests about **370 miles** off the coast of Newfoundland, Canada."

Maya pressed her hand flat against the porthole glass, as if she could touch the old ship goodnight.

"Sleep well down there," she whispered.

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Back on the Carpet
chapters.text:
The blue glow faded. The brass porthole shrank smaller and smaller, until it was just a shiny coin of light on Maya's wall.

"One more thing," said Pip, "before I go. People built a museum in Belfast, shaped like a giant ship's front, right where Titanic began. Years later, someone even made a movie about her, one of the most watched movies ever made."

"People still remember her," Maya said.

"They do," said Pip. "Stories like hers don't really sink. They just wait to be found again."

The porthole winked out completely.

Maya looked down at her drawing. The boat now had four funnels, sixteen little boxes drawn carefully along its side, and a tiny fluffy dog peeking over the railing.

She tucked the drawing under her pillow, climbed into bed, and listened to the quiet of her very own room.

Outside, somewhere far off, a real boat horn gave one soft, sleepy **toot**, almost like it was saying goodnight too.

Maya smiled and closed her eyes.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Maya. Smooth sailing, always.

true_facts.text: Titanic was built by workers at the **Harland & Wolff** shipyard in **Belfast, Ireland**.
Her very first beam, the **keel**, was laid down on **March 31, 1909**, and she slid into the water on **May 31, 1911**.
Titanic stretched **882 feet** long, making her the biggest ship of her time.
Titanic was the middle sister of three ships, alongside **Olympic** and **Britannic**.
Titanic had **four** tall funnels, but only three ever puffed real smoke.
Inside, Titanic had **sixteen watertight compartments**, sealed rooms that led people to call her **nearly unsinkable**.
Titanic left **Southampton, England** on **April 10, 1912**, heading for New York City.
At about **11:40 p.m. on April 14, 1912**, Titanic struck an iceberg in the dark.
Radio operators sent out calls for help using the old signal **CQD** and the brand new **SOS**.
Passenger **Margaret 'Molly' Brown** grabbed an oar and helped row her lifeboat, earning the nickname "**Unsinkable Molly Brown**."
The steamship **Carpathia** raced through the night and rescued survivors from the lifeboats the next morning.
On **September 1, 1985**, explorer **Robert Ballard** finally found the wreck, resting **12,500 feet** down on the seafloor.
After the disaster, new rules meant every ship had to carry enough lifeboats for everyone aboard.

story.title: Ivy and the Rainbow in the Puddle
story.subtitle: A splashy, colorful bedtime adventure with Drip the raindrop

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Glowing Puddle
chapters.text:
Ivy sat on her floor. She painted big blue puddles with her brush.

Rain tapped the window. Tap, tap, tap.

Ivy peeked outside. One puddle glowed gold.

She tiptoed to the door in her socks.

The puddle wiggled. A tiny raindrop popped up with a shiny grin.

"Hello, Ivy! I'm **Drip**," he said. "Want to see where colors hide?"

Ivy grinned back. "Yes! I love colors!"

Drip winked. "Then hold my hand. Sun and rain, colors again!"

Ivy touched the puddle. **WHOOOSH!** The world turned sparkly and small.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Inside a Raindrop
chapters.text:
Ivy landed inside a big round raindrop. It wobbled like jelly.

A beam of sunlight zoomed in from outside.

"Watch the light," said Drip. "It comes right inside the drop."

The light wiggled and bent, like a straw in a cup.

"It **bends**!" Ivy shouted, pointing at the curve.

"You found it," said Drip. "**Sunlight bends when it goes into a raindrop.**"

Ivy clapped. The drop jiggled right along with her.

"Where does the light go now?" Ivy asked.

Drip smiled. "Follow it and see."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Bouncy Back Wall
chapters.text:
The light beam zoomed to the back of the drop.

**SPLAT!** It hit the round wall and bounced, like a ball off a window.

Ivy giggled. "It bounced!"

"Yes," said Drip. "Then it **bends one more time**, right as it leaves the drop."

The light wiggled out the front. Ivy gasped.

Red, orange, yellow, green, blue, and purple spilled out, like wet paint.

"Those colors were hiding inside the white light," said Drip.

Ivy reached out and touched a ribbon of red. It tickled her fingers.

"I want to paint this!" she said.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Sun Behind, Rain Ahead
chapters.text:
Drip floated Ivy back outside, onto a wet sidewalk.

"Look around," said Drip. "Where is the sun?"

Ivy turned in a circle. "Behind me!"

"Good! And where is the rain?"

Ivy pointed ahead. "Over there, still falling!"

"That's the trick," said Drip. "**Sun behind you, rain in front.** Then a rainbow can show up."

Ivy thought for a second. "That's why rainbows come right after a rain shower, when the sun peeks out!"

Drip's eyes went wide. "You figured that out all by yourself!"

A soft rainbow arched over the street. Ivy clapped her hands.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Patient Puddle Thinker
chapters.text:
Drip tugged Ivy toward a cozy little room, long, long ago.

A kind old man sat by a window, watching light through a jar of water.

"This is **Ibn al-Haytham**," said Drip. "A clever thinker. He watched how light moves, a very long time ago."

Ivy peeked at his jar. "Is that like our raindrop?"

"Just like it," said the old man, smiling. "Watching closely helps us learn its secrets."

Ivy picked up a jar of her own and held it to the window.

A tiny rainbow glimmered on the floor.

"I did it too!" Ivy cheered.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Glass Ball Friend
chapters.text:
Next, Drip led Ivy to a sunny workshop.

A man sat surrounded by round glass balls, each one filled with water.

"This is **Kamal**," said Drip. "He used glass balls like big raindrops, to see how light bends inside."

Ivy picked up a little glass ball and held it to the sun.

A rainbow danced across her hand.

"It works just like the real thing!" Ivy laughed.

Kamal nodded. "Looking closely always helps."

Ivy set the ball down gently, so it would not roll away.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Newton's Rainbow Trick
chapters.text:
Drip whisked Ivy to a dusty old room full of books.

A man held up a strange glass triangle. "This is a **prism**," he said. "A glass shape that splits light into colors."

He let sunlight shine through it.

Colors spilled onto the wall: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, and purple.

"Whoa!" Ivy said. "Just like the raindrop!"

"Exactly," said the man. "I'm **Isaac Newton**. White light was hiding colors all along."

Ivy clapped. "Colors were hiding in plain sight!"

Newton chuckled and let her hold the prism.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Home Again
chapters.text:
**WHOOOSH!** Ivy landed back on her bedroom floor.

Her paintbrush was still in her hand.

Outside, the rain had stopped. The sun peeked out, just like Drip said it would.

A real rainbow arched over the yard.

Ivy looked down at her painting. She had painted a puddle with a rainbow inside it, without even knowing.

Drip's voice whispered from a tiny puddle by the door. "Sun and rain, colors again, Ivy."

Ivy yawned and climbed into bed, her painting propped against the wall.

"Goodnight, Drip," she whispered.

Outside, the rainbow glowed softly, then faded into the evening sky.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Ivy. Sun and rain, colors again.

true_facts.text: Sunlight zooms right inside a raindrop.
Inside the drop, the light bends, just like a straw looks bent in a cup.
The light bounces off the back wall of the raindrop.
Then the light bends again as it leaves the drop.
All those bends and bounces split the light into red, orange, yellow, green, blue, and purple.
To see a rainbow, the sun needs to be behind you.
And the rain needs to be out in front of you.
Rainbows need sunshine and rain at the very same time.
That's why rainbows often show up right after a rain shower, when the sun peeks out.

new_recurring.name: Drip
new_recurring.rule: Drip is a friendly talking raindrop who appears glowing in a puddle after rain and invites Ivy into a science adventure. He always says the catchphrase 'Sun and rain, colors again.'

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Ivy returns to her bedroom to find a real rainbow outside her window and realizes she had already painted one hiding in her puddle picture, falling asleep as Drip whispers their catchphrase.

story.title: Leo and the Night Train to Sleepyland
story.subtitle: A choo-choo ride through quiet sleep and dream sleep, with Hoot the Owl.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Owl Wakes Up
chapters.text:
Leo lay on his bedroom floor, way past bedtime. His wooden train track looped in a big circle. On the shelf, his stuffed owl nightlight blinked. Its eyes glowed soft gold.

"Hello, Leo," said a small voice. It was the owl! "I'm Hoot," he said. "Want a ride on the Night Train?"

A tiny glowing train now chuffed along the rug. Leo looked at the loop of tracks. "It goes round and round," he said. "Just like sleep," said Hoot. "Quiet sleep, then dream sleep, over and over, all night long."

Leo hopped aboard. CHUFF CHUFF! Off they went.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Twitchy Eyes Station
chapters.text:
The train screeched to a stop. SCREECH! A sign showed two sleepy eyelids.

Leo peeked through a window. A boy lay sleeping, and his eyelids twitched, fast, like tiny flags. "Why do his eyes wiggle?" Leo asked.

"In **1953**," said Hoot, "two scientists named **Eugene** and **Nathaniel** watched eyes twitch just like that. They found a special dream sleep. Grown-ups call it **REM**. That means Rapid Eye Movement, fast eyes moving while you dream."

Leo tried wiggling his own closed eyes. "Mine won't wiggle!" he giggled.

"That's okay," said Hoot. "It happens all by itself, every single night."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Floppy Noodle Yard
chapters.text:
Next stop: a yard full of toy soldiers, all flopped over like wet noodles.

Leo poked one. Squish! It flopped right back down. "Why so floppy?" he asked.

"During dream sleep," said Hoot, "your brain stays busy, almost like when you're awake. But your arms and legs go **floppy and loose**. That way you can't act out your dreams."

Leo flopped onto the soft grass too, arms wobbly. "I'm a noodle!" he laughed.

Hoot hooted with laughter. "A very safe, floppy noodle," he said.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Grow Big Depot
chapters.text:
A tall measuring pole stood at the next stop, marked with lines. "Why is there a ruler here?" Leo asked.

"Your deepest, quietest sleep," said Hoot, "gives your body a special growing juice. That's one reason sleep helps you grow bigger."

Leo stood against the pole and stretched up on his toes. "Am I bigger yet?" he asked.

Hoot chuckled. "Takes more than one stretch, Leo. But every good sleep helps a little."

Leo decided to stand extra tall, just in case.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Tick-Tock Tower
chapters.text:
A clock tower ticked quietly nearby, its hands shaped like little train tracks. "Does it ever stop?" Leo asked.

"Never," said Hoot. "There's a tiny clock inside your head too. It counts about one whole day, over and over, telling your body when to sleep and when to wake."

"That clock even has a fancy name," Hoot added. "**Circadian**. Old words meaning 'about a day.'"

"Like a train timetable!" Leo said.

"Exactly like that," said Hoot, smiling. Leo waved at the tower as the train rolled on, feeling rather clever.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Remember River
chapters.text:
The train rolled beside a river of floating paper boats. Each boat held one small picture.

Leo spotted a boat with his own red train on it. "That's from today!" he said.

"While you sleep," said Hoot, "your brain sorts pictures like these. It decides which ones to keep. That's how sleep helps you remember things you learned."

Leo reached out and tucked his little boat onto a track marked KEEP. "Keeping that one forever," he said proudly.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Animal Sleep Yard
chapters.text:
The train rumbled into a dark tunnel. Leo grabbed the window ledge. "It's awfully dark," he said in a small voice.

Hoot flicked on the train's lantern. Soft golden light filled the tunnel at once. "Better?" asked Hoot. Leo nodded, brave again.

They popped out into a sunny yard full of animals. A **dolphin** swam past with one eye open, watching for danger. A **giraffe** napped standing up, barely two hours a day. A tiny **bat** hung upside down, snoozing twenty hours straight. A tiny baby, just born, slept in little bursts all day long.

"Who sleeps the most?" Hoot asked. Leo pointed. "The bat!" he said.

"Right again," said Hoot.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Sleepy Juice Station
chapters.text:
A glowing jar sat on the platform, twinkling like stars. "What's that?" Leo asked.

"Scientists found a sleepy juice inside everybody," said Hoot. "Back in **1958**, a scientist named **Aaron Lerner** found it. It makes you feel sleepy when night comes."

Leo peeked at the jar. "Like your eyes, Hoot!" he said, pointing at the owl's glowing eyes.

"Exactly like that," Hoot said, winking. He tipped one tiny drop into his own lantern, and it glowed softer gold.

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Back to the Carpet
chapters.text:
The train chuffed back onto Leo's bedroom carpet. CHUFF... CHUFF... puff. It slowed to a stop right where it started.

Hoot hopped back onto the shelf, eyes glowing soft and low. "Time for your own sleep now, Leo," he said. "Quiet sleep, then dream sleep, round and round, just like our loop."

Leo climbed into bed and pulled his blanket up. The little train sat parked and still, waiting for next time.

"Night night, Hoot," Leo whispered, already drifting.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Leo. Choo-choo to dreamland.

true_facts.text: Sleep moves in loops all night, quiet sleep then dream sleep, over and over.
In **1953**, two scientists named **Eugene** and **Nathaniel** watched a sleeping boy's eyes twitch and discovered dream sleep, called **REM**.
During dream sleep your arms and legs go **floppy and loose**, so you can't act out your dreams.
Your deepest, quietest sleep gives your body a special **growing juice** that helps you grow bigger.
There is a tiny **clock inside your head** that tells your body when to sleep and when to wake up.
That clock has a fancy name, **circadian**, which comes from old words meaning 'about a day.'
While you sleep, your brain **sorts your memories**, deciding which ones to keep.
A tiny baby, just born, sleeps in lots of little bursts all day long.
A **dolphin** can sleep with one eye open, watching for danger.
A **giraffe** naps standing up, sometimes less than two hours a day.
A tiny **bat** can sleep up to twenty hours a day, more than almost any other animal.
In **1958**, scientist **Aaron Lerner** found a sleepy juice inside the body that makes you feel sleepy at night.

new_recurring.name: Hoot the Owl Conductor
new_recurring.rule: Leo's owl nightlight glows soft gold and Hoot invites him aboard a tiny glowing Night Train whenever it's time to learn something new; he always says 'Choo-choo to dreamland' at the end of the ride.

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Leo drifted off to sleep as Hoot the Owl's eyes glowed soft and low on the shelf, with the little toy train parked quietly on its looped track, ready for the next ride.

story.title: Rosa and Isla Learn How Animals Climb Walls
story.subtitle: A sticky, tappy, squishy bedtime adventure

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: Dot Wakes Up
chapters.text:
Rosa sat on her bedroom floor.

She lined up her red ladybird toys. Isla hung from the top of her door frame, practicing her climbing grip.

"Three more seconds," Isla said. She held on tight.

Then Rosa's favorite toy began to glow. It was her littlest ladybird, Dot. Dot blinked twice, bright red.

"Ooooh!" said Rosa.

Dot's tiny wings popped open. "Hello, friends!" she said. "Want to see how bugs climb walls?"

Isla dropped down from the door frame. "Wait. You can talk?"

"Only for adventures," said Dot. She winked one shiny black eye.

She led them through a glowing window. On the other side sat a little lizard. He was upside down, right on the glass.

"Whoa," whispered Isla. "How is he not falling?"

"I'm a gecko," said the lizard. "Look at my toes!"

Isla leaned close. Each toe had rows of tiny hairs. So many hairs. Too small to count.

"These are my sticky toes," said the gecko. "Millions of hairs. Not glue. Just grip!"

Rosa poked the window glass. Her own finger did not stick at all.

"When I want to let go," said the gecko, "I peel my toes up. One at a time. Like peeling tape!"

He peeled one foot. Then another. Then — SCUTTLE SCUTTLE — he ran straight up the wall.

"IT STICKS!" shouted Rosa, clapping both hands.

"Come on," said Dot. "More wall-climbers to meet!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Squishy Pads
chapters.text:
A fly landed on the window glass. It did not slide down at all.

"Hey, that's like you, Dot!" said Rosa.

Dot giggled. "That's right. I'm a beetle. Flies are my cousins."

"So what do you have instead of hairs?" asked Isla.

Dot lifted one tiny foot. A little drop of sticky goo sat on the bottom.

"Squishy pads," she said. "They ooze a bit of sticky stuff. Every single step."

Rosa touched Dot's foot gently. "Squish!" she said, giggling.

"Exactly," said Dot. "Squish, stick, walk. Squish, stick, walk."

The fly buzzed off the glass. It looped right around Isla's head.

"Does it ever get stuck forever?" Isla asked.

"Nope!" said Dot. "We peel up, just like the gecko. Then away we fly."

BZZZZZ went the fly, zooming off at last.

It left one tiny sticky dot on the glass. Rosa pressed her nose close to look.

"Squishy feet are the best feet," Rosa announced.

Dot laughed so hard her wings rattled. "Next stop — somewhere spidery!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Spider on the Glass
chapters.text:
Dot flew them to an old shed. A spider sat very still on the window. High above, a web sparkled.

Isla crept closer. "Is it going to fall?" she whispered.

"Watch," said Dot.

The spider took one slow step. Then another. Right across the smooth glass.

"It's not falling because spiders have tiny hairs too," said Dot. "Thousands and thousands. On every foot. Even smaller than the gecko's."

Rosa squinted hard. "I can't even see them!"

"That's how tiny they are," said Dot.

Isla grinned. "So that's why spiders hang on ceilings. And windows. And never fall off."

"Exactly right," said Dot, bobbing happily.

The spider reached the top corner. It tapped one leg, almost like a wave.

"Bye, spider!" said Rosa, waving both hands back.

Isla laughed. "I don't think it waved on purpose, Rosa."

"It did too," said Rosa, very sure.

Dot chuckled. "Time to go see some claw-climbers now."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Switching Tools
chapters.text:
Outside, a line of ants marched straight up a brick wall.

"Count them, Rosa!" said Isla.

"One, two, three..." Rosa pointed at each tiny ant.

"Ants have little claws," said Dot. "Perfect for gripping bumpy walls, like bricks."

But the ants reached a smooth, shiny drainpipe. They did not slow down one bit.

"Wait," said Isla. "How do claws work on THAT? It's totally smooth!"

"They switch tools," said Dot. "On smooth walls, ants use sticky pads instead. Cockroaches do the same trick."

Isla tapped the drainpipe. "So it's like changing shoes for a different job?"

"Exactly like that," said Dot. "Claws for bumpy. Sticky pads for smooth."

Rosa watched the ants vanish over the top. "Bye bye, ants!"

"Bye bye, ants!" Isla copied, in a silly ant voice.

Rosa giggled so hard she fell backward into the grass. "Again! Again!"

Dot spun a happy circle in the air. "Up next — the biggest climber yet."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Goat Shoes
chapters.text:
Dot flew them over a tall, rocky cliff. It was so steep, Rosa gripped Isla's hand.

A shaggy mountain goat stood near the very top. He looked calm as could be.

"How does he not slip?" asked Isla.

The goat stamped one hoof. "Hard edges on the outside," he said. "Soft, squishy middles too. They squish to fit the rock."

Isla looked down at her own climbing shoes. "Wait. That's just like my shoes! Hard edges. Soft bits too!"

"You noticed something important," said Dot. "Some people study animal feet for a living. We call them scientists — people who study how things work. They used animal feet to help make better climbing shoes. And gloves, too."

Isla's mouth dropped open. "So my shoes are kind of... goat shoes?"

"A little bit," laughed Dot.

Rosa pointed at the goat. "Jump! Jump!"

The goat hopped from rock to rock. He never slipped once. Then he vanished over the top.

"I want goat feet," Isla declared.

"You basically already have them," said Dot, grinning.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Tiny Mountains
chapters.text:
Back in the yard, a squirrel zipped straight up a tree.

"How come he doesn't need sticky feet?" asked Rosa.

Dot pointed at the squirrel's feet. "Look closer."

The squirrel paused. Isla spotted sharp little claws on each toe.

"Those claws dig into tiny cracks," said Dot. "Bumps too small to notice. Even on smooth-looking bark."

"Like tiny mountains!" said Rosa, delighted.

"Exactly like tiny mountains," said Dot.

The squirrel flicked its tail. It ran a silly circle around the trunk, chasing nothing at all.

"Show-off," said Isla, grinning.

Rosa laughed so hard she snorted. That made Isla laugh too.

The squirrel paused near the top. It looked down, almost like a wave goodbye. Then it vanished into the leaves.

"Bye, squirrel!" called Rosa.

"Two wall-climbers left," said Dot. "One wet. One tappy."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Slimy Roads
chapters.text:
Dot led them to a pond. A little tree frog sat on a wet leaf, high above the water.

"Ribbit," said the frog. He did not slide one bit.

"His toes are flat and sticky," said Dot. "Covered in a bit of slime. With tiny bumpy patterns, like a honeycomb. They grip wet leaves. And glass, too."

Rosa touched a leaf. It was slippery and wet, just like the frog's toes. "Slimy and sticky!" she said.

Nearby, a snail inched up a stone wall. It left a shiny trail behind it.

"Ew — I mean, cool," said Isla, grinning. "Is that slime too?"

"Snail slime," said Dot. "They glide along on it. Rippling their one big foot. Up any smooth wall they like."

Rosa pressed her finger near the shiny trail. "Shiny road!"

"A snail-made shiny road," Dot agreed.

The frog gave one more "ribbit." Then he hopped off into the dark. The snail kept gliding, slow and steady, toward the top of the wall.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Home Again
chapters.text:
TAP TAP TAP. A woodpecker hammered at a tree trunk. He stood straight up on the bark.

"How does he stand like that? Without falling backward?" asked Isla.

"Two toes point forward. Two point back," said Dot. "Like a tiny built-in ladder grip. And his stiff tail feathers prop him up. Like a little chair."

Rosa tried standing like the woodpecker. Two fingers forward, two back. She wobbled right over into the grass.

"Needs practice," said Isla, helping her up. Both of them giggled.

TAP TAP TAP went the woodpecker, one more time.

Then Dot's wings began to glow again.

"Time for home," said Dot gently.

The glowing window swirled. Suddenly, Rosa and Isla were back on their bedroom floor. Ladybird toys lay scattered all around them.

Dot folded her wings. She sat still again, just a toy. Except for one last tiny blink and wink.

Rosa hugged the little ladybird toy close. "Goat shoes. Squishy feet. Sticky toes," she murmured sleepily.

Isla tucked her climbing shoes under her bed. She smiled at them in a whole new way.

Outside their window, a real ladybird landed on the glass for just a moment. It did not slide down at all.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Rosa. Goodnight, Isla. Climb well, little bugs.

true_facts.text: Geckos climb glass because their toes have millions of **tiny hairs**.
A gecko's sticky grip isn't **glue** — it can peel its toes up to let go.
Flies and beetles have **squishy pads** that ooze a bit of sticky goo on every step.
Spiders have **thousands of tiny hairs** on their feet, even smaller than a gecko's.
Ants use **sharp claws** on bumpy walls, and switch to **sticky pads** on smooth ones.
Some **scientists** studied animal feet to help invent better climbing shoes and gloves.
Squirrels climb with **sharp claws** that dig into tiny cracks too small to see.
Tree frogs have **sticky, bumpy toe pads** that help them grip wet leaves and glass.
Snails glide up walls on a layer of **slime**, leaving a shiny trail behind.
Woodpeckers grip tree trunks with **two toes forward and two toes back**, plus stiff tail feathers.

editor_notes: Fix the timeline. Have the brick CLICK between eras (Jurassic for Stegosaurus, Late Cretaceous for T. rex and Triceratops) so the trip never implies these animals lived side by side. That also turns the time travel into a shout-along beat for Juno ('CLICK! Next time!'). Change the fossil line to 'millions of years'.

Cut or replace the vague farmer's-dog tale with a genuine hedged legend, or drop it. Prune the repeated tics ('curious instead of...', 'grinning wide', 'smiling wide') and the duplicated 'full of strange shapes' sentence between Chs 4 and 5.

story.title: Milo, Juno and the Dinosaur Brick
story.subtitle: A WHOOOOSH back to the land before time

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Brick Glows Again
chapters.text:
Milo and Juno sat on the carpet. The big LEGO tower from last night stood tall. It still went CLICK and held tight.

Juno hugged his toy dinosaur. "I wish real dinosaurs were here," he said.

Then the red brick on top of the tower began to glow. It hummed like a sleepy bee.

"It's doing the thing again!" Milo said.

Juno poked it. CLICK! The brick lit up bright red.

WHOOOOSH! The room spun. The carpet turned into warm, squishy mud. Trees as tall as houses popped up around them.

"Whoa," Milo whispered. "Where are we?"

A deep voice rumbled. "You are a very, very long time ago."

Milo spun around. A big gray dinosaur with three horns stood smiling at them.

"I'm Terra," she said. "Dinosaurs like me started showing up about **230 million years ago**. That's so long ago, even your grandma's grandma's grandma wasn't born yet!"

Juno's eyes went wide. "That's SO many years."

"The very first dinosaurs were small," Terra said. "But some of us grew up big. Want to meet some?"

Milo grinned. "Yes! And can we see a shark dinosaur?"

Terra laughed, a sound like a trumpet. "No shark dinosaurs here. But I promise you'll love what we find."

She started walking, her big feet going THUMP, THUMP on the soft ground.

"Follow me," she said. "Play well, and watch your step!"

Juno giggled and ran after her, dinosaur toy still in his hand. Milo looked back at the glowing brick, now floating beside them like a little red moon, then ran to catch up.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Terra the Triceratops
chapters.text:
Terra stopped by a big rock. "Look at my face," she said. "What do you see?"

Juno counted. "One, two, three horns!"

"That's right," Terra said. "And see this big bony collar around my neck? We call it a **frill**. It's like a shield, to keep my neck safe."

Milo touched the frill gently. "It's so hard! Like a LEGO shield."

"Exactly," Terra said, pleased. "I use my horns and my frill to stay safe."

Juno gasped. "Does someone chase you?"

"Sometimes," Terra said calmly. "But I'm big and strong, and my horns do the job. No need to worry."

Milo thought for a second. "Could we build a frill out of LEGO bricks?"

Terra tilted her head. "What a good idea."

Milo pictured a wide curved plate, clicking onto a tiny LEGO dinosaur's neck. "We could make tiny horns too," he said. "Three of them, just like yours."

"Dinosaurs like me are called **Triceratops**," Terra said. "It basically means three-horned face."

Juno tried the word. "Try-SAIR-a-tops!"

"Close enough," Terra chuckled.

They walked on, Milo already planning his next LEGO build: a Triceratops with a snap-on frill. Juno marched behind, holding three fingers up to his own forehead like horns.

"Honk honk, I'm a dinosaur!" Juno yelled.

Terra laughed so hard her frill wobbled, and even the tall trees seemed to shake a little.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Giant Long-Neck
chapters.text:
THUD. THUD. THUD. The ground shook under their feet.

Juno grabbed Milo's hand. "Is it mad?"

Terra shook her head. "No, just big. Look up."

Milo tipped his head back, and back, and back. A dinosaur with a neck like a crane reached high into the trees.

"Whoa," Milo breathed. "That's the biggest thing I've ever seen."

"She might be the biggest dinosaur of all," Terra said. "Her kind is called **Argentinosaurus**. She could grow longer than **100 feet**."

Milo's jaw dropped. "That's SO long!"

Milo had an idea. "Let's measure her with our arms!"

He stretched his arms wide. Juno stretched his arms wide too. They stood end to end, trying to match the dinosaur's length.

"One Milo, two Milos, three Milos..." Juno counted, giggling.

They never got close to the end of her, and they both tumbled into the soft mud, laughing.

"Even sharks aren't that big," Milo said, thinking of his favorite ocean giants.

"Nothing swims this big," Terra said. "She eats leaves at the very top of the trees, where no one else can reach."

The giant dinosaur swung her long neck gently, like saying hello.

Juno waved both hands. "Hi, giant dinosaur!"

She blinked slowly, then kept munching leaves, not bothered one bit. A leaf fluttered down and landed right on Juno's head, and he laughed so hard he fell over again.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Terrible Lizard's Name
chapters.text:
A loud ROAR echoed through the trees. Juno jumped. "Who's that?"

Terra smiled. "Don't worry, he's full. That's just him saying hello."

A huge dinosaur stomped closer, his mouth full of enormous teeth.

Milo stared. "Those teeth are huge!"

"Each tooth is about **12 inches** long," Terra said. "That's as long as a ruler."

Juno hid behind Terra's leg, just for a second, then peeked back out. "Is he scary?"

"He looks scary," Terra said, "but right now he's just showing off his smile."

The big dinosaur opened his mouth wide, almost like a yawn, then flopped down in the mud with a SPLAT, perfectly happy.

Milo laughed with relief. "He's kind of silly."

"A scientist named **Richard Owen** looked at bones like these a long time ago," Terra said. "In **1842**, he made up a brand new word for animals like us: **dinosaur**. In an old language, it means 'terrible lizard.'"

Juno repeated it slowly. "Terrible lizard."

"That's a big name," Milo said, "for a guy who just naps in the mud."

"Names don't always tell the whole story," Terra chuckled.

Milo had an idea. "What if we gave him a nicer name? Like... Mud Muncher?"

The huge dinosaur let out a happy snort, as if he liked it just fine.

"Mud Muncher it is," Terra said.

Juno cheered. "MUD MUNCHER!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Sue and the Lucky Dog
chapters.text:
Terra led them to a dusty, rocky place. SCRITCH SCRITCH. Something was digging.

"Who's digging?" Juno asked.

"People called **paleontologists**," Terra said. "They dig up old bones to learn how dinosaurs lived."

Milo watched them brushing dirt off a huge bone. "Is that a real dinosaur?"

"It's what's left of one," Terra said. "Bones that turned hard like rock over a very long time. We call them **fossils**."

Juno touched the ground carefully. "Like a dinosaur puzzle!"

"Exactly," Terra said. "One of the biggest T. rex puzzles ever found got the nickname **Sue**. People found her bones in **South Dakota** in **1990**."

"Sue found a T. rex?" Milo asked, confused.

"No, Sue is the dinosaur's nickname," Terra laughed. "Some people tell a fun story that a farmer's dog once dug up part of a famous dinosaur bone. That part might be a little bit made-up, but it's a fun tale to tell."

Milo grinned. "I like that story anyway."

Juno knelt down and started digging in the soft dirt with his hands, very gently.

"Can I find a fossil too?" he asked.

"Dig carefully," Terra said, "and let's see."

Juno brushed away dirt, and underneath was a curved, hard shape.

"I FOUND ONE!" Juno shouted.

Terra leaned in close. "Well look at that. You found a piece of old dinosaur bone."

Milo clapped. "Juno the fossil finder!"

Juno held it up proudly, grinning from ear to ear, and tucked it carefully into his pocket.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Tiny Turkey Dinosaur
chapters.text:
Something small rustled in the bushes. Juno froze. "What's that?"

A little dinosaur popped out, about the size of Juno's toy chicken.

"That's a Velociraptor," Terra said.

Milo blinked. "Wait, that's it? In my movies they're huge!"

"Movies make them bigger," Terra said. "Really, they were only about the size of a **turkey**."

Juno laughed. "That's not scary at all!"

The little dinosaur hopped closer, covered in soft fluff.

"Feathers?" Milo asked, surprised. "On a dinosaur?"

"Lots of dinosaurs had **feathers**," Terra said, "just like this one."

Juno reached out a careful hand, not touching, just watching. "Can I say hi?"

"You can wave," Terra said. "Let's not touch. Wild animals like to be watched, not grabbed."

Juno waved both hands. "Hi, little feathery dinosaur!"

The small dinosaur tilted its head, then darted off into the bushes, quick as a cat.

Milo giggled. "He's fast for someone so small."

"Small and speedy," Terra agreed. "Not every dinosaur was a giant."

Juno sat back on his heels. "I like this one best. He's turkey-sized, like Thanksgiving!"

Milo laughed so hard he nearly fell over. "Turkey-saurus!"

Terra joined in laughing, her frill shaking, and even Juno did a wobbly little turkey gobble, flapping his elbows like wings.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Spiky Tails and Plates
chapters.text:
CLACK. CLACK. CLACK. A strange sound came from behind a rock.

Milo peeked around. "Whoa, look at those plates!"

A dinosaur with big bony plates down its back walked slowly by.

"That's Stegosaurus," Terra said. "The plates run along her back, and spikes stick out of her tail."

Juno counted the plates. "One, two, three, four..."

"She swings that spiky tail to stay safe," Terra said. "Scientists even gave the tail a silly name: a **thagomizer**. It just means the spiky part of her tail."

Milo tried the word. "Thag-oh-mizer. That's a funny word!"

Juno giggled. "Thagomizer, thagomizer!"

The Stegosaurus swished her tail gently, and CLACK CLACK, the spikes knocked together like wind chimes.

Juno covered his ears, laughing. "It's like music!"

Milo had an idea. "We should build one out of LEGO, with plates that click on like puzzle pieces."

"Snap-on plates," Terra said. "I like how you think."

The Stegosaurus walked on, swishing her tail, CLACK CLACK, like she was waving goodbye with it.

Juno waved back with his whole arm. "Bye bye, thagomizer tail!"

Milo waved too, already sketching the snap-on plates in his head, brick by brick.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Brave Beach Hunter
chapters.text:
They reached a sunny beach cliff. Waves crashed below. WHOOSH, SPLASH.

A girl with a little hammer tapped at the rocks. "Hi!" she said. "I'm Mary."

Milo looked closer. "Are you looking for dinosaurs?"

"Not quite," Mary said, smiling. "I look for old sea creatures that lived back when dinosaurs did. They turn into **fossils** too, but they're big swimming reptiles, not dinosaurs at all."

Juno frowned. "Not dinosaurs? But they're old and giant?"

"That's right," Terra said. "Animals called **plesiosaurs** and **mosasaurs** swam in the ocean while dinosaurs walked on land. They just weren't dinosaurs themselves."

Mary tapped gently, and a curved shape appeared in the rock. "There we go."

"Whoa!" Milo leaned in. "How do you know where to look?"

"Lots of practice," Mary said. "I've been doing this since I was your age. People who study old bones when they grow up are called **paleontologists**. I was one of the very first."

Juno clapped. "You're so brave!"

"Thank you," Mary said, brushing dirt from the fossil. "It takes patience, and a little bit of luck."

Milo picked up a small rock and tapped it like Mary, very gently. "Can I try?"

"Of course," Mary said. "Just be gentle, and careful with the rocks."

Juno tapped too, giggling with each little knock. "Tap tap tap!"

Nothing turned up for the boys that day, but they didn't mind one bit. They had a beach, a hammer, and a brave new friend.

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Dinosaurs Everywhere
chapters.text:
The sky began to turn orange. "It's almost time," Terra said.

Juno tugged her leg. "Do we have to go?"

"Not yet," Terra said. "One more thing first."

She led them to a quiet hill. "A very, very long time after the first dinosaurs, about **66 million years** later, something big changed on Earth. Most dinosaurs disappeared, all around the same time."

Juno's lip wobbled. "All of them? Forever?"

"Not quite all," Terra said gently. "Some small, feathery dinosaurs lived on. Over a very long time, they turned into something you know very well."

Milo thought hard. "Birds?"

"Birds," Terra said, smiling. "Every bird you've ever seen is a tiny bit dinosaur. So really, dinosaurs never totally left."

Juno looked up, and right then, a bird flew overhead, chirping.

"Hi, dinosaur bird!" Juno yelled, waving both arms.

Milo grinned. "That's so cool. Dinosaurs are still everywhere."

"Everywhere you look," Terra agreed.

The red brick floated closer, glowing warm and bright.

"Time to go home," Terra said. "Play well, you two."

Milo hugged her leg. "Bye, Terra! Thank you!"

Juno waved his little fossil bone. "Bye bye, Mud Muncher! Bye, turkey dinosaur!"

WHOOOOSH! The mud and trees spun away into warm, swirly light.

chapters.heading: Chapter 10: Back on the Carpet
chapters.text:
THUMP. They landed back on the soft carpet.

The LEGO tower stood right where they left it, still clicking tight.

Juno looked down at his hand. He was still holding the little fossil bone from the beach.

"Whoa," Milo whispered. "Juno, you brought something back!"

Juno turned it over, and over. "My very own dinosaur treasure."

Milo looked at his own hands, and an idea popped into his head. "Let's build a LEGO Triceratops. With a snap-on frill, just like Terra's."

Juno nodded hard. "And a thagomizer tail!"

They grabbed bricks and started clicking pieces together, right there on the carpet floor. CLICK. CLICK. CLICK.

The red brick on top of the tower glowed one last soft time, then went dark and still, waiting for the next adventure.

Milo yawned, holding up his half-built dinosaur. Juno yawned right back, still gripping his little fossil bone tight.

Outside the window, the moon was already up, round and quiet, like it had been watching the whole time.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Milo. Goodnight, Juno. Play well.

true_facts.text: The very first dinosaurs lived about **230 million years ago**.
A Triceratops has **three horns** and a big bony collar called a **frill**.
Argentinosaurus might have grown longer than **100 feet** — that's really, really long!
A scientist named **Richard Owen** made up the word **dinosaur** in **1842**. It means 'terrible lizard.'
A T. rex tooth could be **12 inches** long, as long as a ruler.
One famous T. rex skeleton is nicknamed **Sue**, found in **South Dakota** in **1990**.
A story says a farmer's dog once dug up a dinosaur bone, but that part might be made up.
A Velociraptor was really only about the size of a **turkey**, not a giant like in movies.
Lots of dinosaurs, like Velociraptor, had soft **feathers**.
A Stegosaurus had bony plates on its back and a spiky tail called a **thagomizer**.
Old dinosaur bones that turned hard like rock are called **fossils**.
Big swimming reptiles called **plesiosaurs** and **mosasaurs** lived in the ocean at the same time as dinosaurs, but weren't dinosaurs themselves.
Birds today are related to dinosaurs, so dinosaurs never totally disappeared.
Most dinosaurs disappeared about **66 million years** after they first showed up.
