story.title: Sam and the Gecko Who Could Climb Anything
story.subtitle: A sticky-footed trip up walls, glass, and one very steep mountain.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Glowing Gecko
chapters.text:
Sam lay on his bedroom floor. He held his rubber spider tight. It was way past bedtime.

On the shelf sat a little toy gecko. Sam had named him Gordon. Gordon never did anything.

Tonight, Gordon's eyes turned bright green. CLICK! His tiny feet twitched.

"Whoa," Sam whispered.

Gordon hopped down. He felt warm in Sam's hand. "Hello, Sam," he said. "Want to see how real geckos climb?"

Sam grinned. "Yes! Spiders and geckos are my favorites!"

A tiny green door opened in the wall. "Climb through," said Gordon.

They squeezed through. Suddenly everything was huge. The glass wall in front of them looked like a cliff.

A real gecko zoomed straight up it. No slipping. No sliding.

"How does he do that?" Sam asked. "He's not even falling!"

"Look close," said Gordon. He pointed at the gecko's toes.

Sam looked hard. He saw rows and rows of tiny lines, like little brushes.

"Those are hairs," said Gordon. "Millions of tiny hairs on every toe."

"Millions?!" Sam's eyes went wide.

"That many," said Gordon. "That's why he can run up glass. He can even walk upside down on a ceiling."

Sam touched the glass himself. His hand just slid off.

"No fair," he laughed.

"You don't have gecko feet," said Gordon, chuckling. "But stick around. There's more."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: No Glue, No Mess
chapters.text:
Sam looked at his own fingers. Once he touched tape. It stayed sticky and gross for hours.

"Does the gecko have glue feet?" Sam asked.

Gordon shook his tiny head. "No glue at all. Watch."

The gecko lifted one toe off the glass. Then another. Peel, peel, peel. Like pulling up tape, but clean.

"No mess!" said Sam. "His feet don't get yucky!"

"Exactly," said Gordon. "It's not glue. It's those tiny hairs again."

"Then how do they stick?" Sam asked.

"They get so close to the glass," said Gordon, "that something invisible grabs on. Too small to see. Even smaller than the hairs. We call those tiny bits molecules."

Sam squinted at the glass. "I still can't see them."

"Nobody can," said Gordon. "But each one holds on just a little. Millions of them together hold on a lot."

Sam thought about that. "So it's like... everybody pushes together?"

Gordon's whole face lit up. "That's it, Sam! Like a hundred hands. Each one holds a little. Together, they hold a lot."

The gecko flicked one foot. He skittered sideways, quick as a blink.

"And when he wants to stop sticking," said Gordon, "he just peels his toes up. One at a time. No glue to scrub off."

Sam clapped his hands. "I want sticky feet like that!"

"Maybe one day," laughed Gordon. "Humans copied this trick. I'll show you later."

Sam's eyes went wide. "Humans copied gecko feet?!"

"Later," said Gordon. "First, somebody else is waiting. Somebody with eight legs."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Spider's Secret
chapters.text:
A new door opened onto a garden wall. A fat, friendly spider sat right in the middle of it.

Sam gasped. "A spider! I love spiders!"

"This one climbs glass too," said Gordon. "Go on. Ask her how."

Sam leaned close, careful not to touch. "How do you climb straight up?" he asked.

The spider waved one leg. Gordon smiled. "She says: look at my feet."

Sam looked closely. Each tiny foot had rows of hairs. Just like the gecko's. Only even smaller.

"Spiders have their own tiny hairs too!" Sam said. "Thousands on every foot!"

"That's right," said Gordon. "That's why so many spiders can run up smooth glass windows."

The spider scuttled sideways, straight up the wall. She didn't wobble once.

Sam clapped. "Go, spider, go!"

The spider paused at the top. She waved one leg down at him, like a little hello.

Sam waved back, grinning ear to ear. "You pick up every bug in your own garden at home," said Gordon. "Next time, look at their feet too."

"I will," said Sam. "I bet ants have secrets too."

Gordon grinned. "Good guess. Let's go find out."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Buzzy Fly
chapters.text:
Buzzzzz! A fat fly landed on a window.

"Watch this one," said Gordon. "Totally different trick."

The fly's feet looked wet and shiny. Sam leaned in close. "Is he sticky too?"

"Sort of," said Gordon. "His feet ooze out tiny drops. Like little glue drops. Flies do this. So do some beetles."

"Goo!" Sam giggled. "Like when I eat jam and get it everywhere."

"A little like that," laughed Gordon. "Except his goo stays right on his own feet. It helps him stick to glass. Even to your ceiling."

The fly buzzed off the glass. He looped in the air. Then — SPLAT! He landed again, feet first.

Sam burst out laughing.

"He's fine," said Gordon quickly. "Flies land like that all the time. It's just how they fly."

Sam pressed close to the glass, but not too close. "His feet are so small. How does goo even fit?"

"Tiny pads," said Gordon. "Built just for this one job."

Sam nodded, very serious. "Spiders have hairs. Geckos have hairs. Flies have goo. Everybody's got their own trick."

"Everybody," agreed Gordon. "Come see the ones with claws."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Sneakers and Slippers
chapters.text:
Next, Gordon led Sam to a crack in an old brick wall. An ant marched straight up it.

"Ants use two different tricks," said Gordon. "Watch what she does."

The ant dug in with tiny claws. Scritch, scritch, scritch, up the rough bricks she went.

Then she reached smooth glass at the top. Her claws stopped working there. She switched to sticky pads instead. She kept right on climbing.

Sam's mouth fell open. "She changed her shoes!"

Gordon laughed so hard his tail wiggled. "Sort of! Rough wall, sharp claws. Smooth wall, sticky pads. Ants do this. Cockroaches do this too."

"That's so smart," said Sam. "Like wearing sneakers AND slippers."

"Exactly like that," said Gordon.

The ant reached the very top. She gave a tiny wave with one leg, like she knew Sam was watching.

Sam waved back. "Good job, ant!"

"Ready for more climbers?" asked Gordon. "These ones live on a mountain."

Sam bounced on his toes. "A mountain! Let's go!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Goats and Squirrels
chapters.text:
The next door opened onto a rocky mountain, cold and windy.

A mountain goat stood on a cliff. It looked much too steep. Sam held his breath. "Is he going to fall?"

"Nope," said Gordon right away. "Watch his feet."

The goat's hooves had a hard rim on the outside. Inside was something softer. It squished around every little bump in the rock.

"His feet are hard outside, soft inside," said Sam. "Like a sneaker with a squishy middle!"

"Just like that," said Gordon.

The goat hopped from rock to rock. He never slipped, not once.

Then a squirrel zipped past them. Straight up a tree trunk.

"What about him?" Sam asked.

"Claws," said Gordon. "Sharp, curved claws. He digs them into tiny cracks. Cracks you and I can't even see."

Sam searched the tree trunk hard. He couldn't spot a single crack. "They must be really, really tiny."

"Tinier than tiny," said Gordon. "But his claws find them anyway."

The squirrel reached the top branch. He chattered loudly, like he was showing off.

Sam laughed and clapped. "Show-off squirrel!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Rain and Slime
chapters.text:
Next stop: a rainy garden, dark and damp.

A little green tree frog sat on a wet leaf. Then he hopped onto a window and stuck there.

"His feet are wet," said Sam. "Won't that make him slip?"

"Should," said Gordon. "But look closer."

Sam looked hard. The frog's toe pads were flat. They had tiny little shapes on them, like a honeycomb.

"Those special pads grip even wet, slippery places," said Gordon. "Wet leaves. Wet glass. No problem at all."

"Cool," breathed Sam.

Down on the ground, a snail glided up the very same window. Slow and steady.

"No hairs. No claws. No sticky pads," said Gordon. "Just slime."

Sam watched the shiny trail behind it. "He's climbing on slime?"

"His whole foot ripples underneath him," said Gordon. "Little waves, over and over. It's slow. But it always works."

"Slow and slimy wins the race," Sam giggled.

"Something like that," laughed Gordon.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Gecko Glove
chapters.text:
"Now," said Gordon, "remember how I said humans copied gecko feet?"

Sam bounced on his toes. "Yes! Show me!"

A new door opened onto a sunny room full of scientists. One of them pressed two small paddles against a tall glass wall. Sam spotted the same pattern from the gecko's toes.

"In **2014**, scientists built paddles just like this," said Gordon. "A whole person climbed a glass wall holding these."

Sam's jaw dropped. "A whole person?! Climbing glass?!"

"A whole person," said Gordon. "No ropes. Just a gecko trick."

The scientist reached the top of the wall. He waved down, grinning.

"People studied gecko feet," said Gordon. "They made new sticky tape. They even made gloves for climbing."

Sam grinned wide. "Geckos are basically inventors."

"Basically," Gordon agreed, laughing.

Then the little green door glowed bright. Sam felt himself grow big again. He blinked, and he was back on his bedroom floor. His rubber spider was still in his hand.

Gordon sat still on the shelf once more, just a toy again. But one eye glinted green, quick as a wink.

On the carpet beside Sam lay something small and shiny. A tiny gecko-foot sticker, like it had traveled home with him.

Sam smiled and held it tight. Tomorrow, he would show it to every bug in the garden.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Sam. Climb well.

true_facts.text: **Geckos** can run straight up glass because their toes have millions of tiny hairs.
A gecko's sticky feet aren't glue — tiny hairs get so close to the glass that **invisible little bits called molecules** hold on, just a little each.
A gecko peels its toes up one at a time, **like pulling up tape**, so its feet never get messy.
Some **flies and beetles** have feet that ooze tiny sticky drops, like little glue drops.
**Spiders** have thousands of tiny hairs on their feet too, which is why many can climb smooth glass.
**Ants** use sharp claws on rough walls and switch to sticky pads on smooth ones, like swapping sneakers for slippers.
**Mountain goats** have hooves with a hard rim outside and a soft, squishy part inside that grips the rock.
**Squirrels** dig sharp, curved claws into tiny cracks in tree bark that are too small for us to see.
**Tree frogs** have flat toe pads with tiny honeycomb patterns that help them stick to wet leaves and glass.
**Snails** climb smooth walls by gliding on a layer of slime, rippling their foot in little waves.
In **2014**, scientists built sticky paddles copied from gecko feet, and a whole person used them to climb a glass wall.

story.title: Finn, Nell, and the Golden Honey Bee
story.subtitle: A hummy, buzzy bedtime trip inside a honey jar.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Jar That Hummed
chapters.text:
Finn sat on his bedroom floor with his honey jar. He had eaten honey toast for supper. Only a little honey was left, stuck to the glass in golden swirls.

Nell sat beside him. She held a yellow flower she had drawn that day. It had five fat, round petals.

The jar began to hum. It glowed soft and gold, like a tiny sunset trapped in glass.

"Finn," whispered Nell. "The jar is singing."

Finn turned the lid. Just a tiny bit. CLICK.

Out popped a bee made of light. He buzzed in a happy circle. His wings sounded like a kazoo.

"Hello, friends," said the bee. "My name is Buzz."

Finn giggled. "You sound funny!"

Buzz landed right on Finn's nose. It tickled. Finn scrunched his face and sneezed a tiny sneeze.

"Want to see how bees make honey?" asked Buzz.

Nell nodded so fast her hair flopped over her eyes. "Yes, yes, YES!"

Buzz sprinkled gold dust over them both. The room spun like a merry-go-round, slow at first, then fast.

When it stopped spinning, Finn and Nell were tiny. Tiny as bees. They stood on a giant green leaf, wind tickling their hair, a whole meadow stretching out before them.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Flower With a Straw
chapters.text:
Buzz led them to a giant yellow flower, taller than Finn's whole bed. Nell gasped. Yellow was her favorite color in the whole wide world.

"This sweet juice inside is called nectar," said Buzz, pointing at a shiny drop. "Nectar means the sugary drink flowers make."

Nell touched a petal very softly. She did not pick it. Flowers like to stay on their stems, she remembered.

"Bees drink nectar with a long, bendy tongue," said Buzz. "It curls up like a party streamer."

Finn tried sipping pretend nectar through pretend straw lips. SLURP! He giggled so hard he nearly fell off the leaf.

A real bee landed nearby and unrolled her long tongue. She sipped the nectar right up.

"WOW!" said Finn. "Her tongue is longer than her whole body!"

"Almost," laughed Buzz. "Bees also carry yellow dust on their fuzzy legs. It's called pollen, and flowers trade it to grow new flowers."

Nell clapped both hands. "Flowers get babies from bees!"

"Kind of," said Buzz, smiling.

Finn noticed something wobbly on the bee's belly. "Does she swallow all that nectar?"

"Not exactly," said Buzz. "Follow me. I'll show you her secret tummy."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Secret Tummy
chapters.text:
They zoomed above the meadow to a cluster of busy bees. Buzz hovered close beside one, round and full.

"Bees have two tummies," said Buzz. "One is for eating. One is just for carrying nectar home."

Finn patted his own belly. "I only have one tummy. For toast."

"This special one is called a honey stomach," said Buzz. "It's like a little backpack inside her, just for nectar."

Nell tilted her head, thinking hard. "So she doesn't eat it on the way home?"

"Exactly," said Buzz. "She saves it, like you save the best bite of toast for last."

Finn grinned so wide his eyes nearly closed. "I always save my honey corner!"

"I knew you were a honey-saving expert," said Buzz, winking.

A bee zoomed past them, her tummy round and full. "She's heading home now," said Buzz. "Let's follow and see what happens next."

Finn grabbed Nell's hand. "Race you!"

They flapped their little arms and zoomed after the bee, laughing the whole way, wind whooshing past their ears.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Pass It Along
chapters.text:
They landed inside a warm, buzzing hive. Bees bustled everywhere, busy as can be.

The nectar bee met another bee right at the door. She opened her mouth. The other bee opened hers too. They passed the nectar, mouth to mouth.

"Ew!" said Finn, then burst out giggling. "That's silly!"

"It's actually clever," said Buzz. "Each time it's passed along, a little bee spit mixes in. That spit starts turning the watery nectar into thick, sweet honey."

Nell thought about this for a second. "Like a magic trick?"

"Kind of like magic," said Buzz, nodding.

Finn wanted to try it himself. He picked up a flower petal and pretended to pass it, mouth to mouth with Nell.

"Blech!" Nell squealed, laughing so hard she snorted.

"Maybe try hand to hand instead," said Buzz, chuckling. "Much less slobbery."

They passed the petal down a whole line of pretend bees, laughing harder with every single handoff. Finn even made a silly bee buzzing voice.

"Now," said Buzz, "let's see where all that nectar finally goes."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Six-Sided Rooms
chapters.text:
Buzz led them deeper into the hive. Tiny walls stretched everywhere, forming hundreds of little rooms.

"This is honeycomb," said Buzz. "Bees build it from wax made in their own bodies. Wax is soft and smooth, like a candle, but bees make it themselves."

Finn pressed one finger against a wall. It felt smooth and a little bit sticky.

"Count the sides with me," said Buzz.

Finn pointed at each wall slowly. "One, two, three, four, five, six!"

"SIX SIDES!" he shouted, bouncing on his tiptoes.

Nell counted too, her finger wobbling with excitement. "Six! My flower only had five petals. This has one more!"

"Six-sided rooms fit together perfectly," said Buzz. "No wasted space at all, like puzzle pieces snapping together."

Bees poured the passed-along nectar straight into these tiny rooms, filling them up like little golden cups.

Finn watched, amazed. "It's like tiny treasure cups!"

"Almost treasure," said Buzz. "But it's not honey yet. It's still thin and watery. Watch what happens next."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Wiggle Those Wings
chapters.text:
Rows of bees lined up beside the wet, shiny cups. All at once, they began to flap their wings. FAST.

"Why are they flapping so hard?" asked Nell, covering her ears just a little.

"They're fanning the nectar," said Buzz. "Flapping wings make a breeze. The breeze dries out the watery part."

Finn flapped his own arms like crazy. WHOOSH! WHOOSH! "Like a tiny fan!"

"A bee's wings flap about two hundred times every single second," said Buzz. "That's what makes their buzzy sound."

Nell flapped too, laughing wildly. "I want to buzz like that!"

She tried her very best, but only made a little hum. Finn laughed so hard he snorted, just like Nell had earlier.

"You sound like a sleepy bumblebee!" he teased, gently, the way sisters and brothers do.

Slowly, the wet nectar turned thicker. Stickier. Glossier. Gold, like Nell's favorite crayon.

"It's turning into honey!" Finn cheered, pointing at the glossy little cups.

"Almost," said Buzz. "One more step to go."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Wax Lid
chapters.text:
When the honey was finally thick and perfect, a bee walked over. She pressed a thin wax lid over the top of the cup, sealing it shut.

"That keeps it clean and safe," said Buzz. "Just like closing a jar."

Finn perked right up. "Like MY honey jar!" He mimed twisting a lid shut, just like he had done at home.

"Exactly like that," said Buzz, smiling warmly.

"Why save so much honey?" asked Nell, gently touching a sealed golden cup.

"For winter," said Buzz. "When flowers stop blooming, there's nothing sweet left to find. So bees eat the honey they saved up all summer."

Finn thought about his own snack drawer at home. "That's smart! Like saving cookies for later."

Nell nodded firmly. "Saving is smart."

Buzz landed on Finn's nose again. Tickle, tickle. Finn giggled and swatted gently at the air.

"Ready to meet the rest of the family?" asked Buzz, buzzing off his nose at last.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Busy Bee Family
chapters.text:
Buzz led them to the very center of the hive. One enormous bee sat there, calm and round.

"This is the queen," said Buzz. "She lays eggs. Sometimes over a thousand in a single day!"

Finn's mouth dropped wide open. "A THOUSAND? That's more than my whole toy box!"

"She's the busy mom of almost every bee here," said Buzz.

Nell looked around at all the bees zooming past. "How many bees even live here?"

"In summer, a hive can hold twenty thousand to sixty thousand bees," said Buzz.

Finn tried counting on his fingers and gave up fast, laughing. "That's SO many!"

"Most of them are girl bees," said Buzz. "Worker bees do every job. Flying for nectar, building rooms, making honey, guarding the door."

Nell puffed up proudly, hands on her hips. "Girls doing everything? I love that!"

"They sure do," laughed Buzz. "Come on, I'll show you how new flower patches get found."

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: The Wiggle Dance
chapters.text:
Outside the hive, one bee was dancing. She wiggled side to side, then looped in a figure eight.

"That's a scout bee," said Buzz. "She found yummy flowers far away."

"Why is she wiggling?" asked Nell, wiggling her own hips to copy.

"Her wiggle dance tells other bees which direction to fly, and how far," said Buzz.

Finn tried the dance too, wobbling and giggling. "Am I doing it right?"

"Close enough for a bedtime bee!" laughed Buzz. "Here's something wild. It takes about twelve bees their whole lives just to make one teaspoon of honey."

Finn gasped. "ONE TEASPOON? That's all I put on my toast!"

"All that work, for one little spoonful," said Buzz. "But that honey lasts a very long time. If it stays sealed up, honey never truly spoils. Not ever."

Nell's eyes went wide. "Never ever?"

"Never ever," said Buzz. "Some honey has stayed yummy for years and years and years."

Finn and Nell looked at each other, both thinking the exact same thing: honey was pretty amazing.

chapters.heading: Chapter 10: Back on the Bedroom Floor
chapters.text:
Buzz flew them gently out of the hive, back toward the big green leaf. "One more stop," he said, "before bedtime."

They landed beside a wooden box in a quiet garden. A kind keeper in a big hat lifted a honeycomb frame, careful and slow.

"That's a beekeeper," said Buzz. "She takes a little honey, gently, and always leaves plenty behind for the bees."

Finn waved at her from far away. Nell waved too, careful to stay back and not get too close.

The gold dust sparkled again, swirling around them. The world spun, slow then fast, just like before.

When it stopped, Finn and Nell were back on their bedroom floor. Their own size again. The honey jar sat quiet, lid back in its place.

But right beside it sat something new: one tiny golden honeycomb charm, no bigger than a button.

"A present," buzzed Buzz softly, "to remember tonight."

Finn held it carefully in his palm. Nell touched its tiny six sides with one gentle finger.

"Goodnight, Buzz," whispered Nell.

The little light blinked once, and faded. Finn yawned a big, sleepy yawn. He set the honeycomb charm on his windowsill, right next to Nell's yellow flower drawing.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Finn. Goodnight, Nell. Bee sweet dreams.

true_facts.text: Bees drink sweet flower juice called **nectar** with a long, curly tongue.
Bees carry yellow dust called **pollen** on their legs, helping flowers make new flowers.
Bees have a special **honey stomach**, just for carrying nectar home, separate from their eating tummy.
Bees pass nectar **mouth to mouth**, and bee spit helps turn it into honey.
The spit mixed in while passing nectar helps turn it from watery to sweet honey.
Bees store nectar in **six-sided rooms** called honeycomb.
Bees make the **wax** for honeycomb right out of their own bodies.
Bees flap their wings fast to dry the nectar into thick, sticky honey.
A bee's wings flap about **two hundred times every second**, making their buzzy sound.
Once honey is ready, bees seal it with a thin **wax lid** to keep it safe.
Bees save up honey so they have food in **winter**, when flowers stop blooming.
A hive can have **twenty thousand to sixty thousand bees** living together in summer.
The **queen bee** lays eggs, sometimes over a **thousand in one day**.
A scout bee does a **wiggle dance** to tell other bees where to find flowers.

new_recurring.name: Buzz the Honey Bee
new_recurring.rule: A tiny glowing bee who appears whenever the honey jar hums and glows, guides the children on honey-and-hive adventures, lands ticklishly on noses for a laugh, and says 'Bee sweet dreams' at the end of each visit.

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Finn and Nell returned to their bedroom floor the same size as always, finding a tiny golden honeycomb charm left beside the honey jar, which Finn set on the windowsill next to Nell's yellow flower drawing.

story.title: Omar and the Wheel That Remembered
story.subtitle: A bedtime ride through two hundred years of bikes

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Running Machine (1817)
chapters.text:
Omar lay on his bedroom floor, BMX flipped upside down, spinning the front wheel with one finger. He was timing how long it could spin before stopping, like the pros did at the skate park.

The wheel spun. And spun. It did not stop. It turned bright green and started to hum.

"Okay," Omar said. "That is not normal."

A tiny voice came from the middle of the wheel. "Normal is boring," it said. A glowing light popped out and became a little spinning wheel with a face. "I'm Spoke. I remember every bike there ever was. Want a ride?"

Before Omar could answer, the floor tipped like a ramp. **WHOOOOSH** — he slid down a tunnel made of spinning wheels.

He landed with a thud on a dusty street. A tall man was pushing a wooden two-wheeler along with his feet, steering it with handlebars just like Omar's bike.

"No pedals?" Omar asked.

"Pedals aren't invented yet," said Spoke. "This is **Karl von Drais**, a German inventor. In **1817** he built the very first two-wheeled riding machine. People called it the running machine, because you ran to make it go."

Omar grinned. "So it's basically a giant balance bike."

"Exactly like one," said Spoke.

Omar hopped on, pushed off with both feet, and wobbled down the street. "I GET IT NOW!" he yelled, feet pedaling air like it was a scooter.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Boneshaker (1860s)
chapters.text:
Spoke spun them forward fifty years. The ground turned to bumpy cobblestones, rattling like a drum.

Omar's teeth buzzed. "Why does everything shake?"

"Because somebody finally bolted pedals straight onto the front wheel," said Spoke. "French builders named **Pierre Michaux** and **Pierre Lallement** made it in the **1860s**. People called it the boneshaker, because the bumpy ride rattled your bones."

A rider pedaled past, bouncing with every bump like he was riding a jackhammer.

"That looks like doing a trick by accident," Omar said.

"Lallement liked his design so much," said Spoke, "he got it officially registered in America in **1866**."

Omar tried a lap himself, feet on the pedals, and nearly bit his tongue on a bump. "OW! Okay — boneshaker is a GREAT name."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Penny-Farthing (1870s)
chapters.text:
The next bike had a front wheel taller than Omar's dad.

"Whoa," Omar said, craning his neck. "That's not a bike. That's a unicycle wearing stilts."

"It's called a **penny-farthing**," said Spoke. "Named after two old coins — one huge, one tiny — because the front wheel is giant and the back wheel is small."

"Why so big?" Omar asked.

"One turn of the pedals rolls you way farther," said Spoke. "Riders went fast. But sitting up that high..."

A rider wobbled, stopped short, and tipped right over his handlebars, landing safely in a soft pile of hay.

Omar winced, then laughed. "Did he just faceplant off a bike?"

"They called that 'taking a header,'" said Spoke. "It happened a lot."

Omar studied the wobbling wheel of another rider nearby. "I bet I could've called that fall before it happened. Look how it's shaking."

"You've got a rider's eye," said Spoke, impressed.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Safety Bicycle (1885)
chapters.text:
The next bike had two wheels the exact same size, and something new — a loop of metal links connecting the pedals to the back wheel.

"That's a chain," Omar said. "Like on my BMX!"

"Good eye," said Spoke. "An Englishman named **John Kemp Starley** built this in **1885**. He called it the Rover Safety Bicycle. Even wheels, a chain to the back wheel — the first bike that really looked like yours."

Omar hopped on and pedaled a smooth circle. "No giant wheel. No header. This is way less scary."

"That's why they called it 'safety,'" said Spoke. "Soon everyone wanted one."

Omar did a little skid stop, sneakers squeaking on the dirt. "Future bikes, please keep the chain."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Squishy Tire (1888)
chapters.text:
Omar's teeth rattled again on hard, solid rubber tires.

"We need the boneshaker fixed for real," he said.

"Coming right up," said Spoke, and the tunnel rolled them into a workshop that smelled like rubber glue.

A man was wrapping a rubber tube around a small tricycle wheel and pumping it full of air.

"That's **John Boyd Dunlop**," said Spoke. "He was a vet from Scotland. In **1888** he built the first good air-filled tire, so his son could ride his tricycle without bumping so hard."

Omar poked the tire. It squished under his finger like a pool float. "That's SO much softer!"

"Dunlop's company is still making tires today," said Spoke. "You've probably seen the name."

Omar thought of the tires on his own bike. "Dunlop. I KNEW that name!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Golden Age (1890s)
chapters.text:
Suddenly the street was packed with bikes, bells ringing everywhere.

"Welcome to the **1890s**," said Spoke. "People called it the Golden Age of Bicycles. Millions of bikes were sold all across Europe and America."

A woman zoomed past wearing puffy pants instead of a long skirt.

"Those pants are cool," Omar said.

"Long skirts used to get caught in the gears," said Spoke. "So the bike craze made baggier pants, called bloomers, popular instead. Bikes also let women travel on their own for the very first time. A famous woman named **Susan B. Anthony** said bikes helped women more than almost anything else in the world."

Omar watched the woman ride off, fast and free. "That's a way bigger deal than just a bike trick."

"Biggest trick of all," said Spoke. "Freedom."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Bike Shop That Learned to Fly (1890s–1903)
chapters.text:
The next stop smelled like oil and metal shavings.

Two brothers were fixing a wheel, spokes gleaming in the sun.

"In **Dayton, Ohio**, in the 1890s," said Spoke, "these two ran a bicycle repair shop. Their names were **Wilbur and Orville Wright**."

Omar blinked. "Wait — the airplane guys?"

"The very same," said Spoke. "They used tricks from building bikes — light metal tubes, spoked wheels — to help build the world's first successful airplane, in **1903**."

Omar picked up a spare spoke, turning it in the light. "So a bike shop invented flying."

"Started with wheels," said Spoke. "Ended up in the sky."

Omar grinned. "Bikes can basically take you anywhere."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Back to the Dirt (1970s to Now)
chapters.text:
The tunnel of wheels spun once more, and Omar landed somewhere that felt like home — a dirt track full of jumps and bumps.

"Now we're talking," Omar said, spotting kids riding small, tough bikes over the jumps.

"**BMX bikes** showed up in the United States in the **1970s**," said Spoke, "copying the dirt bikes used in motorcycle racing. Around the same time, riders out in California built **mountain bikes** with wide, bumpy tires for rough trails."

Omar watched a rider land a jump clean. "That's basically my bike."

"Exactly your bike," said Spoke. "Today there are more than a **billion bikes** in the whole world — more than any other way to get around. In places like the **Netherlands** and **Denmark**, some cities have more bikes than cars."

Omar fist-pumped the air. "Bikes basically won."

The wheel glowed bright green, and the ramp tilted up, up, up — back toward his bedroom floor.

Omar landed with a soft thump on his own carpet. His BMX wheel was spinning slow now, back to plain old silver, its tiny glow fading into the spokes.

He patted the seat. "Thanks for the ride, Spoke."

A tiny whisper came from the wheel. "Anytime, Omar. Ride safe."

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Omar. Ride safe, and dream of wheels.

true_facts.text: In **1817**, a German inventor named **Karl von Drais** built the first two-wheeled riding machine, pushed along with your feet because it had no pedals.
In the **1860s**, French builders **Pierre Michaux** and **Pierre Lallement** bolted pedals onto the front wheel, making the bumpy "boneshaker."
The **penny-farthing** had a giant front wheel and a tiny back wheel, so one turn of the pedals rolled you much farther.
The penny-farthing got its name from two old coins of very different sizes.
Falling off a penny-farthing headfirst was nicknamed "taking a header."
In **1885**, **John Kemp Starley** built the Rover Safety Bicycle, with two same-size wheels and a chain, much safer to ride.
In **1888**, **John Boyd Dunlop**, a Scottish vet, built the first good air-filled tire for his son's tricycle, making rides much smoother.
In the **1890s**, bikes gave women new freedom to travel on their own, and **Susan B. Anthony** said bikes helped women more than almost anything else in the world.
Because long skirts could get caught in bike gears, the bike craze helped make baggier pants called bloomers popular.
**Wilbur and Orville Wright** ran a bicycle repair shop in **Dayton, Ohio** in the 1890s.
The Wright brothers used bike-building tricks, like light metal tubes and spoked wheels, to help build the first successful airplane in **1903**.
**BMX bikes** became popular in the United States in the **1970s**, copying dirt motorcycles.
Today there are more than a **billion bikes** in the whole world, more than any other kind of vehicle.
In places like the **Netherlands** and **Denmark**, some cities today have more bikes than cars.

story.title: Ada and Bolt the Magnet Robot
story.subtitle: A sleepy trip into the invisible pull of magnets.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Glowing Letters
chapters.text:
Ada should have been asleep hours ago.

She tiptoed to the kitchen in her robot pajamas. The fridge magnets were still out from dinner. She liked lining the letters into silly words.

Tonight the letter B started to glow. It went WHIRRR. It popped off the fridge. Little arms and legs popped out too.

"Hiya," it said. "I'm Bolt."

Ada blinked. "Are you a magnet robot?"

"Yep," said Bolt. "Every magnet has two ends. We call them **poles**. One end is north. One end is south."

Bolt turned his north end toward an old letter magnet. CLICK! It snapped on tight.

"**Opposite poles pull together**," Bolt said. Then he flipped around. Two north ends shoved apart like grumpy twins.

"**Same poles push away**," he said.

Ada giggled. "That's like me and my pillow fight."

"Exactly," said Bolt. "Want to see more?"

Ada grabbed her slippers. "Always."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Tiny Teams Inside Metal
chapters.text:
Bolt hopped onto the fridge door and stuck there, humming happily.

"Why do you stick to the fridge," Ada asked, "but not to my wooden spoon?"

"Good question," said Bolt. "Metal like iron has tiny teams inside it. We call them **domains**. Think of them like little arrows."

"When all the arrows point the same way," Bolt said, "the metal turns magnetic. That's why I stick here."

Ada tapped her wooden spoon against the fridge. Nothing happened. Not even a wobble.

"Wood's little arrows all point different ways," said Bolt. "All mixed up, like a messy sock drawer. So wood never turns magnetic."

Ada tried her spoon, her hairbrush, and a plastic cup. None of them stuck.

"None of your sock-drawer arrows line up either," Bolt laughed.

Ada tapped her own arm. "Lucky for me."

Bolt nodded. "Very lucky. Magnet kids would be stuck to everything."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Invisible Hug
chapters.text:
"Can I see the pulling part?" Ada asked. "The part I can't see?"

Bolt grinned. "That's the **magnetic field**. It's the invisible space around a magnet where the pulling and pushing happens."

Ada dug tiny metal shavings from her craft drawer and sprinkled them near Bolt.

The shavings jumped and curled into swooping lines, looping from Bolt's north end to his south end.

"WHOA," Ada whispered. "They made loopy roads!"

"That's the shape of my pull," said Bolt. "You can't see it. But the little bits of metal can show you where it is."

Ada traced one curved line with her finger, careful not to touch the shavings.

"It's like you're wearing an invisible hug," she said.

"Best way anyone's ever put it," Bolt said, puffing up proudly.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Rock That Started It
chapters.text:
Bolt spun in a circle. ZAP! The kitchen melted into warm sunshine and dusty hills.

"Where are we?" Ada whispered.

"Long, long ago," said Bolt, "near a place called Magnesia."

A shepherd nearby gasped as his iron walking stick stuck to a plain black rock on the ground.

"That's a **lodestone**," said Bolt. "A rock that's magnetic all by itself. Finding this rock is how people first learned about magnets."

"Is that where the word magnet comes from?" Ada asked.

"Probably," said Bolt. "Nobody's totally sure, but it's a good guess."

ZAP again, and they landed somewhere else sunny and busy.

"People here used lodestones to make the very first **compasses**," Bolt said. "More than two thousand years ago. A compass is a tool that always points the same way, so travelers never got lost."

Ada spun in place like a human compass needle. "Does it always point this way?"

"Funny you ask," said Bolt. "Next stop."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Earth, the Giant Magnet
chapters.text:
ZAP! They landed back in the cozy kitchen, Bolt holding a tiny toy compass.

"Here's the surprise," Bolt said. "The whole planet Earth is basically one giant magnet."

Ada's eyes went huge. "The WHOLE EARTH?"

"Deep, deep down," said Bolt, "there's swirly melted iron. That swirling makes Earth's own magnetic field, stretching all around us."

He set the little compass on the counter. The needle wiggled, then settled, pointing the same direction every time.

"The needle's north end gets pulled toward Earth's north," Bolt said. "That's why a compass always points the same way, wherever you stand."

Ada spun the compass around three times. Each time, the needle swung back to the same spot.

"It's stubborn," Ada said.

"It's reliable," said Bolt. "Handy thing to be."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Magnets Made of Electricity
chapters.text:
Bolt tugged Ada toward the hallway light switch.

"Magnets don't only come from rocks or robots," he said. "You can make one with electricity."

He showed her a drawing: wire wrapped round and round into a coil, hooked to a battery.

"Wrap wire like that and send electricity through it," said Bolt, "and CLICK — it's a magnet. We call it an **electromagnet**. Flip the switch off, and the magnet turns off too."

"Like a magnet with an on-off button?" Ada said.

"Exactly like that," said Bolt. "Doorbells use them. BUZZ! Speakers use them to make music. And junkyards use giant ones on cranes to lift whole cars."

Ada pictured a crane dropping a car, then gasped and giggled instead. "Imagine a car stuck to YOUR fridge."

"Please don't give Earth ideas," said Bolt.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Snip, Snip, Still a Magnet
chapters.text:
Ada picked up a toy scissors. "What happens if I cut a magnet in half?"

"Try it on me and find out," said Bolt bravely, holding out his arm, which was really just a spare magnet.

Ada pretend-snipped. Bolt popped the arm into two little pieces for the trick.

"You'd think one half gets north and the other gets south," said Bolt. "But nope. Each little piece grows its OWN north and south pole."

"So you get two tiny magnets instead of one big one," Ada said slowly.

"Exactly," said Bolt, snapping his arm back together. "Magnets are sneaky like that."

"One more thing," Bolt added. "Not every metal sticks to me. Gold, silver, and the soda-can metal called aluminum don't stick at all."

Ada ran to test her mom's gold ring. It didn't budge. "You're right. Weird!"

"Metal's full of surprises," said Bolt.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Back on the Fridge
chapters.text:
Ada yawned. Bolt noticed and slowed his beeping right down.

"One last secret," he whispered, pointing to the fridge magnets scattered on the counter. "These are made of soft, bendy rubber mixed with tiny bits of magnet powder. That's why they can bend without losing their stick."

Ada squished a magnet letter between her fingers. It bent, then popped flat again, still ready to stick.

"And somewhere out there," Bolt added, "super strong magnets even help trains float right above their tracks and zoom along without touching them at all."

"Floating TRAINS?" Ada whispered.

"Tomorrow night, maybe," said Bolt with a wink.

He hopped back onto the fridge door. CLICK. He turned back into a plain letter B, glow fading.

Ada pressed all her letters into one neat row, north ends and south ends snapped together snug.

She climbed back into bed, warm and yawning, pulled toward sleep like a needle finding north.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Ada. Sleep tight, and play well.

true_facts.text: Every magnet has two ends called **poles**, a north one and a south one.
**Opposite poles pull together**, and two of the **same poles push apart**.
Inside metal like iron are tiny teams called **domains** that can line up to make it magnetic.
In things like wood, those tiny teams point every which way, so it never turns magnetic.
The invisible space around a magnet where its pull and push happen is called its **magnetic field**.
Sprinkling tiny bits of metal near a magnet shows its field as **curved, looping lines**.
A naturally magnetic rock called a **lodestone** was found near a place called Magnesia long ago.
People used lodestones to make the very first **compasses**, more than **2,000 years ago**.
Deep inside the Earth is swirling melted iron, which makes the whole planet act like a **giant magnet**.
A compass needle always points the same way because it lines up with **Earth's magnetic field**.
Wrapping wire into a coil and running electricity through it makes an **electromagnet**, which can switch on and off.
Electromagnets are used in doorbells, speakers, and even giant **cranes that lift cars**.
If you cut a magnet in half, you don't get a north piece and a south piece — **each half becomes its own tiny magnet**.
Not every metal is magnetic — **gold, silver, and aluminum** don't stick to ordinary magnets.

new_recurring.name: Bolt the Magnet Robot
new_recurring.rule: A small robot who springs to life from one of Ada's fridge magnet letters whenever a new topic starts. He can glow, snap pieces of himself apart to demonstrate magnet tricks, and open short ZAP trips to real places or times, always…

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Ada lined up her fridge magnet letters neatly, north ends to south ends, and climbed back into bed feeling pulled gently toward sleep, with Bolt dozing quietly back into his letter-B shape on the fridge door.

story.title: Priya and Dev and the Rainbow Sprite
story.subtitle: A splashy, colorful bedtime adventure about light, water, and one very excited water pistol.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Backyard Rainbow
chapters.text:
It was way past bedtime. Priya was drawing a shark telling knock-knock jokes. Dev was in the yard, blasting the fence with his favorite water pistol.

"Last squirt before bed!" called Mom.

Dev aimed straight up at the porch light. He squeezed the trigger. WHOOSH-WHOOSH-WHOOSH! Tiny drops flew everywhere. Right there in the mist, a stripe of color popped up. Red. Orange. Yellow. Green. Blue.

Priya ran outside, pencil still in hand. "Did you just make a rainbow with your water pistol?"

A tiny glow blinked out of the colored mist. It had a face, and every color seemed to flicker inside it at once.

"Name's Roy," said the glow. "I show up whenever sunlight and water drops meet. Want to see how this trick really works?"

Dev lowered his water pistol slowly. "Does it involve more squirting?"

"Oh, tons," said Roy. Then WHOOSH — the mist swirled around them, and the backyard melted into something new.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Inside a Raindrop
chapters.text:
They landed inside something round and squishy, with walls that glowed like a giant water balloon.

"Where are we?" asked Priya.

"Inside a raindrop," said Roy. "A big pretend one, so you can actually see."

Dev poked the wall. It wobbled. "It's like a water balloon!"

"Sunlight comes in through here." Roy pointed at a beam shooting through the drop's side. "It bends when it moves from air into water. Scientists call that bending **refraction**. All it really means is light changes direction when it hits something new."

The beam bounced off the back wall of the drop like a mirror. Then it bent again on its way out.

"It bounces AND bends?" said Priya. "That's a trampoline park for light."

"Exactly," said Roy. "That's step one of making a rainbow."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Secret Colors Hiding in White
chapters.text:
Outside the raindrop, a beam of plain white sunlight waited like a stripe of chalk.

"That light looks kind of boring," said Dev. "It's just white."

"That's the trick," said Roy. "White sunlight is actually every color, mixed together and hiding."

Priya gasped. "Like my markers! When I mix all my paints, I get muddy brown. This is the opposite?"

"Kind of," said Roy. "A long time ago, a scientist named **Isaac Newton** shined sunlight through a triangle of glass called a **prism**. The prism split the white light apart. Out came every color, lined up in a row."

Dev squinted. "So the colors were there the whole time? Just hiding?"

"The whole time," said Roy. "Each color bends by a slightly different amount, so the prism spreads them apart, like a deck of cards."

Priya sketched a rainbow bursting from a triangle. "Newton basically unzipped the sunlight."

"Best way I've ever heard it put," said Roy.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Roy G. Biv
chapters.text:
Back outside, Dev raised his water pistol, and a fresh stripe of color arched over them.

"Count them," said Roy. "Every rainbow lines up the exact same way."

Dev counted on his fingers. "Red... orange... yellow... green... blue... purple... and another purple?"

"Close," said Priya. "Those last two are blue, indigo, and violet. Put the first letters together and you get..."

She stopped. She stared at the little sparkle floating beside them.

"R-O-Y-G-B-I-V," said Dev slowly. "That's basically your name!"

Roy did a little spin. "Told you I'm memorable."

"No wonder you're an expert," laughed Priya. "You're named after the whole rainbow."

"Red always sits on the outside edge," Roy explained, "because it bends the least. Violet sits on the inside, because it bends the most."

"So red's the slowpoke and violet's the show-off," said Dev.

"That works," said Roy.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Rainbow That's Actually a Circle
chapters.text:
Roy led them up, up, up, until the backyard looked tiny below.

"Rainbows aren't really arches," said Roy. "They're full circles. We just can't see the bottom half, because the ground blocks it."

Dev's jaw dropped. "A WHOLE circle? Like a hula hoop?"

"Exactly like that," said Roy. "But way up high, like in an airplane, there's no ground to block it. Sometimes people look out the window and see the whole circle, just floating."

Priya pressed her nose to an imaginary window. "I'd draw that so fast. A rainbow donut in the sky."

"Best. Snack. Idea. Ever," said Dev happily.

"It's not actually a snack," said Roy. "But I like your energy."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Nobody Else Sees Your Rainbow
chapters.text:
They floated back down near the fence, where Dev's little rainbow still hung in the mist.

"Quick question," said Priya. "If I stand here and Dev stands there, do we see the exact same rainbow?"

"Nope," said Roy. "You each see your very own rainbow, made from your own raindrops. It depends on the angle between the sun, the water, and your eyes."

Dev stepped sideways. "So if I move, I get a brand new one?"

"A brand new one," said Roy. "That's also why nobody can ever walk up and touch a rainbow, or find its end. The end moves whenever you move."

Priya grinned. "So there's no actual pot of gold at the end?"

"People in Ireland used to tell stories about tricky little leprechauns hiding treasure there," said Roy. "It's a fun story. It's just not really true, since a rainbow doesn't have a fixed end at all."

"Still a great story though," said Dev.

"The best stories don't have to be true to be fun," said Roy.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Rainbows in Waterfalls, Hoses, and Moonlight
chapters.text:
Roy whisked them to a waterfall, roaring and spraying mist everywhere.

"Any splashing water can make one," said Roy. "Waterfalls, garden hoses, even your water pistol."

Dev puffed up with pride. "I knew my water pistol was basically a science machine."

Above the waterfall's rainbow, a second, fainter one glowed, with its colors flipped backward.

"Whoa, there's two!" said Priya.

"A double rainbow happens when light bounces twice inside the drops instead of once," said Roy. "The second one is always fainter, and flipped."

"And at night," Roy added, "moonlight can make a rainbow too. It's called a **moonbow**. It usually looks gray or white to your eyes, but a camera can catch the colors hiding inside it."

"A secret nighttime rainbow," said Priya. "I'm drawing that one in glitter pen."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Home Again
chapters.text:
The mist swirled once more. WHOOSH — they landed back in the yard, Dev's water pistol still dripping in his hand.

"People have told rainbow stories forever," said Roy, its glow dimming softly. "Some say a rainbow is a bridge, called **Bifrost**, for gods to cross. Some say it's a promise, like the one in the story of **Noah**, a sign that a storm has passed and good things are coming."

"I like that one," said Priya. "A promise in the sky."

"Me too," said Dev, yawning hugely.

Roy's glow shrank down to one last sparkle. "Same time next rain?"

"Deal," said Dev, stumbling toward the porch steps.

Priya tucked her comic under her arm. "Goodnight, Roy."

The porch light clicked off. Up where the mist had been, one last shimmer of color blinked out, like a wink.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Priya. Goodnight, Dev. Same time next rain.

true_facts.text: A rainbow forms when sunlight bends going into a raindrop, bounces off the back wall, and bends again coming out.
White sunlight is actually every color mixed together, just hiding, until something splits it apart.
Rainbow colors always line up the same way: **red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, and violet** — which spells Roy's name, Roy G. Biv.
**Red** sits on the outside of a rainbow because it bends the least, and **violet** sits on the inside because it bends the most.
To see a rainbow, the sun has to be behind you and rain or spray has to be in front of you.
Rainbows are actually full circles — we usually only see the top half because the ground blocks the rest.
From an airplane window, with no ground blocking the view, people sometimes see a whole circle rainbow.
Every person actually sees their own private rainbow, made from their own raindrops at their own angle.
Sometimes a fainter second rainbow shows up above the first one, with its colors flipped backward.
Rainbows can show up in waterfalls, garden hose spray, and even moonlight, where they're called **moonbows**.
A scientist named **Isaac Newton** used a glass **prism** to split white sunlight apart into all its colors.
There's an old Irish story about a pot of gold at the end of a rainbow — fun to tell, but not really true.
You can never actually walk up to or touch a rainbow, because its end moves whenever you move.

new_recurring.rule: A tiny sparkle made of all seven colors who appears only when sunlight and water droplets meet at the same time. Speaks in light-and-color wordplay, always ends a visit with 'Same time next rain?'

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Dev and Priya return to the backyard with Roy fading into the mist, promising to meet again next time sunlight and rain cross paths.

story.title: Jack, Ellie, and the Glowing Shark Tooth
story.subtitle: A night swim through four hundred million years of sharks

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Tooth on the Shelf
chapters.text:
It was way past bedtime. Jack had a flashlight under his blanket, reading his shark book again. Ellie lined up her tiny mermaid figures on the windowsill, humming a little tune.

On the shelf between their beds sat the grey rock they'd found on the beach. It was shaped just like a giant tooth.

Then it started to glow. Blue light poured out, like the whole room was underwater.

"Jack," Ellie whispered. "Your rock is doing a thing."

Jack grabbed it. It felt smooth and cool, not hard like a stone at all. "Whoa. It's bendy, Ellie. Feel it."

Ellie poked it. It gave, just a little, like a squishy eraser.

"That's what shark bones are like," said a soft, bubbly voice from inside the glow. "Bendy, not hard like yours. It's called **cartilage** — same stretchy stuff that's in your ear."

Jack pressed his own ear. "Whoa, it IS bendy!"

The light swelled bigger, swirling into a tunnel of blue water right there on the carpet.

"Well?" said the voice. "Divers don't just stand on the shore."

Jack didn't need telling twice. He grabbed Ellie's hand and jumped.

**WHOOOOSH!**

They landed with a **SPLOOSH**, somehow dry, somehow breathing, floating in the biggest, bluest ocean either of them had ever seen.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Older Than Dinosaurs
chapters.text:
Shapes moved in the deep blue below them, long grey shadows gliding in slow circles.

"Are those sharks?" Ellie asked, holding tight to Jack's sleeve.

"Those are some of the very first sharks," said the glowing tooth, now floating beside them like a little blue lantern. "Sharks have been swimming in this ocean for more than **400 million years**. That's way before dinosaurs ever walked anywhere."

Jack's mouth fell open. "Before DINOSAURS?"

"Before dinosaurs," said the tooth. "And today there are more than **500 different kinds** of sharks swimming around the world."

Ellie counted shadows with her fingers until she lost count at seven. "That's a LOT of sharks."

"Which one is your favorite?" the tooth asked.

Jack thought hard. "I want to see the biggest one. And the scariest one. And the weirdest one."

"One at a time, diver," laughed the tooth. "But if you want the oldest and the biggest tooth of all, follow me down."

It spun once and dove. Jack kicked after it like he'd practiced diving in the pool a hundred times. Ellie wrapped her hand around his ankle so she wouldn't drift off, and down they went together.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Giant's Tooth
chapters.text:
At the bottom, half-buried in sand, lay a tooth as long as Jack's whole hand.

"Is that from a monster?" Ellie gasped.

"That's from **Megalodon**," said the tooth. "The biggest shark that ever lived. It's **extinct** now — that means it isn't around anymore, not anywhere."

Jack picked up the giant tooth carefully. It was heavy, like a rock. "How do we even know about it, if it's gone?"

"Mostly from teeth like this one," the tooth explained. "They turned hard as stone over millions of years — we call that a **fossil**. Shark bodies are too bendy to leave much behind, but their teeth tell the story."

"Lucky sharks have so many teeth, then," said Jack.

"Lucky indeed," said the tooth. "A shark loses teeth its whole life, and new ones just slide forward to take their place. One shark can go through thousands of teeth before it's done."

Ellie giggled. "Thousands? Mom would be SO mad if I lost that many teeth."

Jack held the giant tooth up like a trophy. "Can we keep it?"

"Just for now," said the tooth, glowing warmly. "Put it down gently when we go. It's been resting a long time."

Jack set it back in the sand, soft as he could.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Gentle Giant
chapters.text:
A shadow the size of a school bus slid over them, blocking out the sun.

Ellie froze. Jack grabbed her hand. "Wait — it's okay. Look at its mouth. It's not even trying to catch us."

"That's a **whale shark**," said the tooth. "The biggest fish in the whole world, over 40 feet long. But all it eats is **plankton** — tiny floating bits of food, smaller than rice. It just swims along with its mouth open, like drinking through a straw."

"It's gentle," Jack said, soft and sure.

"Can I say hi?" Ellie asked, reaching out her hand.

"You can wave," said the tooth. "But we watch sharks, we don't touch them. Even the friendly ones."

Ellie waved instead, both hands, big as she could. The whale shark's eye rolled slowly toward her, like it noticed.

"Some whale sharks live to be **100 years old**, maybe even older," said the tooth.

"A hundred!" Ellie said. "That's older than Grandpa."

"Way older," Jack grinned.

The giant shark swam on, slow and easy, leaving them bobbing in its wake, both of them still waving goodbye.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Hammers and Sparks
chapters.text:
Something strange poked around a coral wall ahead — a head shaped like a hammer.

"That shark's head is WEIRD," Jack said, laughing.

"That's a **hammerhead**," said the tooth. "Its eyes sit far apart on each side, so it can see almost all the way around itself."

"Like having eyes in the back of your head," Jack said. "Mom always says she has those."

Ellie giggled. "Mom's not a shark, Jack."

"Sharks also have tiny jelly-filled dots on their snouts," the tooth went on. "That's their nose. The dots feel teeny sparks of electricity from other animals, even ones hiding under the sand."

"So it can feel things it can't even see?" Jack asked.

"Exactly," said the tooth.

Sunlight rippled over a passing shark's side, and its skin shimmered rough and grainy. "Its skin looks like sandpaper," Ellie noticed.

"Good eye," said the tooth. "It's covered in zillions of tiny tooth-shaped bumps. That's why it feels so rough, and why real divers never rub a shark's skin the wrong way."

"Noted," said Jack, hands firmly to himself.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Walking Shark
chapters.text:
On a shallow reef, something small flopped between two puddles.

"Jack, is that shark BROKEN?" Ellie asked.

"Nope," laughed the tooth. "That's an **epaulette shark**. It can actually walk, using its flat fins like little paddles, right over the rocky reef and across puddles when the tide goes out."

"No way," Jack said, leaning close to watch it scoot along.

"It can hold its breath for hours too, with hardly any air at all," the tooth added.

Nearby, a wider, sleepier shark lay still on the sandy bottom. "Is that one sick?" Ellie asked.

"That's a **nurse shark**, just resting," said the tooth. "It can pump water over its gills — that's how it breathes underwater — without swimming at all. Sharks can nap too, sort of."

Ellie reached toward it without thinking, then stopped herself. "We watch, not touch," she said proudly.

"That's the rule," said the tooth, glowing a little brighter, like it was proud too.

Jack grinned. "See, Ellie listens better than you think."

"I ALWAYS listen," Ellie said, splashing him on purpose.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Fast, Far, and Mermaid's Purses
chapters.text:
A grey streak shot past them like a torpedo, and was simply gone.

"WHOA! What was THAT?" Jack shouted.

"The **shortfin mako**," said the tooth. "The fastest shark of all. It zooms in quick bursts to catch fast fish like tuna."

"Race you to the coral!" Jack said to no one, and kicked off anyway.

Farther along, the water turned cloudy and brown. "That doesn't look like the ocean," Ellie said.

"That's a river mouth," said the tooth. "**Bull sharks** can swim in salty ocean water AND in rivers with fresh water. Some have even been found far upriver, way past where you'd ever expect."

Then Ellie spotted something snagged on a branch — a dark, leathery little pouch with curly tips.

"What's THIS?" she asked, delighted.

"People call that a **mermaid's purse**," said the tooth. "Some sharks lay their eggs inside pouches like that one. Other sharks just have live babies, called pups, right away."

Ellie held it like a treasure. "A real mermaid's purse. I KNEW mermaids were real."

"Ellie..." Jack started.

"Don't ruin it, Jack," Ellie said, and he didn't.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Shark Lady
chapters.text:
A diver with a notebook floated ahead of them, watching a shark glide by without ever reaching for it.

"Who's that?" Jack asked.

"That's **Eugenie Clark**," said the tooth. "People called her the Shark Lady. She studied sharks for years and years, and showed everyone that sharks are curious — she even trained some to do tricks, like puppies."

The diver turned and smiled at them, then pointed at the shark swimming past.

"Sharks sit right at the top of the sea," said the tooth. "Keeping everything else down here just right, like a king keeping his kingdom balanced."

"Are sharks dangerous?" Ellie asked, quieter now.

"Hardly ever," said the tooth. "Shark attacks almost never happen. Really, people hurt far more sharks than sharks ever hurt us. These days lots of people work hard to look after them instead."

Jack nodded slowly. "So we just... leave them be."

"And wave," said Ellie.

"And wave," the tooth agreed, glowing bright and warm.

The water began to spin, blue turning to carpet, ocean turning to bedroom. Jack and Ellie landed with a soft **thump** right back on the floor, the grey tooth resting cool and still between them, glow fading to nothing.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Jack. Goodnight, Ellie. Swim well, and dream deep.

true_facts.text: Shark bones aren't hard like ours — they're bendy, like the stretchy stuff in your ear. That's called **cartilage**.
Sharks have swum in the ocean for more than **400 million years**, long before dinosaurs.
There are more than **500 different kinds** of sharks living in the world today.
**Megalodon** was the biggest shark ever, but it's extinct now — it isn't around anymore.
We mostly know about ancient sharks from their teeth, which turned hard as stone — a **fossil**.
A shark loses and regrows teeth its whole life, going through thousands of them.
The **whale shark** is the biggest fish in the world, over 40 feet long, but it only eats tiny floating bits called plankton.
Some whale sharks live to be **100 years old** or more.
**Hammerhead sharks** have wide, flat heads with eyes far apart, so they see almost all the way around.
Sharks can feel tiny sparks of electricity from hidden animals, using jelly-filled dots on their snouts.
The **epaulette shark** can actually walk across the reef using its fins, and hold its breath for hours.
The **shortfin mako** is the fastest shark, zooming in quick bursts to catch fast fish.
**Bull sharks** can swim in both salty ocean water and rivers, sometimes far upriver.
Some sharks lay eggs in a leathery pouch called a **mermaid's purse**; others have live babies called pups.

story.title: Nora and the Buried City of Pompeii
story.subtitle: A mosaic tile glows, and a whole Roman town wakes up under the ash.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Tile That Warmed Up
chapters.text:
Nora sat cross-legged on her bedroom floor, snapping tiny glass squares into a picture of a dolphin. It was almost bedtime, but one more tile wouldn't hurt.

She picked up a chip of blue glass. It was warm. Not sun-warm. Glowing-warm.

The tile hummed, soft and low, like a bee caught in a jar. Then the floor tilted, the dolphin picture spun into gold light, and Nora wasn't in her bedroom anymore.

She stood on a stone street, in bright sun, with the smell of bread and the sound of a hundred voices.

"Welcome," said a small voice. The blue tile floated at her shoulder, tiny and bright as a star. "I used to be part of a floor. Floors remember a lot."

"Where are we?" Nora asked.

"A town called **Pompeii**," said the tile. "Near a city called **Naples**, in what is now southern Italy." The word *southern* just meant the bottom part of the map.

Nora looked around. Shops lined the street. People carried baskets. A man sold olives from a big jar.

"How many people live here?" she asked, counting doorways until she lost track at twenty.

"Somewhere between **eleven thousand and fifteen thousand**," said the tile. "Shops, baths, theaters, temples — a whole busy town."

"That's more than my whole school!" Nora said, and the tile wobbled, which was its way of laughing.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Stepping Stones and Secret Pipes
chapters.text:
Nora's shoe splashed in a puddle, and she hopped back with a squeak.

"Careful," said the tile. "But look down."

Across the street sat three flat stones, raised up like little islands, with gaps between them.

Nora hopped from stone to stone, dry the whole way. "It's a bridge for feet!"

"Exactly," said the tile. "The **stepping stones** kept people's sandals dry, while carts still rolled right through the gaps underneath."

A cart rumbled past, its wheels fitting the gaps perfectly, and Nora grinned.

At the corner, water trickled from a stone fountain shaped like a face. Nora cupped her hands and felt it splash cool.

"How does water get all the way up here?" she asked.

"**Pipes**," said the tile. "Long metal tubes carried water under the streets, all the way to fountains like this one."

"So Romans had their own secret water tunnels," Nora said, tracing the fountain's carved eyebrows with one finger. "Sneaky."

"Clever," the tile corrected, bobbing happily. "There's a difference."

Nora splashed one more handful at the tile just to see it dodge, and it did, which made her laugh out loud in the middle of the street.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Stone Bowl
chapters.text:
A roar rolled down the street, and Nora froze. Then she heard clapping, and cheering, and realized it was just a crowd.

Ahead stood a huge oval building, like a stone bowl turned on its side.

"What is THAT?" Nora asked, tipping her head all the way back.

"An **amphitheater**," said the tile. "A giant round stage for games, built about **70 years before the eruption** that buried this town. One of the oldest ever found."

"What kind of games?" Nora asked.

"Contests, called gladiator games," said the tile gently. "People came from all around to watch."

Nora climbed a few stone steps and sat down where thousands once sat. She imagined the noise, the fans, the sun on stone seats.

"It's like a stadium," she said.

"The very first kind," said the tile.

She traced a crack in the step with her finger. "Pompeii even had a nickname," the tile added. "Some people think its name may come from an old word meaning **'five,'** maybe for five little villages that joined together to make one town."

"Five friends who became one team," Nora said, and the tile glowed a little brighter, as if it liked that.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Mountain Wakes Up
chapters.text:
The ground gave a tiny shiver under Nora's shoes, and she grabbed the tile.

"It's all right," said the tile. "That mountain over there has woken up before."

Nora looked past the rooftops at a tall green mountain, smoke curling lazily from its top.

"That's **Mount Vesuvius**," said the tile. "A **volcano** — a mountain that can shoot out hot ash and rock."

"Is it going to do that now?" Nora asked, eyes wide.

"Not while we're standing here," said the tile. "But on **August 24th, in the year 79**, it did."

The sky in Nora's mind turned dark and strange, far across the water.

"A young Roman named **Pliny the Younger** watched it happen from across the bay," said the tile. "He wrote two long letters describing everything he saw — so carefully that scientists still use his words today to understand this kind of eruption."

"So he was like a news reporter," Nora said. "Before cameras."

"Before pencils were even common," said the tile. "Ash fell for two days, until it covered the whole town, as deep as **twenty feet** in places. Deeper than your house is tall."

Nora hugged her knees, quiet for a moment. "That's a lot of ash."

"It is," said the tile softly. "And it's why we can visit here at all."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Bread That Waited
chapters.text:
Nora smelled something warm and crusty, drifting from a little stone oven.

"Someone's baking," she said, stepping closer.

Inside the oven sat a round loaf, scored with lines like a pie, perfectly shaped.

"That loaf has been sitting there for a very long time," said the tile. "Almost **two thousand years**. The ash covered it so fast that it never burned, never crumbled. Diggers found it still marked with the baker's own stamp."

"It's still a bread shape," Nora whispered, leaning in without touching.

"That's the strange magic of ash," said the tile. "It sealed this town shut like a lid on a jar. Paintings on walls stayed bright. Even messages people scribbled stayed readable."

"Like a time capsule," Nora said.

"Like the biggest time capsule anyone ever opened," agreed the tile.

Nora peeked around the corner of the bakery and spotted words painted on the outside wall in faded red letters.

"What does that say?" she asked.

"An old advertisement," said the tile. "Romans painted messages right on their walls — ads for shops, even messages about elections. Like sidewalk chalk that never washed away."

Nora grinned. "I'm definitely painting my door when I get home."

"Please don't," said the tile, and Nora laughed so hard she nearly knocked over the bread.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Town by the Sea
chapters.text:
The tile led Nora along a path that curved toward the water, salty wind in her hair.

"There's another town near here," said the tile. "Smaller, right by the sea, called **Herculaneum**. The same eruption buried it too — but under a different kind of hot, heavy material."

"Different how?" Nora asked.

"It sealed things even tighter," said the tile. "Diggers there found wooden furniture that hadn't rotted away. Even scrolls of paper, still rolled up."

Nora pictured a whole wooden chair, waiting patiently for two thousand years.

"Wood doesn't usually last that long," she said.

"No," said the tile. "But sealed away from air and rain, it can."

They stood at the edge of a cliff, looking down at old stone archways near the water.

"A brave commander named **Pliny the Elder** sailed his ships toward this coast that very day," said the tile, "to try to help the people here."

"That's really brave," Nora said quietly. "Sailing toward the scary mountain instead of away from it."

"It is," agreed the tile. "Some of the bravest people run toward trouble to help, not away from it."

Nora nodded, and tucked that thought away like a little souvenir.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Pictures on the Wall
chapters.text:
Inside a grand house, Nora gasped. The walls were covered in paintings — deep red, bright gold, figures in flowing robes.

"These are called **frescoes**," said the tile. "Paintings made right into wet wall plaster, so they became part of the wall itself."

"They look almost new," Nora said, tracing the air near a painted dancer, careful not to touch.

"The ash protected the colors," said the tile. "This house is famous. People call it the **Villa of the Mysteries**, because nobody is completely sure what the paintings show — maybe a secret ceremony, maybe a celebration."

"A real mystery," Nora said, delighted. "In a house called Mysteries."

"Convenient, isn't it," said the tile.

Nora studied a tiny mosaic on the floor, little colored squares just like the ones in her own bedroom.

"Someone made this with tiles like you," she said.

"Long, long before I was a tile," said the tile, glowing proudly anyway. "Every tiny piece had its place. That's how a mosaic becomes a picture."

"Every tiny piece tells a big story," Nora said slowly, trying the words out.

The tile sparkled. "I like that. Keep it."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Digging It Up Again
chapters.text:
The gold light swirled, and the busy street faded into quiet dirt and stone walls, half-buried under earth.

"Where did everyone go?" Nora asked.

"Time passed," said the tile. "For a very long while, this whole town slept under the ground, forgotten."

"Forever?" Nora asked.

"Not forever," said the tile. "In **1748**, workers digging nearby found old walls and objects poking up from the dirt. People realized a whole town was buried right underneath."

Nora watched shadowy figures with shovels, carefully brushing dirt from a painted wall.

"They dig so carefully," she noticed.

"People who study old places like this are called **archaeologists**," said the tile. "They brush away dirt slowly, so nothing gets broken."

"Like unwrapping a present you don't want to tear," Nora said.

"Exactly like that," said the tile. "And even now, only about **two-thirds** of the town has been uncovered. There's still more town waiting under the ground."

Nora's eyes went wide. "So there could be more bread ovens down there? More paintings?"

"Almost certainly," said the tile. "People find new rooms and new paintings still, every single year."

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Home, With a Tiny Piece
chapters.text:
The gold light swirled one more time, soft and slow, and Nora blinked.

She was back on her bedroom floor, mosaic dolphin still half-finished in front of her.

The little blue tile sat quietly in her palm, not glowing anymore, just an ordinary piece of glass.

"Are you still there?" Nora whispered.

A tiny warmth answered her, like a wink.

"That mountain is still there too," the tile murmured sleepily. "Scientists watch it closely, every day, because so many people live near it now."

"To make sure everyone stays safe," Nora said.

"Exactly," said the tile. "And the buried town you visited is now one of the most visited old places on Earth — millions of people come to walk its streets every single year, just like you did tonight."

Nora pressed the little blue tile into the last empty space of her dolphin mosaic. It clicked into place, perfectly, as if it had always belonged there.

She pulled her blanket up to her chin, thinking of stepping stones, secret pipes, and bread that waited two thousand years just to be found.

"Every tiny piece tells a big story," she murmured, eyes already closing.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Nora. Every tiny piece tells a big story.

true_facts.text: **Pompeii** was a real Roman town near the city of **Naples**, in southern Italy.
Before the mountain erupted, about **eleven to fifteen thousand people** lived in Pompeii, with shops, baths, theaters, and temples.
Pompeii's streets had raised **stepping stones** so people could cross without wet feet, while carts still rolled through the gaps.
Pompeii had **pipes** carrying water under its streets, all the way to public fountains.
Pompeii's huge oval **amphitheater**, built about seventy years before the eruption, is one of the oldest ever found.
On **August 24th, in the year 79**, the volcano **Mount Vesuvius** erupted and buried Pompeii.
Ash from the eruption covered the town as deep as **twenty feet** in places.
A young Roman named **Pliny the Younger** watched the eruption from across the bay and wrote two letters describing it so carefully that scientists still use them today.
Diggers found a **loaf of bread** in a Pompeii oven, still shaped and stamped by its baker, almost two thousand years later.
The ash sealed the town so fast that paintings and even scribbled messages on walls stayed in place for centuries.
A nearby seaside town called **Herculaneum** was buried too, under material that preserved even wooden furniture and rolled-up scrolls.
Pompeii was rediscovered in **1748**, when workers digging nearby found old walls and objects.
Pompeii is now one of the most visited old places on Earth, with millions of visitors every year.
Only about **two-thirds** of Pompeii has been dug up so far, and new paintings and rooms are still being found.
