story.title: Maya and the Race to the Stars
story.subtitle: A splashy bedtime trip through the Space Race, with Barnacle the seal along for the ride.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: Bathtub Liftoff
chapters.text:
Maya sat in the bathtub with her waterproof crayons. She drew a round ball with a wiggly antenna on the foggy tile.

It had been one whole week since Barnacle waved his flipper at the last rivet on that humming bridge. Tonight the water felt extra fizzy.

"Five more minutes, Maya!" called her mom from the hallway.

Maya kept drawing. She liked drawing best right before bedtime, when the tub was warm and quiet.

SPLOOSH! A round, whiskery face popped up between her knees.

"All aboard, Maya!" said Barnacle, the harbor seal, shaking water off his nose.

"Barnacle!" Maya laughed. "Look what I drew."

The little ball on the tile began to glow. It lifted off the wall and floated into the bathwater. Then it started to beep.

BEEP. BEEP. BEEP.

"Why is it beeping?" Maya asked, because asking why was her favorite thing to do.

"That's **Sputnik 1**," said Barnacle. "The very first **satellite**. A satellite is just a little metal moon that circles a planet instead of falling down."

"When was it?" Maya asked.

"**October 4, 1957**," said Barnacle. "It was only **fifty-eight centimeters** wide. About the size of a beach ball."

Maya held her hands apart to show how small that was. "That tiny? And everyone heard it beep?"

"On ordinary radios, everywhere," said Barnacle. "People pointed their antennas at the sky just to listen."

Maya reached out and touched the glowing ball. The bathwater shivered. Then it turned into a thousand tiny stars, swirling like bubbles.

The tub tipped back like a rocket on a launchpad.

"Hang onto your crayons!" shouted Barnacle.

WHOOOOSH! The little boat Maya had drawn rose up out of the water. It grew big enough to sit in, with Maya and Barnacle aboard, zooming through a tunnel of starlight.

"Where are we going?" Maya asked, gripping the sides.

"Back to 1957," said Barnacle. "The year two countries, America and the Soviet Union, started racing each other to space."

Maya looked down. The bathroom was gone. Below them, Earth spun, blue and round, with the little beeping satellite looping around it.

"It beeps," Maya whispered, "like it's saying hello to everybody."

Barnacle smiled his whiskery seal smile. "I'd say hello back. But I'm a seal. I only know how to say SPLOOSH."

Maya giggled so hard she nearly let go of the boat.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Laika's Brave Ride
chapters.text:
A soft bark echoed through the starlight.

Maya sat up. "Was that... a dog?"

The little boat drifted toward a silver capsule — a kind of sealed space car — tumbling gently through the dark.

"That's Sputnik 2," said Barnacle. "Launched **November 3, 1957**, just one month after the first satellite. And yes, there's a dog inside."

"A dog? In space?" Maya pressed her nose to the boat's rail.

"Her name was **Laika**," said Barnacle. "She was the first living creature ever to circle the Earth."

Maya peered through the capsule's little window. Two big brown eyes peered back.

"She looks lonely," Maya said. "Can I draw her something?"

"Go ahead," said Barnacle. "Nobody rushes anybody around here."

Maya flipped to a clean page. She drew a soft, round cushion with a bone on it. The picture glowed, lifted off the page, and floated straight through the capsule wall, landing beside Laika with a gentle plop.

Laika pressed her paw to the window. A little foggy paw print bloomed on the glass.

"Why did they send a dog instead of a person?" Maya asked.

"Because nobody knew yet if a living creature could survive up here," said Barnacle. "Laika went first, so braver trips could follow."

Maya waved at the window. "Thank you for going first, Laika."

The paw print on the glass shimmered brighter. Tiny silver sparkles floated off the capsule, drawing a trail through the stars like a path to follow.

"Looks like she's pointing the way," said Barnacle.

"Where to?" asked Maya.

"Follow the sparkles and find out," said Barnacle, paddling his flippers like oars.

The little boat turned, caught the glittering trail, and sailed on, leaving Laika's capsule tumbling peacefully behind, her paw print still glowing warm on the glass.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: America Catches Up
chapters.text:
A buzzer rang out, loud and urgent, like a school bell gone wild.

"Uh oh," said Maya. "Someone's in a hurry."

The boat floated down past a building full of blinking lights and scribbling scientists.

"Sputnik gave the United States a scare," said Barnacle. "So on **October 1, 1958**, they started a brand-new space team called **NASA**."

Maya looked at a chalkboard covered in numbers and arrows. "What are they trying to find?"

"Watch," said Barnacle, pointing a flipper at a thin, pencil-shaped ship on the launchpad. "That's **Explorer 1**, America's first satellite. It went up **January 31, 1958**."

The little ship roared off the pad and climbed high above Earth. Maya watched its dials wiggle and spike on a screen nearby.

"Why's it doing that?" she asked.

"It just found something nobody knew was there," said Barnacle. "An invisible ring of fizzy space weather, circling the whole planet like a giant hula hoop."

Maya's eyes went wide. "A ring you can't even see?"

"Not with your eyes," said Barnacle. "But Explorer 1's instruments felt it."

Maya grabbed her sketchbook. She drew her own little satellite, with the same thin antennas as the real one, and a dotted loop all around Earth to show where the hidden ring sat.

The drawing glowed and zipped off the page, joining Explorer 1 in **orbit** — the word for circling all the way around a planet.

On the screen, the dotted loop lit up gold, matching Maya's picture exactly.

"FOUND IT!" Maya shouted, pointing.

The scientists below cheered. One of them taped a copy of her drawing right onto the chalkboard.

"Nicely spotted," said Barnacle. "Next stop, the big one — the year humans finally leave the ground."

The boat rose through the cheering room and out into the stars once more.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Gagarin's Giant Loop
chapters.text:
A streak of silver shot past the boat so fast it rocked side to side.

"Whoa!" Maya grabbed the rail. "What was that?"

"That was Vostok 1," said Barnacle. "Inside it is a very brave pilot named **Yuri Gagarin**."

"Is he going in a loop?" Maya asked, watching the silver ship curve around the blue Earth below.

"The whole way around," said Barnacle. "On **April 12, 1961**, he became the first human ever in space. One full orbit took about **108 minutes**."

Maya counted on her fingers, then gave up. "That's a long time!"

"Not even two hours," said Barnacle. "Shorter than a movie."

Maya grabbed her crayons. She drew a big looping racetrack around a picture of Earth, to show the whole path Gagarin had flown. The loop glowed gold where his ship had already passed.

"Who else is racing?" Maya asked.

Right on cue, a stubby little capsule zoomed by below them, going up and straight back down, like a diver doing a quick bounce.

"That's **Alan Shepard**," said Barnacle. "On **May 5, 1961**, he became the first American in space, aboard Freedom 7. His trip was short. He didn't make it all the way around like Gagarin did."

Maya drew a short dashed line next to her big loop, to show Shepard's quicker bounce.

Then a deep voice rang out across the stars, like a speech from a podium.

"We choose to go to the Moon," the voice said, "and do the other things, because they are hard."

"Who's that?" Maya whispered.

"**President John F. Kennedy**," said Barnacle. "On **May 25, 1961**, he dared his whole country to land someone on the Moon, and bring them home safe, before ten more years had passed."

Maya's eyes lit up. "It's a race to the Moon! Like a boat race, but with rockets!"

"Exactly like that," said Barnacle, and together they watched Kennedy's words sparkle across the sky like a finish line waiting to be drawn.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Valentina's Vostok
chapters.text:
Crackly static buzzed from a little radio bolted to the boat's dashboard. Then, through the static, came a woman's voice, calm and clear.

"Who's that?" Maya asked, turning the dial.

"**Valentina Tereshkova**," said Barnacle. "She used to work in a factory. Then she trained to fly. On **June 16, 1963**, she became the first woman ever in space."

A silver ship called Vostok 6 sailed past, circling Earth again and again.

"She's going around and around," said Maya, watching it loop. "Like me doing laps at swim practice!"

"A bit faster than swim practice," said Barnacle, chuckling.

Maya tore a page from her sketchbook and drew a little checkered racing flag. "For her," she said. "Since it's a race."

She held the flag up out of the boat and waved it as hard as she could.

The moment she waved, Vostok 6 dipped one wing, almost like a wave back. A shower of silver sparkles drifted from its hull toward the little boat.

"She saw you," said Barnacle softly.

Maya beamed, tucking her flag into her sketchbook like a prize. "Why did it take so long for a woman to go?" she asked. "Gagarin went first, and that was two whole years before."

"Lots of people had to say yes first," said Barnacle. "But once Valentina got her chance, she circled this whole planet again and again, proving she belonged up here just as much as anyone."

The sparkles gathered into a swirling silver trail, curling away through the dark like a ribbon.

"Follow that?" Maya asked, already steering.

"Follow that," said Barnacle, and the little boat chased the glittering ribbon deeper into the stars.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Floating Free
chapters.text:
Something — or someone — floated right outside the boat's window, tumbling slowly in the dark.

Maya gasped. "Barnacle! A person!"

A figure in a big, puffy white suit drifted at the end of a long cord, like a kite on a string.

"That's **Alexei Leonov**," said Barnacle. "On **March 18, 1965**, he opened his hatch and stepped outside his ship. Nobody had ever done that before."

"Stepped outside?" Maya pressed close to the glass. "Isn't that scary? Won't he float away?"

"That's what the cord is for," said Barnacle. "It kept him tied to the ship, so he couldn't drift off. A bit like how you wear a pool noodle at swim practice, so you always float back to the edge."

Maya grinned. "I love floating in the pool."

"Leonov floated for about ten minutes," said Barnacle, "then climbed carefully back inside."

Maya grabbed her crayons and drew her own cord, stretching from the little boat all the way to Leonov's drifting boots, just to be extra safe.

The drawn cord glowed. It stretched across the stars and gently tugged Leonov back toward his open hatch, right on schedule.

He gave a thumbs-up through his visor before disappearing inside.

"Nice knot," said Barnacle.

"I learned it tying up our rowboat," said Maya proudly.

The hatch sealed with a soft clunk. A comet streaked by overhead, trailing a long tail of light.

"That comet's headed somewhere," said Maya, pointing.

"Then let's follow it," said Barnacle, and the little boat turned to chase the comet's glowing tail into the dark.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Earthrise
chapters.text:
The boat slid around the gray, bumpy edge of the Moon, and Maya gasped out loud.

There, rising over the Moon's horizon, hung the whole Earth — blue, white, and small enough to cover with her thumb.

"Barnacle," Maya whispered. "It's rising. Like a sunrise. But it's Earth."

"They call it **Earthrise**," said Barnacle. "In **December 1968**, three astronauts aboard **Apollo 8** became the first people ever to circle the Moon. One of them took a photo of exactly this."

"Can I draw it?" Maya asked, already flipping to a fresh page.

"Nobody's rushing you," said Barnacle.

Maya drew carefully: the gray Moon ground in front, the small blue Earth hanging above it, swirled with white clouds. She colored the ocean her favorite shade of boat-blue.

When she finished, her drawing glowed softly. So did the real Earth outside the window, as if the two pictures were shaking hands.

"It's so small," Maya said quietly. "Everyone I know is on that little ball."

"Every boat, every bathtub, every bed," said Barnacle.

Maya tucked her drawing into her sketchbook, right next to her racing flag. "What happens next?" she asked.

"Next," said Barnacle, "people stop circling the Moon, and finally land on it."

A bright dotted line sparked to life across the sky, leading off toward a nearby crater glowing gold.

"That way?" Maya asked, already steering the boat toward the light.

"That way," said Barnacle, and off they sailed.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: One Giant Leap
chapters.text:
A rocket stood on a distant launchpad, so tall it poked through the clouds.

"That's a **Saturn V** rocket," said Barnacle. "**363 feet** tall. Taller than the Statue of Liberty."

Maya tipped her head all the way back. "That's HUGE."

"Two men built rockets like it," said Barnacle. "**Wernher von Braun** led the American team. In the Soviet Union, a quiet genius named **Sergei Korolev** led theirs. It was such a secret that almost nobody knew his name until after he died, in 1966."

"That's sad," Maya said softly.

"It is," said Barnacle. "But his rockets flew on without him."

The Saturn V roared off the pad in a sheet of fire and smoke. The little boat shot forward in time, all the way to **July 20, 1969**.

A ladder unfolded from a spindly spacecraft. A boot touched gray dust.

"**Neil Armstrong**," Barnacle said. "The first person to ever walk on the Moon."

"That's one small step for man," crackled a radio voice, "one giant leap for mankind."

Maya watched, barely breathing, as a second astronaut climbed down to join him.

"That's **Buzz Aldrin**," said Barnacle. "And up above, circling all alone, waiting for them, is **Michael Collins**, flying the ship called Columbia."

"He's all by himself?" Maya asked.

"For a while," said Barnacle. "But he knew exactly what he was doing, and exactly when his friends were coming back."

Maya pulled out her sketchbook one more time. She drew two bootprints in gray dust, side by side.

The drawing glowed, and real bootprints appeared beside Armstrong's and Aldrin's, right there on the Moon.

"They're not alone," Maya grinned.

"Over the next few years," said Barnacle, "ten more astronauts followed those very first footprints, across five more landings."

Maya traced her bootprints with one finger. "Twelve people," she whispered. "Twelve people on the Moon."

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Splashdown and a Handshake
chapters.text:
The boat rocked suddenly, hard, and a warning light flashed red on the dashboard.

"What's wrong?" Maya grabbed the rail.

"This is **Apollo 13**, in **1970**," said Barnacle. "An air tank on board just had a problem. It gave the astronauts quite a jolt."

Maya's stomach dropped. "Are they okay?"

"They are," said Barnacle quickly. "Clever engineers back on Earth figured out a fix, step by step. The whole crew splashed down safely. Nobody was hurt."

Maya let out a breath she didn't know she was holding. "Good," she said firmly. "That's the most important part."

"Always is," said Barnacle, patting her hand with one flipper.

The warning light faded. The boat drifted on, calm again, toward one last glowing date: **July 17, 1975**.

Two spacecraft, one American and one Soviet, floated nose to nose in the quiet dark.

"After all that racing," Barnacle said, "the two sides finally decided to meet instead."

A hatch opened. An American hand reached through. A Soviet hand reached back, and the two shook, right there above the Earth.

"They're not racing anymore," Maya said. "They're friends."

"The Space Race was over," said Barnacle, "and everybody had won."

Maya pulled out her sketchbook one last time. She drew the two hands shaking, with Earth glowing blue behind them. The picture shimmered, and the stars around the boat began to melt back into warm, soapy bathwater.

SPLOOSH!

Maya blinked. She was back in the tub, water gone lukewarm, her sketchbook open on her knees to a brand-new page: two hands, shaking, in crayon.

"Five minutes was actually fifteen," called her mom, "but I'll let it slide tonight."

Barnacle winked one whiskery eye before sliding beneath the bubbles. "All aboard, Maya," he said. "Same time next sleep?"

Maya hugged her damp sketchbook to her chest and grinned all the way to her pajamas.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Maya — all aboard for dreamland.

true_facts.text: **Sputnik 1** was the first **satellite**, launched by the Soviet Union on **October 4, 1957**.
Sputnik 1 was about **fifty-eight centimeters** wide — the size of a beach ball — and sent out a simple **beep** anyone could hear on a radio.
A brave dog named **Laika** flew aboard Sputnik 2 on **November 3, 1957**, the first living creature to circle Earth.
The United States started a new space team called **NASA** on **October 1, 1958**.
America's **Explorer 1** satellite, launched **January 31, 1958**, found a hidden ring of space weather circling Earth.
On **April 12, 1961**, **Yuri Gagarin** became the first human in space, circling Earth once in about **108 minutes**.
On **May 25, 1961**, **President Kennedy** challenged America to land someone on the Moon and bring them home safe within ten years.
On **June 16, 1963**, **Valentina Tereshkova** became the first woman in space.
On **March 18, 1965**, **Alexei Leonov** became the first person to float outside his ship in space, tied on by a cord.
In **December 1968**, the crew of **Apollo 8** became the first people to circle the Moon, and took the famous **Earthrise** photo.
On **July 20, 1969**, **Neil Armstrong** became the first person to walk on the Moon.
In **1970**, an air tank problem on **Apollo 13** gave the crew a scare, but they all made it home safely.
The **Saturn V** rocket that carried astronauts to the Moon stood **363 feet** tall — taller than the Statue of Liberty.
On **July 17, 1975**, American and Soviet spacecraft met in space and the crews **shook hands**, ending the Space Race.

story.title: Zara and the Glowing Rock
story.subtitle: A sleepover trip to the fiery insides of the Earth

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Rock That Glowed
chapters.text:
Zara sat on her bedroom floor long after lights-out, sorting her rock collection by flashlight. Shiny ones here. Bumpy ones there. Sparkly ones in a pile all their own.

At the bottom of the box sat a smooth black rock she almost never noticed. Tonight it felt warm in her hand. Then it started to glow, soft and orange, like a tiny coal.

"Whoa," Zara whispered. "Rocks don't do that."

"This one does," said a small, crackly voice. The rock had a face now, barely there, like light flickering on glass. "I'm Glimmer. I used to be melted rock, bubbling hot underground. Down there we call it **magma**. The second I spilled out into the air and cooled down hard, I became something else — **lava** that turned to stone."

Zara grinned. "So you're a leftover splash?"

"A very old splash," Glimmer said. "Want to see where I came from?"

Before she could answer, the room filled with orange light. **WHOOOOSH!**

They landed on a black rocky slope in Hawaii, warm air pressing on Zara's cheeks. Below them, a lake of melted rock glowed and popped like soup left too long on the stove.

"This is **Kilauea**," Glimmer said. "A **volcano** — that's any spot where hot melted rock, ash, and gas escape up from under the ground."

Zara studied the mountain's shape. It wasn't pointy at all. It spread out low and wide, like an upside-down dinner plate.

"It's not a sharp mountain," she said slowly. "It's more like... a shield lying flat?"

"Exactly right," said Glimmer. "We call that a **shield volcano**, because that's just what it looks like. And Kilauea barely ever stops. It has been erupting on and off for decades — that's years and years."

The lava lake burped a bubble the size of a beach ball. Zara jumped back, then laughed so hard she snorted.

"Soup rock!" she shouted. "Bubbling SOUP ROCK!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Ring Around the Ocean
chapters.text:
Glimmer floated them up high, above the clouds, until Hawaii shrank to a green speck in a huge blue ocean.

"Look down," Glimmer said. "See how the ocean has an edge, almost all the way around, shaped like a horseshoe?"

Zara traced it with her finger. Japan. The Philippines. Down to South America and back up to Alaska.

"People call this the **Ring of Fire**," said Glimmer. "It's the spot where most of the world's volcanoes live — about three out of every four."

"Why there, though?" Zara asked. "Why not just anywhere?"

"Good question," Glimmer said. "The ground under your feet isn't one solid piece. It's cracked into giant puzzle pieces called **plates**, and they're always moving, just super slowly. Where two plates push together, or pull apart, or scrape past each other — that's where volcanoes love to pop up."

Zara squinted at one crowded little country near the middle of the ring. "That one has a LOT of dots."

"Sharp eyes," Glimmer said. "That's **Indonesia**. It has more active volcanoes than anywhere else on Earth."

"More than anywhere?" Zara repeated, delighted. "Like, the champion?"

"The champion," Glimmer agreed.

Zara counted dots on the map until she lost track, giggling every time she had to start over. "This is better than counting sheep," she said.

"Just wait," said Glimmer, glowing a little brighter. "There's one spot that breaks the whole rule."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Hot Spot Under Hawaii
chapters.text:
They dropped back down toward Hawaii, and Zara noticed something odd right away.

"Wait," she said. "You said volcanoes are at the edges of those puzzle pieces. But Hawaii's way out in the middle of the ocean!"

"Caught me," Glimmer said, sounding pleased. "Hawaii's volcanoes don't sit on an edge at all. They sit over a **hotspot** — a place deep down where extra-hot rock keeps rising up, like a candle flame that never blows out, no matter where the puzzle piece drifts on top of it."

Zara looked out at a second mountain nearby, even bigger than Kilauea, its wide shoulders rolling for miles.

"That one's huge," she breathed.

"That's **Mauna Loa**," said Glimmer. "The biggest active volcano on the whole planet, over four thousand meters tall from the sea up to its top. Bigger than it looks from here, and it already looks enormous."

Zara spread her arms wide, trying to show how big that felt, then gave up and just flopped backward dramatically onto the warm black rock.

"I can't even arms it," she said.

"You can't even arms it," Glimmer agreed, in a very serious voice, and Zara laughed so hard she rolled sideways.

She sat back up and pointed between the two mountains. "They're both the same shape, though. Both shields."

"Right again," said Glimmer. "Wide and gentle, built from lava that flows a long way before it cools. Not every volcano looks like this one. Some are tall and pointy instead, built from thicker, stickier stuff. We're headed to meet one of those next — and it has quite a story."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Day the Sky Went Dark
chapters.text:
The light shifted. Zara blinked, and suddenly she stood on a hillside above a sparkling blue bay, ancient stone buildings dotting the shore below.

"Where are we now?" she asked.

"Italy," said Glimmer. "The year is **79**. That mountain across the water is **Vesuvius**."

It didn't look scary. It looked almost sleepy, green and quiet. Then a thread of gray smoke curled up from its top, and Zara's stomach did a little flip.

"Is it going to blow up?" she asked.

"It already did, a long time before your today," Glimmer said gently. "This is just us watching it happen, safe and far away, like a movie. Vesuvius erupted so hard it covered two whole towns, **Pompeii** and **Herculaneum**, under thick, heavy ash."

Zara watched the smoke thicken into a tall gray cloud, shaped almost like a tree. A man stood on a rooftop nearby, scribbling fast on a scroll.

"Who's that?" Zara asked. "Shouldn't he run?"

"He's far enough away to be safe," said Glimmer. "His name is **Pliny the Younger**, and he's writing down everything he sees, because nobody has ever described an eruption like this before."

Zara watched him writing and writing. "He's basically taking notes on a volcano."

"He did it so well," Glimmer said, "that scientists still use his name today. Any volcano that blasts a tall cloud like that one gets called a '**Plinian**' eruption, after him."

"So he got a whole kind of explosion named after him just for writing a good letter?" Zara said, grinning. "I should start writing letters."

"Start with your rock collection," Glimmer suggested, and Zara decided that was actually a wonderful idea.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Loudest Bang Ever
chapters.text:
Next, the air turned warm and salty, and Zara found herself standing on a faraway beach, staring at an island with smoke pouring from its middle.

"This is **Krakatoa**," Glimmer said. "The year is **1883**. Cover your ears, just in case."

Zara clapped her hands over her ears and waited. Nothing happened.

"When does it—"

**BOOM.**

Even far away, even just watching, the sound rolled through her chest like thunder with no end.

"That's one of the loudest sounds ever made on Earth," said Glimmer. "People heard this very bang almost **three thousand miles away**, on a tiny island called Rodrigues."

Zara's mouth fell open. "Three THOUSAND? That's like... that's so far I can't even picture it!"

"Picture your town," Glimmer said. "Now imagine someone on the very other side of the whole country hearing you pop a balloon."

"No WAY," Zara said, delighted and a little bit stunned. "That's the loudest pop in the history of pops."

"Pretty much," said Glimmer, glowing with what might have been a laugh.

Zara sat down right there on the sand, still a little wide-eyed, and asked Glimmer to say the number again, just to hear it twice.
chapters.shout_line: THE LOUDEST POP IN THE HISTORY OF POPS!

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Summer That Never Came
chapters.text:
They traveled again, this time to a quiet mountain in Indonesia, the year **1815** hanging in the air like a label.

"This is **Tambora**," said Glimmer. "It had the biggest eruption anyone has ever recorded."

The mountain let out a huge dark cloud that spread and spread, drifting up high into the sky until it wrapped halfway around the whole Earth.

"All that ash floated so high," Glimmer explained, "that it blocked some of the sun's warmth, far away, for a whole year."

"Wait," Zara said, counting on her fingers. "So people somewhere else just... didn't get a summer?"

"Exactly. The next year, **1816**, people in Europe and America called it the 'Year Without a Summer.' Snow in June. Crops that wouldn't grow properly."

Zara looked up at the drifting ash cloud, trying to imagine snow falling in the middle of summer vacation.

"That's wild," she said. "One mountain, way over here, messed with people's SUMMER way over there?"

"One mountain," Glimmer confirmed. "That's how big these things can be."

Zara shivered, even though the air around them was warm, and tucked that thought away carefully, like a rock worth keeping.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Mountain That Lost Its Top
chapters.text:
The scene changed to green forest and a tall, snow-capped mountain that looked almost too perfect, like a drawing.

"Washington State," Glimmer said. "**Mount St. Helens**. The date is **May 18, 1980**."

"It's so pretty," Zara said. "Why do I feel nervous?"

"Scientists felt it too," Glimmer said. "For weeks, they'd been watching this mountain closely, using machines called **seismographs** that feel tiny wobbles in the ground, way too small for people to notice on their own."

As Zara watched from a safe distance, far up in the clear sky with Glimmer, the whole side of the mountain suddenly slid away in a massive landslide — the biggest ever recorded. A second later, the mountain itself burst open behind it.

**CRACK — WHOOOOSH!**

When the dust and ash finally settled, the mountain's whole top was gone — about **thirteen hundred feet** of it, simply blown away.

"Whoa," Zara breathed, eyes huge. "It just... doesn't have a top anymore."

"It doesn't," Glimmer agreed softly. "The scientists who studied this mountain worked hard to understand it, so that towns nearby would know when to stay away and stay safe."

Zara looked at the strange, flat-topped mountain for a long moment, then reached out and patted the air near it, the way she'd pat a dog that had been in a fight and won.

"Good job healing," she whispered. "You look tough now."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Baby Island
chapters.text:
The last stop smelled like salt and steam. Gray ocean stretched in every direction, and right in the middle of it, smoke hissed up out of the waves.

"Iceland, nearby waters," Glimmer said. "The year is **1963**. Keep watching the water."

Zara watched. Steam. A rumble. Then, slowly, black rock began poking up out of the sea, piece by piece, like a shy animal peeking out of its den.

"Is that..." Zara gasped. "Is a volcano building an ISLAND?"

"It is," said Glimmer. "A brand new island, called **Surtsey**, rising right out of the ocean because an underwater volcano kept on erupting."

"From nothing? From just... water and fire?"

"From nothing," Glimmer said. "Iceland sits on a spot where two of those giant puzzle pieces are pulling apart from each other, which is exactly why it has so many volcanoes of its own."

Zara watched the baby island grow a little more rock, a little more shape. "It's like the ocean is hatching an egg," she whispered.

"There's one more volcano I should mention," Glimmer added, "so you don't worry later. There's a giant one sleeping quietly under a place called Yellowstone. Its last big eruption was about **six hundred forty thousand years** ago, and nothing right now says it's waking up soon."

"So it's basically just... napping. Forever."

"Forever napping," Glimmer agreed. "Some volcanoes build you a new island. Some just nap for hundreds of thousands of years. Earth keeps all kinds."

Zara nodded slowly, watching Surtsey's dark rock gleam in the sunset. "Earth's weird," she said happily. "The best kind of weird."

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Back on the Carpet
chapters.text:
The glow folded in on itself, and Zara blinked — and there she was, back on her bedroom carpet, rock piles still sorted around her exactly as she'd left them.

Glimmer sat small and dark in her palm again, barely glowing now, just a faint ember-orange line along one edge.

"Did that really happen?" Zara whispered. "All of it? The soup lake, and the island being born, and the mountain that lost its top?"

"Every bit," Glimmer said. "You saw real places. Real mountains. Real splashes of me, a long, long time ago."

Zara turned the little black rock over in her fingers, looking at it completely differently now — not just a rock, but a tiny piece of something enormous, cooled down and carried all this way.

"You're basically a souvenir," she said. "From the whole entire Earth."

"I like that," said Glimmer, glowing just a touch brighter, pleased. "Keep me safe on your shelf. Next time your rocks start feeling warm, you'll know it's me, ready for another trip."

Zara set Glimmer gently on the very top of her tallest pile, right where she'd see it first thing, and pulled her blanket up to her chin.

"Goodnight, Zara," Glimmer murmured, glow fading to a whisper of orange, then nothing at all. "Sleep well, little rock hound."

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Zara. Sleep well, little rock hound.

true_facts.text: A **volcano** is any spot where hot melted rock, ash, and gas escape from under the ground.
Melted rock underground is called **magma**; once it spills out and cools, it becomes hard **lava** rock.
Hawaii's wide, gently sloping mountains are called **shield volcanoes**, because they're shaped like a shield lying flat.
**Kilauea** in Hawaii has been erupting on and off for decades, barely ever stopping.
The **Ring of Fire** is a horseshoe-shaped stretch around the ocean holding about three out of every four of the world's volcanoes.
**Indonesia** has more active volcanoes than any other country on Earth.
Hawaii's volcanoes sit over a **hotspot**, a place deep down where extra-hot rock keeps rising, even though it's far from the edge of any puzzle piece of ground.
**Mauna Loa** in Hawaii is the biggest active volcano on the whole planet, over four thousand meters tall.
In the year **79**, **Vesuvius** erupted so hard it buried the towns of **Pompeii** and **Herculaneum** under thick ash.
**Pliny the Younger** watched Vesuvius erupt and wrote it all down, so tall, explosive eruptions are still called '**Plinian**' after him.
In **1883**, **Krakatoa**'s eruption was so loud it was heard almost **three thousand miles** away.
In **1815**, **Tambora**'s huge eruption sent ash so high it helped cause snow in June the next year, a time people called the 'Year Without a Summer.'
On **May 18, 1980**, **Mount St. Helens** erupted and blew about **thirteen hundred feet** off its own summit.
In **1963**, the brand new island **Surtsey** rose straight up out of the ocean near Iceland from an underwater volcano.

new_recurring.name: Glimmer
new_recurring.rule: A small, smooth black rock in Zara's collection that warms up and glows soft orange when a new adventure is ready. It speaks in a gentle, crackly voice, always begins trips with a WHOOOOSH, and signs off each night calling Zara 'little…

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Zara returns to her bedroom floor and sets the now-quiet black rock Glimmer at the very top of her rock pile before falling asleep, certain it will warm up again for the next adventure.

scenarios.why: #48: B15 cell. A long story on a topic the children know better than the writer - accuracy and no brand worship.
scenarios.best_moment: "Everything's basically Minecraft to you," said Byte. Ben shrugged. "It's a good game."
scenarios.worst_moment: "In 2011, someone who makes games, in Sweden, named Markus Persson — folks called him 'Notch' — released a game," said Byte.
editor_notes: Fix the factual slips. Say Miyamoto's Mario first appeared in 1981 and starred in Super Mario Bros. in 1985. Credit Pong to Atari (or engineer Allan Alcorn). Drop Ben's claim that the Odyssey had only one built-in game.

Rebuild Level 8 around one hands-on beat for Ben instead of a four-stop montage. For example, let Ben race Sonic, or build something in early Minecraft, and cover the PlayStation and Hall of Fame in a line each.
Vary the chapter endings and cut repeated tics ("like it agreed," "Good eye"). Not every level needs the same "SHOUT CHAMPION!" closer.

story.title: Ben and the Pixel Time Machine
story.subtitle: One glowing block, every game that ever was.

chapters.heading: Level 1: The Green Wiggly Line (1958)
chapters.text:
Ben lay on his bedroom floor, controller in his lap, way past bedtime.

He was building a pixel art dragon in Minecraft, block by block, scale by scale.

Outside, the house was quiet. Only his screen glowed blue-white in the dark.

Then the screen flickered. A thin green line wiggled across it, bouncing like a tiny ball.

"Weird," Ben whispered. "That's not part of my build."

The line bounced faster. Then — **POP!** — a small blocky shape hopped right out of the screen and landed on his carpet.

It was pixelated all over, like a tiny person made of squares. It had a joystick for an arm and a smile made of three pixels.

"Hiya," it said. "Name's Byte. Wanna see where all this started?"

Ben blinked. "Started? Games have always been around."

"Nope," said Byte. "Press start and find out."

The carpet melted into a green glow, and Ben felt himself shrink down, down, down — until he was standing in a huge humming room full of machines.

A man in a lab coat stood at a round glowing screen, drawing with a little dial.

"That's **William Higinbotham**," said Byte. "In **1958**, he worked at a science lab called Brookhaven. He built a game called **'Tennis for Two.'**"

The screen was an **oscilloscope** — a machine that was really just for drawing wiggly lines, not games at all.

Ben watched the little green dot bounce back and forth over a line, like a ball going over a net.

"That's... tennis," Ben said slowly. "On a science machine."

"Bingo," said Byte. "First video game a lot of folks ever played."

Ben grabbed the dial. He turned it a little too far, and the green dot zoomed way up high.

"Whoa — is it gonna break?" Ben asked.

Byte laughed. "Nah. Just turn it back."

Ben turned the dial back. The dot settled down and bounced along the line again, steady as ever.

"PLAY BALL!" Ben shouted, and the little green dot bounced extra high, like it agreed.

chapters.heading: Level 2: The Dot Fight (1962)
chapters.text:
The green glow faded, and Ben found himself in a room stuffed with metal cabinets.

They hummed and clicked, taller than Ben's dad.

"This is a **PDP-1**," said Byte. "A giant computer — way, way bigger than yours."

Ben craned his neck to look up at it. "This is like ten of my computers stacked together."

"More buttons than your controller, too," said Byte.

A college student leaned over a small round screen, tapping two switches fast.

"That's **Steve Russell**," said Byte. "In **1962**, he and his friends at MIT made a game called **'Spacewar!'**"

On the screen, two tiny pixel spaceships spun around a dot in the middle, shooting little dashes at each other.

Ben leaned in. "Is that a star in the middle?"

"Yep," said Byte. "Pulls the ships in if they fly too close."

One ship swerved too near the star and spiraled in, spinning out of control.

"Watch the pull!" Ben called out, and the student yanked his switch back just in time, steering his ship away.

"Nice call," said Byte. "Took you one game to learn space flying."

"I just didn't want the ship to crash," Ben said.

He tried the switches himself, zooming his pixel ship in a loop around the star, dodging the other ship's shots.

**PEW PEW PEW**, went the tiny dashes across the screen.

"This is basically Minecraft, but in space," Ben said.

"Everything's basically Minecraft to you," said Byte.

Ben shrugged. "It's a good game."

He steered his ship around the star one more time, and the little screen beeped happily, like it agreed too.

chapters.heading: Level 3: The Brown Box and the Ping-Pong Game (1972)
chapters.text:
Next stop: a cozy workshop with wires everywhere.

A man with glasses fiddled with a wooden box hooked up to a TV.

"That's **Ralph Baer**," said Byte. "Folks later called him the 'father of video games.' He built a TV test box — he called it the **'Brown Box.'**"

Ben peered at the screen. Two white squares moved up and down, batting a white dot between them.

"It's like... ping pong," Ben said. "On a TV!"

"Exactly," said Byte. "And in **1972**, his box turned into a real toy you could buy — the **Magnavox Odyssey**. First game machine ever made for your living room."

Ben pressed a button, and his square bumped the dot back across the screen.

"Can I keep this?" Ben joked.

"Patience," said Byte. "There's more. Same year, at a company called Atari, two guys named **Nolan Bushnell** and **Ted Dabney** made their own bouncing-ball game for arcades — big rooms full of coin machines. They called it **Pong**."

The scene shifted. Now Ben stood in a noisy, blinking arcade, coins jingling in every pocket.

A line of kids waited to play one single machine with a screen that said PONG.

"People really liked this one," said Byte. "Story goes, one machine got so many quarters stuffed inside, it actually jammed shut."

"No way," Ben said.

"Might be a bit of a tall tale," said Byte, "but it tells you how wild everybody went for it."

Ben hopped up to the machine and spun the knob. His white paddle zipped up, smacking the dot clean past the other player.

**BOOP. BEEP. BOOP.**

"PING PONG CHAMPION!" Ben shouted, pumping his fist, and the whole arcade line cheered for him.

chapters.heading: Level 4: The Cartridge Trick (1977)
chapters.text:
The arcade noise faded into a quieter living room, carpet and a big boxy TV.

A kid about Ben's age held up a flat plastic rectangle, turning it over in his hands.

"That's a **cartridge**," said Byte. "A little plug-in game card."

"Wait," Ben said. "Didn't the machine before only play one game, stuck inside forever?"

"Good memory," said Byte. "But in **1977**, Atari made a new machine called the **Atari 2600**. Instead of one game stuck inside, you could pop in a different cartridge whenever you wanted."

The kid slid the cartridge into a slot on top of the machine — one you hook up to your TV to play games.

**CLICK.**

The TV blinked on, showing a totally new game.

"So it's like..." Ben thought for a second. "Minecraft worlds. You don't have to pick just one."

"Kind of exactly like that," said Byte.

Ben grabbed a second cartridge off the shelf and swapped it in himself.

**CLICK.** A whole different game popped up, bright and blocky.

"Whoa, that was fast," Ben said.

"That's the whole trick," said Byte. "One machine, tons of different games, easy as swapping a cartridge."

Ben counted the cartridges stacked on the shelf. "One, two, three," he said, holding up each one. "Three totally different games, same machine."

He swapped a third one in, just to prove he could.

**CLICK. CLICK. CLICK.**

"SWAP AND PLAY!" Ben yelled, holding up a stack of cartridges like trophies, and the kid on the carpet laughed and gave him a high five.

chapters.heading: Level 5: Invaders and the Missing Slice (1978–1980)
chapters.text:
The living room dissolved into another buzzing arcade, rows of glowing screens.

Rows of little pixel aliens marched slowly across one screen, side to side.

"That's **Space Invaders**," said Byte. "Made in **1978** by a designer named **Tomohiro Nishikado**, for a company called Taito. It kicked off a huge arcade craze — everybody wanted to play."

Ben watched the aliens march down, row by row, getting closer to the bottom.

"They're getting faster," Ben noticed.

"Sharp eyes," said Byte. "Fewer aliens left on screen means the rest speed up."

Ben grabbed the little cannon at the bottom and fired straight up.

**PEW!** One alien blinked out. The rest sped up again, marching quicker.

"They're not gonna reach me," Ben said, firing again and again, clearing the whole screen.

**ZAP ZAP ZAP!**

"Nice sweep," said Byte, and the machine next to them lit up with a new game.

A little yellow circle with a wedge cut out of it zipped through a maze, gobbling rows of dots.

"Is that... missing a slice?" Ben asked. "Like a pizza?"

"Good eye," said Byte. "This one's **Pac-Man**, made in **1980** by a designer named **Toru Iwatani**, for a company called Namco. Story goes, he got the idea staring at a pizza with one slice gone."

"Might not be totally true," Byte added, "but it's a fun story, and it sure looks like one."

Ben took the little joystick and steered Pac-Man around a corner, just missing a ghost.

"Left, left, up!" Ben called to himself, zooming through the maze and gobbling the last dot.

**WAKA WAKA WAKA WAKA.**

"CHOMP CHAMPION!" Ben shouted, and the screen flashed a happy little tune.

chapters.heading: Level 6: The Big Oopsie (1983)
chapters.text:
The arcade lights dimmed, and Ben found himself in a big, messy store, shelves stuffed with games.

So many games, boxes were falling over each other.

"Something went wrong here," Byte said, kicking a toppled box gently. "By **1983**, stores had way too many games, and a bunch weren't very good. People stopped buying as much, and lots of game companies had a tough time. Folks later called it the **video game crash** — not a crash like a car, just the games business getting a whole lot smaller for a while."

Ben picked up a box and frowned at the cover art, which didn't match the blocky picture on screen at all.

"That's kind of a bummer," Ben said.

"It was, for a while," said Byte. "But here's the funny part."

The store faded into a dusty desert, flat and sandy, under a big sky.

A line of diggers in hard hats stood around a huge hole.

"Story goes," said Byte, "that a bunch of unsold game cartridges got buried out here, in a big dump in New Mexico. People had heard about it for years, like a legend."

"Did anyone ever check?" Ben asked.

"In **2014**, they finally dug," said Byte. "And they found them. Cartridges, right there in the dirt."

One of the diggers held up a dusty cartridge, grinning, and wiped it clean with his sleeve.

Ben crouched down and brushed sand off a second cartridge himself, like a treasure hunter.

"Found one!" Ben called, holding it up.

"Nice digging," said Byte. "Turns out even a big oopsie makes a pretty good story."

Ben tucked the dusty cartridge under his arm. "I'm keeping this one."

"You can't," said Byte. "It's eighties sand. Nice try, though."

Ben laughed, dropped it back in the pit, and the diggers waved them both goodbye.

chapters.heading: Level 7: Falling Blocks and a Jumping Plumber (1984–1985)
chapters.text:
The desert spun away into a snowy, humming room full of computer screens, somewhere far from home.

"This is Moscow," said Byte, "and that's **Alexey Pajitnov**, a scientist who loved puzzles."

On his screen, blocky shapes drifted down from the top, stacking up at the bottom.

"In **1984**, he made this puzzle game," said Byte. "It's called **Tetris**. Shapes fall, and you fit them together."

Ben watched a long shape drop. "Turn it! It fits better sideways!"

Pajitnov spun the shape with a tap, and it slid neatly into a gap, clearing a whole row.

**CLEAR!** The row vanished, and everything above dropped down one.

"You called it," said Byte. "Good eye for shapes."

"I build with blocks every day," Ben said. "This is basically survival mode, but way more stressful."

The room shifted into a cozier spot — an office with a man sketching a round-faced character with a hat and mustache.

"That's **Shigeru Miyamoto**," said Byte. "He designed a jumping plumber hero in **1985**."

"Mario!" Ben shouted. "I know Mario!"

"Everyone does now," said Byte. "That same year, Nintendo put him on a new game machine called the **NES**, and packed it together with his game, **Super Mario Bros.** It helped bring video games back strong in America."

Ben grabbed a controller and hopped Mario clean over a gap, landing square on a floating block.

**BOING!**

A little coin popped out, spinning and chiming.

"JUMP TIMING!" Ben yelled, hopping Mario over a second gap just as smoothly.

Miyamoto looked over and gave Ben a thumbs up.

"Not bad for a kid who's never held this controller," Byte said.

"I've held a controller my whole life," Ben said. "Just not this one."

chapters.heading: Level 8: Blue Hedgehogs, Shiny Discs, and a Block from Home (1991–2015)
chapters.text:
The office melted into a blur of colors, fast as a racetrack.

A small blue creature zipped past Ben in a flash, curled into a spinning ball.

"That's **Sonic the Hedgehog**," said Byte. "Sega made him in **1991** — a fast blue character built to represent the company, racing against Mario."

Ben tried to keep up, running alongside the blur of blue.

"He's way faster than Mario," Ben panted.

"That was the whole point," said Byte.

The scene shifted again — a cozy room with a TV and a strange silver disc spinning inside a machine.

"In **1994**, a company called Sony made the **PlayStation**," said Byte. "It used shiny discs instead of cartridges, so games could look and sound way fuller than before."

Ben peeked at the disc spinning, watching a game load up on screen, full of smooth, round shapes.

"Cool," Ben said. "But I still like blocky better."

Byte grinned. "Funny you say that."

The room dissolved into green hills, blocky trees, a blocky sun — Ben's own world, almost.

"In **2011**, someone who makes games, in Sweden, named **Markus Persson** — folks called him **'Notch'** — released a game," said Byte. "You might know it. **Minecraft**."

Ben's jaw dropped. "Wait — this is MY game!"

"It became the best-selling video game ever made," said Byte. "Guess all those blocks really stuck with people."

Ben reached out and placed one pixel block on a blocky hill, just to say he'd done it.

**CLICK!**

The hills faded into a museum hallway, glass cases glowing softly, trophies lined up neat.

"This is the **World Video Game Hall of Fame**," said Byte. "Opened in **2015**, in Rochester, New York, to remember all the games that mattered."

Ben spotted a glowing case with a tiny green dot bouncing inside, just like the very first one.

"That one started it all," Ben said quietly.

"Every single game you've ever played," said Byte, "started with that one wiggly line."

The museum blurred, green light rushing past, and Ben felt the carpet under his knees again.

He was back in his room, controller still warm in his hand.

On his screen, his pixel art dragon stood finished, scales and all — and beside it, one tiny new block glowed bright green, one he was sure he hadn't placed.

Ben grinned and pulled his blanket up.

"Good game," he whispered.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Ben. Game saved — see you at the next level.

true_facts.text: A scientist named **William Higinbotham** made one of the very first video games, called **'Tennis for Two,'** in **1958**.
In **1962**, **Steve Russell** and his friends at MIT made a space game called **'Spacewar!'** on a giant computer called a **PDP-1**.
**Ralph Baer** built an early TV game box called the **'Brown Box.'**
In **1972**, Baer's box became the **Magnavox Odyssey** — the first game machine made for home TVs.
Also in **1972**, **Nolan Bushnell** and **Ted Dabney** started a company called **Atari** and made the arcade game **Pong**.
In **1977**, the **Atari 2600** let players swap in different game **cartridges** instead of playing just one game.
In **1978**, **Tomohiro Nishikado** made **Space Invaders**, starting a huge arcade craze.
In **1980**, **Toru Iwatani** made **Pac-Man** — some say he got the idea from a pizza missing a slice, though that part might be a bit of a tall tale.
By **1983**, too many games — and not very good ones — made people stop buying as much, which hurt the game business for a while.
In **2014**, diggers found old, unsold game cartridges buried in a big dump in New Mexico, just like the old story said.
In **1985**, Nintendo's new **NES** machine came packaged with **Super Mario Bros.**, helping bring video games back strong.
In **1984**, **Alexey Pajitnov** invented the falling-block puzzle game **Tetris** in Moscow.
In **2011**, **Markus 'Notch' Persson** released **Minecraft**, which went on to become the best-selling video game ever made.
The **World Video Game Hall of Fame** opened in **2015** in Rochester, New York, to remember games that mattered.

story.title: Lena and the Ball Called Match
story.subtitle: A four-thousand-year dribble through the history of soccer

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: A Ball That Talks Back
chapters.text:
Lena was supposed to be asleep. Instead she was diving across her bedroom carpet, goalkeeper gloves on, saving a balled-up sock from an invisible striker. Ten o'clock. Eleven more saves and she'd call it a night.

On the shelf above her bed sat the ball she'd found at a flea market last summer — brown leather, scuffed bald in spots, laces crossed in a stitched X. It had never done anything interesting. Until tonight.

Its seams lit up gold, like it had swallowed a floodlight. A hum rolled out of it, low and crowded, like a stadium breathing. Lena froze, sock-ball still in her glove.

The ball rolled off the shelf, bounced once on her rug, and spoke in a voice like a radio stuck between stations. "AND SHE SAVES IT," it crackled. "Finally. A keeper who actually dives."

"You talk," Lena said, which seemed like the important part.

"I'm Match," said the ball. "Get your gloves. We've got thousands of years of football to watch, starting with a game that didn't even use a round ball."

Green light swallowed the bedroom. When it cleared, Lena stood on hard-packed dirt, and a dozen players were booting a leather ball between two bamboo poles.

"**China**," said Match. "More than **2,000 years ago**. This game is called **cuju** — 'kick ball.' No hands, same as now. A lot of people think it's the oldest football game anyone's found."

A player flicked the ball off his shoulder, juggled it twice, and threaded it through the poles without it touching ground. Lena's jaw dropped.

"That's a better first touch than half my team," she said.

Match bounced twice, pleased. "AND WHAT A MOMENT THIS IS."
chapters.shout_line: AND WHAT A MOMENT THIS IS!

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Too Wild for London (1314)
chapters.text:
The green light faded into a muddy street, and chaos arrived with it. Dozens of men were shoving down a lane after a ball, smashing through fences, crashing into a fruit stall.

"WHOA," Lena said, stepping back fast. "Is this a game or a riot?"

"Bit of both," said Match, rolling to dodge a flying cabbage. "They call it **mob football**. Whole villages play at once, no teams marked out, barely any rules. Sometimes the whole town is the field."

A crier climbed onto a barrel and bellowed something official-sounding.

"**King Edward II**," Match translated, "just banned this in **London**, in **1314**. Too much property getting flattened."

Lena watched a man sprint past clutching the ball to his chest like a loaf of bread. "They don't even kick it much," she said.

"That's the problem," said Match. "Nobody's agreed on rules yet. That's still five hundred years away."

Lena ducked a swinging gate someone had torn off its hinges. "I vote we find somewhere with a referee."

"Your wish," said Match, "in three seconds."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: One Rulebook to Rule Them All (1863)
chapters.text:
Lena landed in a tidy room full of young men arguing over a chalkboard.

"**Cambridge University**, **1848**," said Match. "Students from different schools learned football with different rules — some let you catch it, some let you trip people. So they sat down and wrote the **Cambridge Rules**: one version everyone could agree on."

Lena pointed at a man scribbling furiously, ink-stained to the elbow. "Who's that?"

"**Ebenezer Cobb Morley**," said Match. "Jump forward fifteen years with me."

The scene shifted to a smoky meeting room crowded with top hats. Morley stood reading from a stack of papers.

"The **Football Association**," Match said. "Founded right here in **London**, on **26 October 1863**. Morley wrote the first official rulebook, the **Laws of the Game**. Rule everyone remembers: no carrying the ball with your hands."

"Finally," Lena said. "Keepers get the exception, right?"

"Not yet, actually," said Match. "You're ahead of your time."

Lena grinned and mimed catching a cross anyway. "Somebody had to be."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Nil-Nil and a Nickname (1872)
chapters.text:
Fog rolled across a Glasgow pitch, and two teams lined up in long sleeves and heavy boots.

"**Scotland** versus **England**," said Match. "**1872**. The first official international match in the sport's history."

Lena squinted at the scoreline chalked on a board. Ninety minutes later, it still read nothing to nothing.

"That's it?" Lena said. "Zero-zero?"

"A scoreless draw," Match agreed. "Still the start of something enormous."

Lena noticed a schoolboy nearby calling the game "soccer" instead of football, and asked Match why.

"English schoolboys in the **1880s** loved shortening words," said Match. "'**Association** football' got chopped to '**assoc**,' then to '**soccer**.' Same game, just a nickname that stuck."

"So I'm playing assoc right now," Lena said, flexing her gloved fingers.

"Technically," said Match, "you're about to referee a scoreless draw forever if we don't move on."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The First World Cup (1930)
chapters.text:
The fog cleared into a packed stadium roaring in Spanish.

"**Montevideo, Uruguay**," said Match. "**1930**. The first ever **World Cup**."

"Who even runs that?" Lena asked.

"**FIFA**," said Match. "Football's world organizer. Seven countries founded it in **Paris**, back in **1904**, so everyone everywhere could play by the same rules. A man named **Jules Rimet** pushed hardest to get a real World Cup started — they even named the first trophy after him."

On the field below, Uruguay scored again, and the home crowd roared loud enough to rattle Lena's teeth.

"Uruguay's winning," she said, reading the scoreboard.

"They beat **Argentina** in the final," said Match. "Hosts, and champions, in the very first tournament."

Lena watched the home goalkeeper punch a cross clear, mud to his eyebrows, grinning the whole time. "I'd dive in that mud all day," she said.

"AND WHAT A MOMENT THIS IS," crackled Match, and for once Lena said it right along with him.
chapters.shout_line: AND WHAT A MOMENT THIS IS!

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Banned, Then Unstoppable (1921–1991)
chapters.text:
The scene jumped to a packed English stadium, thousands of fans crammed in to watch women's football.

"The **Dick, Kerr Ladies**," said Match. "One of England's most popular teams, thanks partly to a forward named **Lily Parr** who could blast a ball harder than most of the men around her."

Lena watched a player smash a shot into the top corner, and the crowd came off their feet.

Then Match's voice dropped, less crackle, more serious. "In **1921**, the people running English football banned women's teams from their grounds. Fifty years, for no good reason."

Lena's stomach sank. "That's not fair."

"It wasn't," said Match. "But it didn't stick forever. The **FA** finally lifted the ban in **1971**."

The light shifted into a stadium in **China**, banners snapping in the wind.

"**1991**," said Match. "The first official **Women's World Cup**. The **United States** won it."

Lena watched the American keeper leap full stretch to tip a shot over the bar, and pumped her fist like she'd made the save herself. "That's the one I'm stealing for practice," she said.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: A Dog Named Pickles (1966)
chapters.text:
Lena landed beside a glass case, empty where a golden trophy should have sat.

"Someone stole the actual **World Cup trophy**," said Match, "right here in **London**, before the **1966** tournament even started."

"They just... took it?" Lena said.

"For a week," said Match. "Until a dog out for a walk sniffed it out, wrapped in newspaper, under a hedge. His name was **Pickles**."

Lena laughed so hard she nearly fell over. "A dog solved it?"

"A dog solved it," Match confirmed. "That same year, **England** hosted the tournament and won the whole thing — their only title so far."

Match rolled her toward a wall of old photos — a Brazilian forward in yellow, mid-leap, chest out.

"**Pele**," said Match. "The only player ever on three World Cup-winning teams: **1958, 1962, and 1970**. Brazil's won it five times total, more than anybody."

Lena studied the photo's perfect balance in the air. "I want to save one of his shots someday."

"Good luck with that," said Match.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Red Light, Yellow Light (1970)
chapters.text:
The last stop smelled like fresh-cut grass. A referee jogged across the pitch and pulled a bright square of colored card from his pocket.

"**Ken Aston**," said Match. "A referee who got the idea sitting at a stoplight — red means stop, yellow means slow down. He brought yellow and red cards into the game at the **1970 World Cup**, so everyone, in any language, could see a warning coming."

Lena watched the referee flash yellow at a player who'd slid in late, and the whole stadium understood instantly, no translator required.

"That's actually clever," Lena admitted.

"Told you," said Match. "Now. Bedtime."

Green light rushed back in, and Lena landed on her own carpet, gloves still on, sock-ball still by her foot. The old leather ball sat on the rug, seams dim again, looking exactly as scuffed and ordinary as it had three hours — or four thousand years — ago.

Lena picked it up and set it back on the shelf, a little more carefully than usual.

"Goodnight, Match," she whispered.

The seams gave one last small flicker, like a wink, and went dark.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow at practice, Lena had a save to try — one she'd borrowed from 1991.

The first **World Cup** was held in **Uruguay** in **1930**, with Uruguay beating **Argentina** in the final.
**Jules Rimet** pushed hardest to create the World Cup, and the first trophy was even named after him.
**Lily Parr** helped make the **Dick, Kerr Ladies** one of England's most popular teams.
The **FA** finally lifted its unfair ban on women's football in **1971**, fifty years after it began.
The first official **Women's World Cup** was held in **1991**, and the **United States** won it.
In **1966** the World Cup trophy was stolen in **London**, then found safe a week later by a dog named **Pickles**.
**England** hosted and won the **1966 World Cup**, its only title so far.
**Pele** is the only player ever on three World Cup-winning teams: **1958, 1962, and 1970**.
Referee **Ken Aston** invented yellow and red cards, inspired by a traffic light, debuting at the **1970 World Cup**.

story.title: Stumps, Arjun: The Night Cricket's Guide to Sleep
story.subtitle: A bedtime report from the world's strangest commentator.

chapters.heading: Over 1: The Boy Who Twitched (1953)
chapters.text:
Arjun was lying flat on his stomach, flashlight under the blanket, reading the newest issue of his favorite comic for the fourth time.

"Five more minutes," he whispered to no one, the way he did every single night.

Then the flashlight flickered green, and the comic's last panel began to glow like a firefly had moved in. Something small and shiny popped out of the page and landed on his pillow. It had wings like a cricket — the chirping kind — and tiny sunglasses pushed up on its head.

"Nibs," it said, bowing. "Night Cricket. I commentate on sleep, the way your telly commentates on actual cricket. Fancy a look at tonight's match?"

Arjun sat up so fast the comic slid off the bed. "Sleep has a *match*?"

"Every night," said Nibs. "First ball's in **1953**, University of Chicago. Two scientists, Eugene Aserinsky and Nathaniel Kleitman, were watching a boy sleep."

"That's... creepy?" Arjun guessed.

"Science," corrected Nibs. "They noticed the boy's eyes twitching back and forth under his eyelids, fast, like he was watching a rally. They called it **REM sleep** — Rapid Eye Movement. Eyes racing, even though the boy looked totally still."

Arjun pressed his own eyes shut, trying to feel them move. Nothing happened, obviously — you can't catch yourself dreaming.

"Kleitman spent his whole life watching people sleep," Nibs said. "People still call him the father of the whole science of it."

"So I've got a secret eye-match going on every night?" Arjun said. "Nobody told me!"

"Lean in," said Nibs, "and I'll show you the whole innings."

chapters.heading: Over 2: The Ninety-Minute Over
chapters.text:
A glowing line now rippled across the dark like a scoreboard. It dipped low, then spiked, then dipped again.

"Every sleep is divided into rounds," Nibs said, "about **ninety minutes** each — roughly one half of a football match, if that helps."

Arjun squinted at the spikes. "They're like overs. Quiet, quiet, quiet, then — action!"

"Close enough," said Nibs. "The quiet part is called **non-REM** — your body resting, heart slowing down. Then it flips into REM, where you dream hardest and your brain gets almost as busy as when you're awake."

"But I don't sleepwalk every night," Arjun said. "So what stops me acting it out?"

"Good question — the exact one scientists asked," Nibs said. "During REM, your muscles basically switch off. Go floppy. Your brain can run around all it wants. Your body just lies there like a sack of kit bags."

Arjun tried to imagine his arms gone totally limp while his brain played test cricket inside his own skull. "That's either amazing or terrifying."

"Bit of both," Nibs agreed. "Now — count the spikes with me. How many rounds in a normal night?"

Arjun counted along the glowing line. "Four? Five?"

"Four or five," Nibs confirmed. "A whole tournament, every single night."
chapters.shout_line: A WHOLE TOURNAMENT, EVERY SINGLE NIGHT!

chapters.heading: Over 3: The Clock Behind Your Eyes
chapters.text:
Nibs led him through a corridor shaped like the inside of a comic panel, until they reached a glowing knot of light shaped like a tiny stadium clock, nestled right behind Arjun's own eyes.

"That," said Nibs, "is the **suprachiasmatic nucleus**. Say it three times fast and you win a prize."

Arjun tried. He did not win a prize.

"Everyone just calls it the master clock," Nibs said. "It sits exactly where the nerves from your two eyes cross over, and it keeps your whole body on schedule — sleepy at night, awake in the day."

"So that's why I get tired at the same time every night," Arjun said, "even on holiday, even with no clock in the room."

"Exactly. Scientists have a word for a clock that runs about once a day: **circadian**. It comes from old Latin words that basically mean 'about a day.'"

"Circa-day," Arjun repeated, liking the sound of it. "Like a day-shaped boomerang."

"Not far off," said Nibs. "It keeps coming back whether you want it to or not — which is bad news for anyone hoping for five more minutes."

Arjun groaned. The clock had clearly heard that joke before.

chapters.heading: Over 4: Three Scientists and a Fly (2017)
chapters.text:
A tiny fly buzzed past Arjun's ear and landed, dead still, on the scoreboard clock.

"Is it... sleeping?" Arjun asked. "It's a fly. Its brain's the size of a comma."

"Even flies go still like they're asleep," Nibs said. "Scientists think sleep might be one of the oldest tricks in the whole animal game — older than cricket, older than comics, older than pretty much everything alive."

Arjun looked at the fly with new respect.

"The clock behind your eyes runs on tiny genes," Nibs went on, "switches inside your cells that tick off the hours. In **2017**, three scientists — Jeffrey Hall, Michael Rosbash, and Michael Young — won the **Nobel Prize**. That's basically the gold medal of science. They won it for finding those very genes."

"They won a medal," Arjun said slowly, "for other people's bedtimes."

"For *everyone's* bedtimes," said Nibs. "Fly bedtimes included."

The fly gave what might have been a shrug, and went straight back to sleep.

chapters.heading: Over 5: The Lights-Out Hormone (1958)
chapters.text:
The stadium floodlights began to dim on their own, dropping from white to orange to a sleepy purple.

"Who's doing that?" Arjun asked.

"A little chemical messenger called **melatonin**," said Nibs. "Scientists call it a hormone — basically a note your body sends itself. This note says: lights out."

"Where does it even come from?"

"A pea-sized part of your brain makes it, as soon as the room goes properly dark. In **1958**, a scientist named Aaron Lerner led the team that first managed to pull it out and study it closely."

Arjun watched the lights fade almost to nothing, like a stadium after the last ball of the day.

"So melatonin's basically an umpire," he said, "calling stumps on the whole day?"

"Best comparison I've heard all night," said Nibs, sounding genuinely impressed.

"I have good ones sometimes," Arjun said, trying not to look too pleased with himself.

chapters.heading: Over 6: The Rinse Cycle and the Growth Spurt
chapters.text:
They moved to a part of the stadium where everything looked freshly mopped, pipes gurgling overhead.

"Every night your brain runs its own rinse cycle," Nibs said. "Scientists call it the **glymphatic system** — think of it as a cleaning crew flushing out waste while you're deep asleep."

"Gross," said Arjun, "but also kind of great."

"During the deepest part of non-REM sleep," Nibs went on, "your body releases the most **growth hormone** — the stuff that helps you grow taller. One reason kids need more sleep than grown-ups."

Arjun perked up. "So sleep makes me taller? For cricket?"

"Partly," said Nibs. "It also sorts your memories, filing the important stuff into long-term storage. Like that bowling grip you practiced today."

"So if I sleep well tonight," Arjun said, working it out loud, "I'll remember it better tomorrow?"

"That's the theory," said Nibs. "Sleep's basically doing your homework while you're unconscious."

Arjun decided, right there, that sleep was extremely underrated.

chapters.heading: Over 7: The Sleep Scoreboard
chapters.text:
A glowing scoreboard rose up, shaped like the ones at the cricket ground, except it listed animals instead of teams.

"Sleep records," Nibs announced. "Pick one."

Arjun pointed straight at the dolphin. "Dolphins can't fully fall asleep, right? They'd drown."

"They solve it by sleeping with half their brain at a time," Nibs said. "One eye stays open, watching for danger, while the other half rests. Seals do something similar."

"Next," said Arjun, scanning down. "Giraffe — only two hours?"

"Sometimes under two, in short naps, standing right up," Nibs confirmed. "Shortest sleeper of any big animal."

"And bats pull the opposite stunt," Nibs added before Arjun could even ask. "Some small ones sleep up to **twenty hours** a day. Laziest mammals on record."

"What about baby humans?" Arjun asked, thinking of his cousin's new little sister.

"Newborns sleep **fourteen to seventeen hours**, in short bursts, nearly half of it in REM," said Nibs. "All that dreaming helps build a brand-new brain."

Arjun did some quick math in his head. "So by the time I'm old, I'll have slept through, what, a third of my whole life?"

"Just about," said Nibs. "Which means you're basically a professional at this already."

chapters.heading: Over 8: The Boy Who Stayed Awake (1964)
chapters.text:
"One more player," said Nibs, the lights dropping low, almost stumps. "In **1964**, San Diego — a seventeen-year-old called Randy Gardner stayed awake for about **eleven days** straight, for a school science project."

Arjun's mouth fell open. "ELEVEN DAYS? That's basically a whole series!"

"It's one of the longest stretches anybody's ever properly recorded," Nibs said. "But listen close — doctors do not want anyone trying to break that record. Go without sleep that long and your mood crashes, your attention goes to pieces, you forget everything. Randy turned out fine, but nobody recommends the stunt."

Arjun thought about his own nightly argument for five more minutes, multiplied by eleven days, and felt a little ill.

"Message received," he said. "Five more minutes is my absolute limit."

"Good," said Nibs, folding his wings. "Stumps."

The stadium lights dimmed to nothing. The comic slid shut on its own, its glowing edge fading back to ordinary paper. Nibs hopped onto the last panel and gave a small salute.

"Same time tomorrow?" Arjun whispered.

"Every innings needs a tomorrow," said Nibs, and blinked out.

Arjun set the flashlight down, pulled the blanket up, and for once did not ask for five more minutes.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow's nets could wait; tonight was for letting that bowling grip settle in, rested and ready to remember itself.

true_facts.text: In **1953**, two scientists at the University of Chicago discovered **REM sleep** by watching a sleeping boy's eyes twitch back and forth under his eyelids.
A night's sleep comes in repeating rounds about **ninety minutes** long, moving between quiet rest and busy, dreaming REM sleep.
During REM sleep the brain gets almost as busy as when you're awake, but your muscles go floppy so you can't act out your dreams.
A tiny part of the brain called the **suprachiasmatic nucleus**, sitting right where the eye nerves cross, works as the body's master clock.
The word **circadian**, used for the body's about-a-day clock, comes from old Latin words meaning "about a day."
In **2017**, three scientists won the **Nobel Prize** for finding the tiny genes that keep the body's clock ticking.
The sleepy-time chemical messenger **melatonin** was first pulled out and studied by Aaron Lerner's team in **1958**.
The deepest part of sleep releases the most **growth hormone**, one reason growing kids need extra sleep.
Sleep helps sort the day's experiences into long-term memories, which can help you remember what you practiced.
Every night the brain runs a kind of rinse cycle, called the **glymphatic system**, flushing waste out while you sleep.
Dolphins and seals sleep with only half their brain at a time, keeping one eye open to watch for danger.
In **1964**, seventeen-year-old Randy Gardner stayed awake for about **eleven days** for a science project — one of the longest stretches ever properly recorded.
Doctors say nobody should try to beat that no-sleep record, since going without sleep quickly wrecks your mood, attention, and memory.

new_recurring.rule: A tiny glowing cricket who hops out of a comic page at bedtime to commentate on sleep science using cricket-match language. He ends every visit by saying "Stumps."
