story.title: Tom and the Wheel That Remembered Everything
story.subtitle: Nine stops on two hundred years of bicycles

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Running Machine (1817)
chapters.text:
Tom had the garage light on an hour past bedtime, his mountain bike flipped upside down on the workbench, back wheel spinning free.

The derailleur — the little arm that slides his chain between gears — had skipped on the trail today, dumping him into the wrong gear halfway up Devil's Elbow. He wanted to know why.

He spun the wheel again, listening to each click. On the third spin, the hub — the metal center where all the spokes meet — glowed warm gold and hummed like a tuning fork.

"Finally," said a voice from inside the metal. "A mechanic who actually listens to his bike. Most people just pedal."

Tom nearly dropped his wrench. "Bikes don't talk."

"This one does," said the voice. "I'm Hub. Want to meet the man who built the first one? Hang on to the frame."

The garage walls smeared sideways. WHOOOOSH. Cobblestones replaced concrete under his sneakers.

A man in a long coat strode along a park path on two wooden wheels, pushing off the ground with his feet like he was running on rolling stilts.

"Karl von Drais," said Hub. "**1817**. He calls it his 'running machine' — no pedals at all. You just push."

The wheels wobbled, then steadied the instant von Drais leaned into a turn and steered the handlebars — exactly like cornering on a trail.

"He's basically scootering," Tom said. "Lean into the turn, not away from it."

Von Drais rolled past, grinning. "Some call her the **hobby horse**, young man. But she steers — handlebars, same as yours."

Tom grinned back. The man had basically invented steering, and he looked thrilled about it.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Boneshaker (1860s)
chapters.text:
Hub spun faster, and the cobblestones turned into a Paris workshop that smelled of hot metal.

A man was bolting a pedal straight onto a front wheel — no chain, just a crank fixed to the hub itself.

"Pierre Michaux and Pierre Lallement," said Hub. "**1860s**. They called it the velocipede. Riders called it something else."

"Let me guess," Tom said, eyeing the solid iron wheels. "Nothing soft between you and the road."

"They called it the **boneshaker**," Hub said. "No rubber, no suspension. Every cobblestone, straight into your teeth."

Tom swung a leg over and pedaled onto the street. The front wheel juddered over the stones so hard his vision blurred. RATTLE-RATTLE-RATTLE.

"This needs cushioning," he shouted over the noise, bracing his arms the way he braced on rock gardens back home. "Something in the wheel, not just on top of it."

Lallement laughed, jogging alongside. "Already thinking like an engineer. Patent that idea and it's yours — I patented mine for pedals, in **1866**, over in the United States. First to register it as my own invention."

Tom climbed off, rubbing his arms. "Pedals were a great idea. The ride still needs work."

"Everything does, at first," said Hub, sounding pleased.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Penny-Farthing (1870s)
chapters.text:
The workshop dissolved into a sunny street lined with top hats and stares, all pointed at one enormous wheel.

A front wheel taller than Tom himself carried a tiny back wheel behind it like an afterthought.

"The **penny-farthing**," said Hub. "**1870s**. Named for two old coins — a big penny and a tiny farthing."

Tom studied the gearing. No chain, no derailleur — the pedals bolted straight to that giant front hub. "One turn of the pedals," he said slowly, "and you roll forward as far as the whole wheel goes around. That's like riding in your highest gear, permanently."

"Exactly," said Hub. "Fast, if you can reach the seat."

A rider wobbled past, perched impossibly high, then hit a stone. The front wheel stopped dead. The rider pitched forward over the handlebars — and caught himself, rolling neatly onto the grass, hat rolling after him.

Tom winced, then laughed when the man sat up, unhurt, brushing off his coat. "They call that **taking a header**," Hub said. "Common enough that everybody had a name for it."

"Big wheel, big gear, big problem if you stop fast," Tom said. "Somebody needs to build this lower to the ground."

"Patience," said Hub. "Fifteen years."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Safety Bicycle (1885)
chapters.text:
The street blurred, and Tom landed in an English workshop full of metal tubing and two wheels — the same size.

A chain looped from a pedal crank back to the rear wheel, just like the one Tom had been oiling an hour ago.

"John Kemp Starley," said Hub. "**1885**. He calls it the Rover Safety Bicycle."

Tom crouched by the chain, tracing it with one finger. "This is basically my drivetrain. Pedals turn a gear, the gear pulls a chain, the chain spins the back wheel. No giant front wheel at all."

"Lower seat, even wheels," said Starley, wiping grease from his hands. "Nobody takes a header off this one."

Tom swung a leg over and pushed off. It rolled smooth and level, nothing like the wobbling tower from before. "This is just... a bike," he said. "A normal bike."

"That's the point," said Hub. "Within a few years, this became the standard, everywhere."

Tom pedaled a slow circle around the workshop yard, grinning. It felt like coming home two hundred years early.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Air in the Tire (1888)
chapters.text:
Hub's hum shifted lower, and the workshop became a Scottish yard, a boy on a wooden tricycle bumping over gravel.

A man knelt beside the trike, wrapping a rubber tube around the wheel rim and pumping it full of air with a hand pump.

"John Boyd Dunlop," said Hub. "**1888**. He's a vet, not an engineer — just wanted a smoother ride for his son's tricycle."

"A **pneumatic** tire," Hub added. "Air-filled rubber, instead of solid metal or wood."

The boy rode off across the gravel, and the rattling stopped completely. Tom could hear the difference from across the yard — just the quiet hiss of rubber rolling.

"That's suspension," Tom said, crouching to press the tire with his thumb. It sank and sprang back. "Same idea as the shocks on my mountain bike. Air soaks up the bumps before they reach you."

Dunlop looked up, surprised. "Soaks up the bumps. I like that."

"His company's still around," Hub said. "You've probably seen the name on tires."

"Dunlop," Tom said. "Yeah. Didn't know it started with a kid's tricycle."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Golden Age (1890s)
chapters.text:
The yard became a crowded avenue, bicycles everywhere, bells ringing like a flock of birds.

"The **Golden Age of Bicycles**," said Hub. "**1890s**. Millions sold, across Europe and America."

A woman rode past in puffy, practical pants instead of a long skirt, pedaling fast and laughing at nothing in particular.

"Long skirts used to catch in the chain and gears," Hub said. "So women started wearing **bloomers** instead — looser pants, safer around moving parts."

"That's a design problem," Tom said. "The clothes were wrong for the machine, so the clothes changed."

"Exactly how an engineer would put it," Hub said. "A reformer named Susan B. Anthony said cycling had done more to **emancipate** — to free — women than anything else in the world. Suddenly they could go wherever they wanted, whenever they wanted."

Tom watched the woman disappear around a corner, pedaling hard, going nowhere in particular and everywhere she chose. "That's not a small thing," he said. "That's just... freedom with wheels."

"Most good inventions are," said Hub.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Bicycle Shop in Dayton (1890s)
chapters.text:
The avenue narrowed into a small American shop, tools hanging on every wall, the smell of oil and sawdust.

Two brothers were bent over a wheel, threading thin spokes through a hub, their hands quick and sure.

"Wilbur and Orville Wright," said Hub. "They repair and build bicycles here, in Dayton, Ohio, in the **1890s**."

Tom picked up a length of metal tubing from the workbench — light, almost hollow, barely heavier than a straw. "This is why racing bikes are light," he said. "Thin tubes, strong metal, no wasted weight."

"Keep that thought," Hub said. "These two use those same tricks — light tubing, spoked wheels — on something else entirely, a few years later."

"What else needs to be light and strong?" Tom asked.

Orville looked up, almost smiling. "Something that needs to leave the ground."

Tom's eyebrows went up. "Wait. You're not — the Wright brothers? The actual first airplane?"

"**1903**," said Hub. "Bicycle mechanics first. Flyers second."

Tom looked at the spoked wheel in Wilbur's hands with new respect. Turns out the sky owed bicycles something.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Dirt Trail (1970s)
chapters.text:
The shop spun away into a blur of gears and finish lines, and Tom landed somewhere that finally felt like his own backyard.

"Quick stops first," said Hub. "**1930s**: multi-speed gears, called derailleurs, let riders shift up or down for hills."

"I know derailleurs," Tom said. "Mine broke yesterday."

"**1903**: the Tour de France starts. Today it covers about **3,500 kilometers**, over three weeks, across France."

Tom whistled. "That's insane."

"**1970s**: sturdy little **BMX** bikes show up in America, built for tricks and dirt, copying off-road motorcycle racing — motocross."

Then the trail itself appeared under Tom's feet — real dirt, real roots, a hill dropping away below him.

A group of riders in Marin County, California, were bolting wide, bumpy tires onto old heavy frames, grinning like they'd invented Christmas.

"**Mountain bikes**," Hub said. "Same decade. Built by riders who wanted to go down rough trails, not just up paved roads."

Tom looked down at his own bike, waiting back in the garage a hundred years away, and understood exactly where it came from.

"That's my bike," he said. "That's literally my bike."

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Back to the Garage
chapters.text:
The trail spun away, and concrete replaced dirt under Tom's sneakers. The garage light was still on. The wheel was still spinning, slowing now, clicking down to a stop.

"One more thing," said Hub, glowing softer. "There are over **one billion** bicycles in the world today. More than any other kind of vehicle, anywhere."

"A billion," Tom repeated.

"In places like the Netherlands and Denmark, some cities have more bikes than cars, with wide lanes built just for riders. And the fanciest racing bikes now weigh under **eight kilograms** — lighter than your backpack."

Tom crouched and spun the back wheel one last time. It ticked around smooth and even, no skip, no catch.

"Fixed," he said, surprised. He hadn't touched the derailleur in an hour.

"You didn't fix the bike," Hub said. "You just finally understood it. Same thing, usually."

Tom flicked off the garage light and looked back once at his bike, hanging quiet on its hook, two hundred years of other people's ideas built into every bolt.

Tomorrow, Devil's Elbow was waiting, and this time he knew exactly what was turning under him.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow, he had a trail to ride, and a derailleur that finally made sense.

true_facts.text: In **1817**, Karl von Drais built a wooden two-wheeler called a **running machine** that had no pedals — riders pushed it along with their feet.
Von Drais's invention was nicknamed the **hobby horse**, and it steered with handlebars, just like bikes today.

In the **1860s**, French makers Pierre Michaux and Pierre Lallement bolted pedals straight onto a front wheel, building the **velocipede** — riders called it the **boneshaker** because it rattled so hard on cobblestones.
The **penny-farthing** had a giant front wheel and a tiny back wheel, named after two old coins of very different sizes.
Riding a penny-farthing was risky — a sudden stop could throw the rider forward, a fall nicknamed **taking a header**.
In **1885**, John Kemp Starley built the **Safety Bicycle**, with two even-sized wheels and a chain driving the back wheel.
In **1888**, John Boyd Dunlop invented the **pneumatic tire** — an air-filled rubber tire — to give his son's tricycle a smoother ride.
In the 1890s, reformer Susan B. Anthony said bicycles helped **emancipate**, or free, women more than almost anything else, letting them travel on their own.
Wilbur and Orville Wright ran a bicycle shop in Dayton, Ohio, in the 1890s, before building the first successful airplane in **1903**.
The **Tour de France**, the world's most famous long bike race, began in **1903** and today covers about **3,500 kilometers**.
**Mountain bikes**, built with wide, bumpy tires for rough dirt trails, were developed in the 1970s in Marin County, California.
Today there are more than **one billion** bicycles in the world — more than any other kind of vehicle.
In places like the Netherlands and Denmark, some cities have more bicycles than cars, with wide lanes built just for riders.

new_recurring.rule: Hub is the glowing, humming voice living inside any bicycle wheel's center hub Tom is working on. He appears when Tom is fixing or spinning a wheel late at night, speaks in a dry, steady, slightly pleased-with-itself tone, and always…

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Tom's garage wheel clicks to a smooth, un-skipping stop, Hub's glow fades, and Tom heads to bed knowing exactly how his mountain bike's drivetrain works for tomorrow's ride.

story.title: Hana and the Titanic's True Course
story.subtitle: One brass compass, one old chart, and a ship that still has stories to tell.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Compass That Would Not Point North
chapters.text:
Hana was supposed to be asleep an hour ago. Instead she sat cross-legged on her bedroom floor with a ruler, tracing a line across an old chart of the North Atlantic Ocean pinned above her desk. It had belonged to her grandfather, a merchant sailor, and so had the brass compass sitting next to her knee.

The compass had never worked right. Its needle never settled on north. Tonight it spun faster than ever, then stopped dead and glowed a soft, sudden green.

Hana leaned closer. The needle began to twitch in a pattern — short, short, long, short — like it was tapping out a message in some code she almost recognized. A thin ribbon of green light unrolled from the compass's open lid, and inside that light, a chart drew itself: a shipyard, a river, the shape of a half-built hull.

"Belfast," Hana whispered, reading the tiny glowing letters. "Ireland."

The light swallowed her bedroom whole.

When it let go, she was standing on a wooden platform above a river, under a sky loud with hammering. Below her, a steel spine as long as a city block lay propped on wooden blocks, men crawling over it like ants.

"That's not a ship," Hana said to a passing workman, pointing at the giant backbone of steel. "That's just... a beam."

"That's her keel, miss," the workman said, wiping his hands on his apron. "The spine we build everything else onto. We laid the first piece of it back in **March of 1909**. Build the spine first, then the ribs, then the skin."

Hana looked past him and counted — not one hull taking shape on the slipways, but two, side by side, nearly identical.

"There are two of them," she said slowly, tracing the twin shapes with her finger the way she traced coastlines on her own maps. "They're the same ship. Built twice."

The workman grinned, impressed. "Sharp eyes. That one's to be called **Olympic**. This one — the one you're standing over — will be **Titanic**. Built right here at **Harland & Wolff**, for a company called **White Star Line**. There's a third sister coming after, too, name of **Britannic**. Three ships, cut from the same plan."

Hana grinned back. Her grandfather's map had never shown her a city where ships were born in twins and triplets. She was starting to like Belfast.

"When does she get to go in the water?" Hana asked.

"Patience," said the workman. "A ship this size doesn't rush."

The compass in Hana's pocket buzzed, as if it agreed.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Launch Day
chapters.text:
Two years disappeared in a single green flash, and Hana found herself jammed into a crowd on the Belfast dockside, everyone craning their necks at the same enormous black hull.

"That's the same ship," Hana said, amazed. "It's finished. It's huge."

A woman beside her, holding a parasol against the sun, laughed. "Finished enough to float, dear. Not finished enough to sail. Today she only launches."

Hana checked the compass, which had gone warm and still in her pocket, like it trusted her to work this one out herself. She studied the hull from bow to stern, counting four tall smokestacks rising above the deck.

"Four funnels," she murmured. Then she noticed something — the fourth one, at the very back, had no soot streaking its paint. "Wait. That one's fake?"

The woman peered where Hana pointed. "Clever girl. Three funnels carry smoke from her boilers. The fourth is mostly there to look grand and let out extra air. A ship this size needs to look the part."

Somewhere, a bottle did not smash — White Star Line ships launched without the champagne ceremony other companies used — and instead a cannon of grease and tallow sent the hull sliding down the slipway on its own enormous weight.

**SPLOOOOSH!**

Spray exploded upward as nearly **882 feet** of steel hit the river for the first time, afloat for the first time in its life. The crowd roared.

"SHE FLOATS!" Hana shouted, along with everyone around her, and for once nobody told her to be quiet.

When the cheering settled, the woman explained the part Hana's map could never have shown her: below the waterline, the hull was divided into **sixteen separate watertight compartments** — rooms with doors that could seal shut so that water flooding into one wouldn't spread to the rest.

"That's why people are already calling her nearly unsinkable," the woman said.

Hana looked at the huge black hull floating calmly on the river, and believed it completely. She didn't know yet how much weight that word "nearly" was carrying.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Southampton, 10 April
chapters.text:
The green light set Hana down on a crowded pier, gulls wheeling overhead, a brass band somewhere playing loud enough to be heard over the crowd. The ship towering beside the dock was finished now — painted, polished, flags snapping from every mast.

"She sails today," said a woman in a wide hat, checking a small travel case at her feet. She had a brisk, cheerful voice, like someone used to being listened to. "**10 April, 1912**. Southampton to New York. My first time crossing on anything this grand."

"I'm Hana," said Hana, and because the woman seemed like someone worth asking, she asked: "Are you nervous?"

"Nervous? I once rowed myself out of worse scrapes than an ocean crossing." The woman winked. "Margaret Brown. Friends call me Maggie. You'll hear people call me other things eventually, after this trip — something about being unsinkable myself." She laughed at her own joke before Hana even understood it.

A whistle shrieked, long and deep, shaking the planks under their feet. Hana watched ropes thick as her arm get hauled in, watched the gap between hull and dock widen into open water.

She pulled her grandfather's compass from her pocket and lined it up with the ship's bow, the way she lined up her ruler on a chart at home. "New York's that way," she said, pointing west across the water.

"Not quite yet," Molly said. "We stop first in France, then Ireland, to pick up more passengers. Then it's open ocean, all the way across."

Hana watched the English coastline shrink behind them, green light humming faintly in her pocket like a held breath. She thought of her own bedroom map, the thin blue line she'd traced so many times between Europe and America, never quite able to picture how big that empty space really was until she was standing in the middle of it, deck thrumming under her sneakers, the whole Atlantic stretched out ahead like a chart waiting to be filled in.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Night of the Fourteenth
chapters.text:
Four days later, Hana stood at the rail in the dark, breath showing in the cold air. The sea around the ship had gone glassy and still, and the stars overhead were almost too bright to be real.

"Too calm," Molly Brown said beside her, pulling her coat tighter. "My grandmother always said still water hides things."

Hana checked her compass. The needle, usually lazy, was spinning in slow, uneasy circles.

Then, far ahead in the blackness, something pale slid past the edge of sight — gone before Hana could point at it.

A bell rang out from high in the ship, three sharp strikes, and a voice somewhere above shouted down to the bridge.

Hana felt the whole deck shiver, a long, grinding shudder she felt through her shoes more than heard. It passed in a few seconds. The ship didn't stop. It didn't even seem to slow.

"What was that?" Hana asked.

"Ice," said Molly, frowning now, all the cheerfulness gone quiet. "We've grazed an iceberg."

It was **11:40 at night**, on **14 April, 1912**, and Hana realized with a small cold jolt that nothing around her looked frightened yet — stewards were still smiling, the band was still tuning up somewhere below. Just a bump in the night, everyone seemed to think. A story to tell at breakfast.

Hana's compass had stopped spinning. It simply glowed, steady and green, pointing — not north, not anywhere on a map — straight down, toward the hull, toward the sea below the waterline where nobody could see what the ice had really done.

She didn't know yet how much those sixteen watertight rooms were about to be tested. But she knew, the way she always knew when a map was about to show her something new, that the next part of this voyage would not be dull.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: CQD, SOS
chapters.text:
Hana followed the glow of her compass down a narrow companionway and found a small room crackling with static, two men hunched over a brass machine covered in dials.

"Is that a telephone?" Hana asked.

"Wireless," said the nearer man, not looking up, fingers tapping a small lever in short, sharp bursts. "Sends messages through the air, no wires needed, to any ship close enough to listen."

Hana recognized the rhythm instantly — dots and dashes, the same pattern her compass had tapped out in her bedroom.

"That's Morse code," she said. "What are you saying?"

"**CQD**," he answered. "Old distress call — means 'all stations, danger.' We're sending the newer one too, just in case. **SOS**. Easier to tap out fast when your hands are shaking."

Hana looked at his hands. They were shaking.

"Is it bad?" she asked.

He paused just long enough to answer honestly. "Bad enough. We're asking every ship within reach to come now."

Hana thought of the sixteen sealed rooms below the waterline, built to stop water from spreading. She thought of the long grinding shudder she'd felt through her shoes.

"Will someone hear you?" she asked.

"Someone's already answering," he said, and for the first time he smiled, pointing at a scribbled line of dots and dashes on his notepad. "Ship called **Carpathia**. Fifty-eight miles off. Turning around, full speed, heading straight for us."

Hana let out a breath she hadn't noticed holding. Fifty-eight miles had sounded enormous a minute ago. Now, with a ship already turning through the dark toward them, it felt more like a distance a determined friend could cross.

"Keep tapping," she told him, which was a silly thing to say to a man who clearly already knew his job, but he laughed anyway, just a little, and kept tapping.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Boats and Band
chapters.text:
Up on deck, the calm from before had cracked into something busier, though not yet frightened — crewmen swinging lifeboats out on their davits, passengers in coats and life belts being helped in, one by one, down the side of the tilting ship.

Hana counted the boats as they filled. She counted again, comparing against the crowd still waiting on deck, and didn't like the number she got.

"There aren't enough," she said to Molly, who was helping an older passenger into a boat with one strong arm. "The boats only hold about **eleven hundred seventy-eight** people. There are more than that still standing right here."

"I know," Molly said, grim for one second, then brisk again, because brisk was useful and grim wasn't. "Ships back then only had to carry enough boats for a ship half this size, not one this big. Nobody's updated the rule yet. Into the boat, Hana."

"Wait — I need to find the captain."

She found him instead on the bridge, a steady, grey-bearded figure giving quiet orders, the most experienced captain White Star Line had. **Captain Edward Smith** was staying with his ship, the way captains of his time believed they should.

Somewhere below, music was still playing — a hired band, led by a man named **Wallace Hartley**, keeping their instruments going on the sloping deck. Nobody could later agree exactly which songs they played, or for how long, but more than one survivor swore they heard music right until the very end, something steady to hold onto in the cold and the dark.

A small, indignant yip made Hana turn. A woman nearby was climbing into a lifeboat with a trembling Pomeranian tucked inside her coat. Another dog, just as small, was already curled in a different boat two rows down.

"Dogs get a seat too?" Hana asked, half laughing despite everything.

"If they're small enough and someone loves them enough," Molly said, and pulled Hana firmly toward the last open boat. "Now. In. You can ask questions from the water."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Lights on the Water
chapters.text:
The lifeboat rocked gently on black water, crowded and quiet, everyone's eyes fixed on the same dark horizon.

Hana held her compass tight. It had stopped glowing green. Now it simply sat warm in her palm, needle trembling very slightly, like it was holding its breath with her.

More than fifteen hundred people did not make it off the ship that night. Hana would learn that fact later, plainly, the way you learn something true and sad and important all at once. Right now, in the boat, nobody said numbers out loud. They watched the water and waited.

It was Hana who saw it first — a single light, low and steady, growing on the horizon where there had only been stars.

"There," she said, pointing, and her voice cracked a little with how much she wanted to be right. "That's not a star. Stars don't move."

Molly followed her finger and went very still, then let out a whoop that startled half the boat awake.

The light grew into a shape, and the shape grew into a ship — the **Carpathia**, exactly as the wireless man had promised, steaming through waters littered with ice that had slowed every other ship for miles, risking the same danger Titanic had met, to reach them anyway.

By morning, every lifeboat had been found and pulled alongside, passengers hauled up rope ladders onto Carpathia's deck, wrapped in blankets, counted, and counted again until the counting finally stopped.

Hana sat wrapped in a scratchy wool blanket, compass warm in her lap, and watched the empty horizon where the biggest ship in the world had been the night before.

"She's really gone," Hana said quietly.

"She is," said Molly, settling beside her. "But you're not. That's the part worth holding onto tonight."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Rule That Came After
chapters.text:
The green light pulled at Hana again, gentler this time, and set her down somewhere dry — a paneled office hung with ship's charts, a world map spread across a long table.

A man in a dark coat was marking a new line across the North Atlantic in red pencil.

"What's that line?" Hana asked.

"A patrol route," he said, barely looking up. "After what happened to Titanic, ships started watching for ice and warning each other. We call it the **International Ice Patrol**. Someone always keeping a lookout now, every spring."

Hana leaned over his map, tracing the red line with one finger the way she'd traced her own chart back home. "And the lifeboats?"

"New rule for that too," he said. "A treaty called **SOLAS** — ships now have to carry enough lifeboats for every single person aboard. No more counting on 'probably enough.'"

Hana thought of the boat she'd sat in, of counting heads and running out of room. It felt, suddenly, like the whole miserable night had at least taught the world something it couldn't un-learn.

"That's good," she said, and meant it completely.

The man finally looked up, noticing her properly for the first time, and smiled like someone meeting a question he enjoyed answering. "Would you like to see where she ended up?"

Hana's compass answered for her, flaring bright green before she could even say yes.

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Found Again
chapters.text:
The light set her down on the deck of a research ship, salt wind in her hair, a screen in front of her glowing with grainy green shapes from a camera somewhere far below.

"That's the seafloor," said a man watching the screen with total focus, headphones around his neck. "**Robert Ballard**, oceanographer — someone who studies what's down in the ocean. We've been looking a long time."

The screen flickered, and a shape swam into view that made the whole room go silent: a great dark hull, a rust-streaked bow, half-buried after seventy-three years on the bottom.

"That's her," Hana breathed. "That's Titanic."

"**1 September, 1985**," Ballard said, voice careful, almost reverent. "Nearly **twelve thousand five hundred feet** down — deeper than most ships could even reach her before now. About **370 miles** off the coast of Newfoundland, Canada. She broke into two main pieces on the way down."

Hana studied the wreck on the screen, matching its position against the chart burned into her memory from the beginning of the night. The math worked. The map and the mystery finally lined up.

"FOUND HER!" she said, and nobody on the research ship seemed surprised that a ten-year-old was the one to say it first.

The green light caught her gently this time, and the research ship dissolved into her own bedroom, lamp still on, chart still pinned to the wall, exactly as she'd left it.

On her desk sat one new thing: a small brass button, green with age, resting beside the compass. A keepsake from somewhere she had never technically been able to visit.

She thought of a museum built decades later on the very shipyard where the keel had first been laid, shaped like a ship's prow, opened for the hundredth anniversary of a voyage that never finished. She thought of a movie people still watched, of dinner plates and shoes pulled gently from the sea and placed behind glass so nobody would ever quite stop remembering.

Hana set the compass down, picked up her ruler, and drew one last careful line across her chart — not where the ship had been going, but where it had finally been found.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow, Hana decided, she would draw a map of every ship still waiting to be found.

true_facts.text: **Titanic** was built in **Belfast** at a shipyard called **Harland & Wolff**, for a company named **White Star Line**.
Titanic had two sister ships built to the same plan: **Olympic** and **Britannic**.
The finished ship was about **882 feet long** — the biggest ship afloat at the time.
Titanic had **four funnels**, but only three ever let out real smoke — the fourth was mostly for looks.
Below the waterline, Titanic had **sixteen watertight rooms** meant to stop flooding from spreading, which is why people called her nearly unsinkable.
Titanic left **Southampton on 10 April 1912**, heading for New York.
A passenger named **Molly Brown** helped row her own lifeboat and later earned a famous nickname for it.
Titanic hit an iceberg at about **11:40 at night on 14 April 1912**.
The wireless operators tapped out both the old distress call **CQD** and the newer one, **SOS**.
The lifeboats only had room for about **1,178 people**, far fewer than everyone aboard.
**Captain Edward Smith**, one of the line's most experienced captains, stayed aboard as the ship went down.
The steamship **Carpathia** raced through icy waters and rescued the survivors the next morning.
The disaster led to two big safety changes still used today: the **International Ice Patrol**, and a rule called **SOLAS** requiring enough lifeboats for everyone aboard.

new_recurring.name: The Wayfinder Compass
new_recurring.rule: A brass compass, inherited from Hana's sailor grandfather, that never points north. When a story is ready to begin, it spins, glows green, and taps out a short pattern in Morse code before unrolling a thread of green light that pulls Hana…

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Hana returned safely to her own bedroom to find a small age-green brass button from the wreck resting beside her grandfather's compass, having traced Titanic's whole course from Belfast's slipway to the seafloor where Robert Ballard finally found her.

request.care_notes: Focus on the engineering marvel of the ship, how it was built, the safety systems of the time, and the rescue efforts. Avoid graphic descriptions of the disaster, drowning, or the suffering of passengers. Emphasize how this tragedy led to improved maritime safety rules we still follow today.

story.title: Max, Sami, and the Brick That Would Not Quit
story.subtitle: A night of carpenters, tubes, and one very stubborn brick

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Brick That Wouldn't Stay Still (Billund, 1932)
chapters.text:
Max and Sami lay on their bedroom floor at eleven at night, which was two hours past the time either of them was supposed to be awake. Between them sat a half-finished LEGO Technic crane, its gears not quite meshing the way Max wanted. Sami was ahead on his own build and was not about to let his brother forget it.

Max dropped a brick in the wrong spot and muttered something under his breath. Sami laughed. "Lego loser," he said.

That is when the brick in Max's hand started to glow.

It did not glow like a nightlight. It glowed like something that meant it. Gold light spilled out between the studs, and the brick grew warm, then grew, period — doubling, then doubling again, until a doorway stood where a Technic beam had been.

Through it, they saw a cramped wooden workshop. Sawdust covered the floor. A man with a thick mustache was sanding a stepladder.

"Well," Sami said. "That's new."

They stepped through anyway.

The man turned out to be Ole Kirk Christiansen, a carpenter who had just started a little company in a small Danish town. "Billund," he said, when Max asked where they were. "The year is **1932**." He waved at the stepladders and wooden ducks stacked against the wall. "I build whatever people need. Mostly furniture. Sometimes toys, when the furniture orders slow down."

Sami picked up a wooden duck on wheels and turned it over. "You made this?"

"I made whatever kept the workshop open," Ole Kirk said. "A carpenter who only builds one thing starves in a bad year."

Max, who liked knowing how things worked, asked the obvious question: "So how does a stepladder company end up making the thing we were just building?"

Ole Kirk smiled like a man who already knew the ending. "Come back and find out."

The glow pulled at them again, and the workshop folded away like a page turning.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Play Well (1934)
chapters.text:
They landed two years later, in front of a wooden sign hanging crooked above the workshop door. A painter balanced on a ladder, brush in hand, paint dripping.

"What's it going to say?" Sami asked.

The painter squinted at a scrap of paper. "Boss wants it to say LEGO."

Max frowned. "Lego? Like — 'I put together'? That's Latin. We did it in school."

Ole Kirk, arms crossed below, laughed. "Funny coincidence, that one. People like to say that's where the name came from. It isn't. I took it from two Danish words — *leg godt*. It means **'play well.'** I shortened it to LEGO in **1934**." He shrugged. "The Latin thing's a nice story. Just not the true one."

Sami grinned. "So it's a happy accident."

"Exactly that," said Ole Kirk.

The painter climbed down to let the paint dry. Sami — who never went anywhere without a pencil — borrowed the painter's chalk and sketched the letters bigger and bolder on a scrap of board, just to see how they'd look over the door. Ole Kirk held it up against the sign.

"That's better than mine," the painter admitted.

Max rolled his eyes. "Don't let it go to your head."

"Too late," said Sami.

Ole Kirk clapped them both on the shoulder. "Play well, you two. Both of you, not just the one with the pencil." Then he nodded toward the road, where a truck was unloading strange gray drums. "Come see what just arrived. It's going to change everything."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Plastic Problem (1947–1949)
chapters.text:
The gray drums turned out to be plastic pellets, and the machine they fed into looked like nothing Max had ever seen — a squat iron beast with a hand crank and a mold clamped to its front.

"**1947**," Ole Kirk said, patting it like a horse. "One of the first machines in Denmark that can melt plastic and push it into a mold, like filling an ice tray that never melts. Out comes a toy."

Max circled it twice. "Can I try?"

Ole Kirk handed him the crank. Max pulled it. The machine groaned, hissed, and spat out a small hollow brick with four studs on top. Sami caught it before it hit the floor.

"**1949**," Ole Kirk said. "We call them Automatic Binding Bricks." He pressed it onto another brick. It sat there. It did not click. One light push and it slid right back off.

Sami tried. Same result. "They don't really... bind," he said. "The name's a bit hopeful."

"They hold a little," Ole Kirk said, a touch defensive. "Not perfectly. Yet."

Max turned the brick over and peered at the hollow underside, his brain already chewing on the problem the way it chewed on gear ratios. "What's under here?"

"Nothing," said Ole Kirk. "Just hollow."

"That's the problem," Max said. "There's nothing to grab onto."

Ole Kirk raised an eyebrow. "My son's been saying the same thing for weeks. Maybe you should tell him yourself."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Tube Idea (1958)
chapters.text:
Godtfred Kirk Christiansen's desk was buried under loose bricks, pencil stubs, and three mugs of cold coffee.

"You're the kid who found the problem," he said, without looking up. "Good. Now help me find the fix."

Sami sorted the sketches scattered across the desk — tubes, pegs, little plastic rings — the way he'd sort a drawing into a keep pile and a bin pile.

Max picked up a brick, turned it over, and said the thing that had been bugging him since the workshop. "What if the bumps on top had something to grab, instead of just sitting in a hole?"

Godtfred stared at him. Then he grabbed a pencil and sketched little round tubes hanging down inside the bottom of a brick, built to hug the studs of the brick underneath.

They built a test one right there. Sami lined up two bricks and pressed.

**CLICK.**

He pulled. It held.

"IT HOLDS!" Sami yelled, loud enough that Godtfred flinched.

Max grabbed the two bricks and yanked harder, because Max could not let a win go unchallenged, even when it wasn't his win. It still held. He stacked a third brick on top. Still held.

"**January 28, 1958**," Godtfred said, writing the date on a form. "That's the day we make this official." He signed at the bottom. "A patent — it means this design is written down and dated as ours, so nobody else gets to copy it and call it theirs."

Max turned the brick over again, grinning despite himself. "This is the exact same tubes as the brick I was holding back home."

"It should be," Godtfred said. "We never really changed it after this. A brick from today should fit one made fifty years from now."

Sami tucked one of the test bricks into his pocket when nobody was looking. Max noticed and said nothing, because some wins you let your little brother have.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Night the Warehouse Burned (1960)
chapters.text:
Smoke was already curling into the evening sky by the time the glow dropped them on a hill above the factory, well back from the buildings below.

"**1960**," Godtfred said quietly, standing beside them, older now, his hair gray at the edges. "The wooden-toy warehouse. Everything in it is gone."

Sami's stomach dropped. "Is everyone okay?"

"Everyone's fine," Godtfred said quickly. "Nobody was hurt. Just years of wooden toys and stepladders and ducks on wheels, gone in a night."

Max watched the firefighters working, well clear of the flames, hoses arcing over the roofline. "So what happens now? Do you start over with wood?"

Godtfred shook his head slowly, like a decision that had been building for a while and had just finished arriving. "We'd already mostly stopped making wooden toys anyway. This just makes the choice for us. From here, it's plastic bricks. Only plastic bricks."

Sami looked at the smoke a moment longer, then at the brick still riding in his pocket from the last chapter — small, plastic, untouched. "It can't burn as easy as wood, right?"

"That's one way to think about it," Godtfred said. "A fresh start, whether we wanted one or not."

Max, who liked a clean decision, nodded slowly. "Sometimes the plan only gets simple after something forces it to."

"That's the most grown-up thing you've said all night," Sami told him.

"I contain multitudes," said Max, who had heard that phrase once and had been waiting for an excuse.

By the time the glow pulled them onward, the fire crews had it under control, and the sky over Billund was already clearing.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Bricks for Everyone (1963–1978)
chapters.text:
A worker nearby was bending a brick back and forth, testing it like he didn't quite trust it. "**1963**," he said. "New plastic — **ABS**. Doesn't crack as easy, keeps its color way longer than the old stuff." He handed it to Max, who bent it himself, impressed despite himself.

The glow shifted, and suddenly the air smelled like a carnival — sugar, sawdust, hot plastic — while a Ferris wheel built entirely out of bricks turned slowly against the sky.

"**1968**," said Godtfred, older still, beaming like a man standing inside his own dream. "The first LEGOLAND. Right here in Billund, next door to the factory."

Sami spun in a circle trying to look at everything at once. "You built a whole theme park out of your own toy?"

Max picked up a brick from a nearby bin — bigger, chunkier, clearly meant for smaller hands. "What's this one?"

"**DUPLO**," Godtfred said. "**1969**. Sized for little hands, so toddlers don't choke on the small ones. Still clicks onto a regular brick, though."

The glow shifted again, and the park dissolved into a workshop full of gears, axles, and long gray beams.

"**1977**," Godtfred said, handing Max a box. "**Technic**. Real moving parts. I hear you already like this kind of thing."

Max tore into the box like it was Christmas morning and had a small crane built, gears turning, before Sami had even found the instructions.

"Showoff," Sami muttered — then spotted a tray of tiny yellow heads with blank faces. He grabbed one, borrowed a marker from the table, and sketched a grin and two raised eyebrows onto it.

"**1978**," Godtfred said, examining Sami's work. "First year we made little people at all. Arms that move, hats and heads you can swap around." He held Sami's doodled face up to the light. "This one's better than most of ours."

"Obviously," said Sami.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Hard Years (2000s)
chapters.text:
The next room had no sawdust and no sugar smell. Just fluorescent lights, stacks of paper, and a man rubbing his eyes over a desk covered in spreadsheets.

"Rough few years," said Kjeld Kirk Kristiansen, Ole Kirk's grandson, now running the whole company. "Early **2000s**. We tried watches, clothes, parks all over the world, video games — too many things at once. We nearly ran out of money."

Sami, who'd been having a great time right up until now, looked worried. "Nearly ran out? Like — forever?"

"Close," Kjeld said. "Not quite."

A new man walked in — younger, calmer, carrying nothing but a single box of plain bricks. "**Jorgen Vig Knudstorp**," he said, introducing himself. "**2004**. New here." He set the box on the desk. "I've got one idea. Stop chasing every new thing. Get back to this."

Max picked up a brick from the box — plain, four studs, nothing fancy. "That's it? That's the fix?"

"That's the fix," Jorgen said. "Fewer distractions. Better bricks. Let the brick do the work it's always done."

Max turned it over in his hand, thinking of a crane, a theme park, a tube design that still worked fifty years later. "Because it already works. You don't fix something that isn't broken. You just stopped paying attention to the thing that was actually good."

Jorgen pointed at him. "That's exactly it."

The room brightened, and somewhere a screen flickered to life, showing bright yellow figures racing across a brick-built city. "**2014**," Kjeld said, nodding at it. "A whole movie, starring bricks like these. People loved it."

Sami watched, delighted, momentarily forgetting to be worried about anything. "We're going to go home and tell nobody about this and have them think we're insane."

"Welcome to the club," said Max.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Back on the Carpet
chapters.text:
The glow dimmed, and the workshop smell gave way to the familiar mess of their own bedroom — Technic gears, a half-built crane, a scatter of plain bricks across the carpet.

Max sat up first, blinking. "Did that actually just happen?"

Sami checked his pocket. The test brick from Godtfred's desk was still there, small and real, with a date scratched faintly into its underside. "**1958**," he read aloud. "It's not a dream if there's proof."

Max picked up his half-finished crane. The gears that had refused to mesh an hour ago suddenly made perfect sense — he snapped two Technic beams together and felt the quiet, satisfying click of a part that was always going to fit.

"Still in Billund," Sami said, half to himself, remembering the sign, the factory, the whole company standing on the same patch of ground the entire time.

"Some things don't move," Max said. "They just get better at being themselves."

Sami flipped his drawing pad to a blank page and started sketching a tiny grinning face with raised eyebrows — his own minifigure, for whenever he got around to actually building it.

Max glanced at the clock. Nearly midnight. "We should sleep."

"In a minute," Sami said, still drawing. "I want to finish this one first."

Max didn't argue. He picked the glowing brick up off the carpet — ordinary and gray again, just a brick like any other — and set it on the shelf, studs facing the ceiling, ready for whenever the gold light decided to come back.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow, there was a crane to finish — and Max still intended to win.

true_facts.text: LEGO started as a small carpenter's workshop in **Billund, Denmark**, run by **Ole Kirk Christiansen**, starting in **1932**.
In **1934** Ole Kirk named his company **LEGO**, short for the Danish words *leg godt* — which means **'play well.'**
People love to say *lego* also means 'I put together' in Latin — that's probably just a fun coincidence, not the real reason for the name.
By **1949** the workshop was making early plastic bricks called **Automatic Binding Bricks** — though they didn't bind together very well yet.
**Godtfred Kirk Christiansen** fixed that by adding little tubes under each brick to grip the bumps below, officially dated **January 28, 1958**.
Because the design barely changed, a brick made in **1958** still clicks perfectly onto a brick made today.
In **1960** a fire burned down the wooden-toy warehouse, and nobody was hurt — afterward the family decided to make only plastic bricks from then on.
In **1963** LEGO switched to a tougher plastic called **ABS**, which cracks less and keeps its color much longer.
The first **LEGOLAND** theme park opened right next to the factory in Billund in **1968**.
**DUPLO** bricks, sized just right for little hands, came out in **1969** — and they still click onto regular LEGO bricks.
The **LEGO Technic** line, with real gears and moving parts, launched in **1977**.
The very first tiny LEGO people, with arms that move and swappable heads, showed up in **1978**.
In **2004**, **Jorgen Vig Knudstorp** became the new leader and helped the company get back to basics after some very hard years.
In **2014**, **The LEGO Movie** brought LEGO bricks to movie screens everywhere.

story.title: Isla and the Lamp of Pompeii
story.subtitle: A midnight dig through the town the mountain buried

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Lamp That Woke Up
chapters.text:
Isla was supposed to be asleep.

Instead she was cross-legged on her bedroom floor at 11:47 p.m., headlamp on, sorting through the dusty cardboard box her grandfather had left her — the one marked, in his looping handwriting, FINDS. HANDLE WITH CARE. ASK QUESTIONS FIRST.

He had been an archaeologist, the real kind, the kind who dug holes in the ground for a living and got excited about broken pots. Isla liked to think she'd inherited at least the excited-about-broken-pots part.

Tonight's find was a lump of bronze the size of her fist — a cracked old oil lamp, the kind Romans used before electricity existed, with a worn thumbprint pressed into the handle where someone had held it, two thousand years ago, exactly the way she was holding it now.

She rubbed the dust from the grooves. The lamp went warm. Then warmer. Then it began, very softly, to hum.

"Okay," Isla said, to nobody. "That's new."

Light poured out of the crack in the spout in one long golden rope, and it did not stop at her bedroom wall. It kept going straight through, like the wall wasn't fully convinced it was a wall. Isla had about half a second to decide whether this was a problem, and then the light pulled her through it.

She landed — feet first, like the lamp had been practicing — on a stone street warm from somewhere she couldn't see the sun. A cart wheel rattled nearby. Someone was shouting about fish.

The street in front of her wasn't flat. Big square stones crossed it in a raised line, a hand's width above the road, with gaps between them just wide enough for a wheel to pass through.

She'd seen a photo of stones exactly like these in one of her grandfather's books. "This is a crossing," she said slowly. "For people, so you don't have to step in the—" she glanced at the stained gutter and decided not to finish that sentence. "And carts still get through, because the gaps are exactly cart-wheel width."

The lamp pulsed once, satisfied, like a small nod.

"You're not just a lamp, are you," Isla said.

It hummed again. Close enough to a yes.

She stood looking at red-tiled roofs and a mountain rising green and calm in the distance, in a town that was very much alive, and very much not supposed to still exist.

"Where—" she started.

"Pompeii," said a voice behind her, and it did not belong to the lamp.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Five Villages and a Painted Insult
chapters.text:
Isla turned to find a boy about seventeen, wax tablet under one arm, looking at her like she'd appeared out of thin air — which, fairly, she had.

"I'm Gaius," he said, then caught himself. "Gaius Plinius. People call me Pliny. The younger one. There are two of us."

Isla knew that name. It had sat under a photo in her grandfather's book, next to the words eyewitness account. "You wrote letters," she said. "About—" she stopped, unsure if that was a secret she was meant to know yet.

Pliny just looked pleased. "I write things down. Useful. You never know what's going to matter later."

He was, Isla would decide, dramatically right about that.

He walked her into the square, past a building with huge curved stone benches rising in rows, big enough to swallow thousands of people.

"The amphitheater," he said, waving a hand. "A giant oval stage, built for games. Big crowds. One of the oldest of its kind anywhere."

Painted on a nearby wall, in letters a foot tall, was a scrawl of red paint.

"What's that say?" Isla asked.

"An advertisement," said Pliny. "For rooms to rent. And someone's opinion, right next to it, about who should win the next election." He said it the way someone might say and here's the weather report, which told Isla that painted walls doing the job of flyers was just Tuesday here.

She studied the word carved above the gate they'd just come through. POMPEII. Something about it nagged at her.

"That doesn't sound Latin," she said slowly. "It sounds like it's doing something with numbers."

Pliny raised an eyebrow, surprised. "Go on."

"There's a word — I read it somewhere — from an older language people spoke here before Latin took over. It means five." She looked at the streets fanning outward. "Was this five towns that joined into one?"

Pliny didn't answer right away, which from a boy who enjoyed being the smartest person in most rooms was as good as a yes.

"Nobody is completely certain," he admitted. "But that's the best guess anyone has. Five villages, one town, one name." He looked at her with new interest. "You might be useful to have around."

Isla decided she liked Pompeii. It was a town that argued in paint, named itself after arithmetic, and had just complimented her thinking within ten minutes of her arrival.

"What's for breakfast around here?" she asked instead, because the smell drifting down the street was extraordinary.

Pliny grinned. "Follow me."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Bread Still in the Oven
chapters.text:
The smell belonged to a bakery wedged between two shops, where a man with flour to his elbows slid round loaves into a domed brick oven on a long wooden paddle.

Each loaf had a pattern pressed into the top — lines cutting it into eight wedges, with a small stamped mark near the crust.

"That's a signature," Isla said, pointing. "A maker's mark. So people know whose bakery it came from."

The baker, who did not speak English and had no reason to, looked pleased that someone had noticed his stamp anyway, and handed her a warm end-piece of dough.

"Every baker marks his own," Pliny confirmed. "No point making the best bread in the street if nobody knows it was yours."

Isla chewed and thought about her grandfather's box, and the thumbprint on the lamp, and decided people had been signing their work since approximately forever.

Outside, a public fountain gurgled at the corner, water running continuously from a carved stone spout into a trough.

"It never stops?" Isla asked, crouching to look.

"Why would it?" said Pliny, like this was an odd question. "Lead pipes bring water down from the hills into fountains all over town. Shops, baths, houses that can afford it. It just keeps coming."

Isla traced the pipe where it vanished into the wall. A whole town, she thought, plumbed like a single machine, water finding its way to a hundred spouts without anyone pumping a handle. It was the kind of engineering people usually assumed came much later than two thousand years ago, and here it was, running quietly in the background of somebody's Tuesday.

"You people are extremely organized," she said, "for a town that also paints insults on walls."

"We contain multitudes," said Pliny solemnly, and went back to his bread.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Room That Kept Its Secrets
chapters.text:
Pliny led her up a street of grand houses until they reached one with painted walls so bright Isla actually gasped — reds and golds, floor to ceiling, covering every inch of plaster.

"Frescoes," said Pliny, watching her face. "Painted straight into wet plaster, so the color sinks in and never fades. This house has some of the best in town."

One room stopped her completely. Life-sized figures wound around the walls in a painted procession — a woman with a whip, dancers, something being revealed beneath a cloth — a scene that clearly meant something, urgently, to whoever had paid for it.

"What is this showing?" Isla breathed.

Pliny shrugged, and for the first time all night, looked genuinely stumped. "Nobody who lives here will tell outsiders. A ceremony, maybe. People argue about it." He tilted his head at the room. "That's rather why everyone just calls it the room of mysteries."

Isla, who had been waiting her whole life for someone to hand her an actual unsolved mystery, felt something click into place behind her ribs. "So nobody ever figures out what it means?"

"Not that I've heard," said Pliny, with the easy honesty of someone who did not know he was talking to a girl who would, in roughly seventeen centuries, be very good at exactly this kind of question.

Under the house, the ground gave the faintest shiver — so small Isla nearly missed it. Pliny didn't even look up.

"Does that happen a lot?" she asked.

"Since the big one, seventeen years back, smaller ones all the time," he said, already moving on. "Everyone's used to it by now."

Isla looked back at the painted room over her shoulder, the dancers frozen mid-step, the mystery exactly as unsolved as it had been a minute ago. She didn't know yet it would stay that way for a very long time — long enough that she herself, one day, might be one of the people still arguing about it.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Mountain Opens
chapters.text:
They were in the market square, Pliny haggling cheerfully over olives, when the sky did something wrong.

Isla saw it first — a column rising straight up from the mountain behind the town, fast, white and gray, climbing higher than anything had a right to climb.

"Pliny." Her voice came out flatter than she meant it to. "Look at the mountain."

He looked. He went very quiet.

"That's Vesuvius," he said, confirming it to himself as much as to her. The calm green mountain Isla had noticed on arrival wasn't calm anymore.

Isla's brain, unhelpfully, chose that exact moment to supply a fact. "You write about this," she said. "In letters. People study your words for two thousand years because you're the only one who wrote down exactly what this looked like." She grabbed his sleeve. "That means you need to leave. Now. With your mother. That's what you do."

Pliny stared at her, and for once asked no clever question. He ran.

Isla watched the date settle around her like a fact finally becoming a place she stood in: August 24th, in the year 79. The mountain on every postcard, the one everyone called a gentle old neighbor, was erupting in front of her, exactly the way the letters said it would.

Ash began to fall — fine, gray, endless, drifting down like dirty snow, settling on rooftops and the painted wall still advertising rooms to rent. Mixed in were small, pale stones that bounced rather than thudded when they landed.

"That's pumice," Isla murmured, catching one — rock so full of trapped air bubbles it was nearly light enough to float.

The ash and pumice kept falling, that day and the next, until it had piled up over the whole town — eventually as deep as thirteen to twenty feet, burying streets, burying roofs, burying the oven with its bread still inside.

Thousands of people in and around the town died that day. But thousands more got out — including the boy who had just sprinted off toward his mother's house, who would live another forty years and write it all down so carefully that scientists, nineteen centuries later, would name this exact kind of eruption after him: a Plinian eruption.

Isla didn't move. The lamp in her pocket was warm against her leg, steady, like it was waiting for her to decide something.

"We're not done yet," she said. "Are we."

It hummed.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Sailing Toward the Smoke
chapters.text:
The lamp pulled her sideways this time, not forward — across the bay, to a coastline where warships sat moored, crews staring, like everyone else, at the impossible cloud over the water.

A heavyset man in uniform stood at the rail of the largest ship, watching through narrowed eyes, utterly unbothered, while his sailors looked considerably more bothered.

"That's the other one," Isla guessed. "Pliny the Elder. His uncle."

The man turned at the sound of his own family name, raised an eyebrow at the girl who had apparently materialized on his deck, and decided — with the brisk practicality Isla was starting to recognize as a family trait — that there were more urgent matters than how she'd gotten there.

"People along that shore need boats," he said, mostly to his crew, but loud enough for her benefit. "So we will be the boats."

"You're sailing toward it," Isla said. "Not away."

"Famous last words tend to be more interesting that way," he said, which Isla chose to find reassuring rather than alarming, mostly because his crew were already hauling the oars and did not look like they planned on dying about it.

She watched the ships push across water gone the color of wet ash, sails cutting through floating pumice like it was sea foam, aimed straight at a coast everyone else was desperate to leave. It was, she thought, the single bravest thing she had ever personally watched — a man steering his ships toward danger on purpose, because people on the other side needed somewhere to stand.

"Will they make it?" she asked the lamp quietly.

The lamp didn't answer that one. Some things, apparently, even a magic oil lamp knows better than to promise.

What she did know, holding the rail as the fleet pulled away from view, was that because of ships like this one, people who'd have had nowhere to go got pulled out of the ash and onto a deck instead. She chose to hold onto that part.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Other Town
chapters.text:
The light shifted again, gentler this time, and set her down in a town that looked, at first glance, almost identical to the one she'd just left — same red roofs, same stone streets, same mountain looming behind it.

"Herculaneum," hummed the lamp, somehow managing to sound like a word despite not having a mouth. "Smaller than Pompeii. Same mountain. Same day."

But something here was different, and it took Isla a minute of walking to spot it.

In Pompeii, everything wooden had burned or rotted away over the centuries, leaving only holes where beams and furniture used to be. Here, through a doorway, she saw an actual wooden bed frame, scorched black but still standing, and on a shelf nearby, something that might once have been a scroll, rolled tight and blackened like a stick of charcoal.

"That's wood," Isla said slowly. "Actual wood. After two thousand years."

"Different kind of burying," the lamp hummed. "Pompeii got ash and stone from the sky. This town got something hotter and faster, moving along the ground — it buried things so completely, so fast, there was no air left to rot anything. Furniture. Scrolls. Even loaves, here too."

Isla crouched by the doorway, turning the idea over. Same volcano, same afternoon, two towns captured by two different kinds of disaster, like two photographs taken with completely different cameras.

"So the thing that destroyed it," she said slowly, "is also the reason we still have it."

The lamp didn't need to confirm that one. She could tell, by its warmth in her hand, she'd gotten it exactly right.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Found Again
chapters.text:
The light swirled a final time, and when it cleared, centuries had gone with it. Pompeii lay in front of her again, quiet now in a completely different way — no carts, no shouting fish-sellers, just low stone walls half-buried in soft earth, and tourists in sun hats taking photographs behind a rope.

"Nobody remembered this was even here," the lamp hummed, "for almost seventeen hundred years. Buried. Forgotten. Just a hill people planted grapes on."

"Until?" Isla asked, already knowing there had to be an until.

"1748," said the lamp. "Workers digging nearby hit stone where there shouldn't have been stone. Walls. Pots. A whole town, exactly where they left it."

Isla walked the quiet street slowly, past the same stepping stones, the same gutter, the same gate stamped POMPEII. It was unmistakably the place she had stood that morning — if that morning was even the right way to describe something that had happened nearly two thousand years ago and also several hours ago, depending who was counting.

A sign near the entrance, printed in six languages, named the place a UNESCO World Heritage Site — Isla had seen the term on a poster in her school library, and finally understood it properly: a place the whole world had formally agreed was too important to lose twice.

"How much of it has even been dug up?" she asked.

"About two-thirds," said the lamp. "The rest is still down there. Every year, somewhere under all that dirt, someone finds a fresco nobody's seen since the day it was painted."

Isla looked out at the green, ordinary-looking mountain still standing patiently behind the ruins — the same one that had done all of this, the same one people still lived beside today, the same one scientists still watched, every single day, because it had never actually stopped being a volcano.

"It's still active," she said. It wasn't really a question.

"Still watched. Closely," the lamp confirmed. "Just in case."

The light rose around her one more time, the ruins folding away like a page turning, and Isla landed — feet first, same as before — back on her own bedroom carpet, headlamp still on, the box from her grandfather still open beside her.

The lamp in her hand had gone cool and ordinary again, bronze and cracked and quiet. Except — she turned it over — where there had only been a worn thumbprint before, there was now a second mark pressed faintly beside it. Small. Fresh. Shaped exactly like her own thumb.

Isla sat very still, looking at the two prints side by side, separated by two thousand years and about four hours.

Then she reached for her notebook, because she had several hundred questions, and tomorrow she intended to start answering them.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow, she had an entire town's worth of questions to ask the dust.

true_facts.text: Its streets had raised **stepping stones** so people could cross without stepping in the muck, with gaps just wide enough for **cart wheels**.
The name **Pompeii** probably comes from an older word meaning **five** — maybe because five villages joined to make one town.
Lead pipes carried water from the hills to fountains all over town, running almost constantly.
Bakers stamped their own mark into every loaf of bread — one whole loaf, stamp and all, was found still sitting in its oven.
One house held a painted room now called the **Villa of the Mysteries**, showing a ceremony nobody has ever fully explained.
On **August 24th, in the year 79**, the volcano **Mount Vesuvius** erupted and buried the town.
Ash and **pumice** — light volcanic rock full of air bubbles — buried Pompeii as deep as **thirteen to twenty feet**.
A young writer named **Pliny the Younger** watched it all and wrote it down so carefully that this kind of eruption is now called a **Plinian eruption**.
The nearby town of **Herculaneum** was buried by the same eruption, but under different material — one that preserved actual wood and scrolls.
Pompeii was lost for almost **seventeen hundred years**, until workers rediscovered it in **1748**.
Pompeii is now a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**, a place the whole world has agreed to protect.

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Isla returned to her bedroom with the oil lamp gone cool again, now marked with a fresh thumbprint beside the ancient one, and a notebook full of questions she planned to start answering the next day.

request.care_notes: Focus on the archaeology, engineering of Roman cities, and how we learn from preserved artifacts. The story should convey the drama of a natural disaster without graphic descriptions of suffering or death; emphasize rescue and discovery rather than catastrophe.
